subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF SOLDIERS' CIVIL REESTABLISHMENT ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
One thing that has been brought to my attention in regard to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, I think, I might bring to the attention

D.S.C.R. Act Amendment
of the committee, as the constitution of new appeal boards will certainly increase the number of officers in that department and the amount of salaries which is now payable by that department. What strikes one at the present moment in regard to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, is that, out of the large amount which is annually paid out by the department, a very small amount of the money ever reaches the soldier or is ever used for the purposes of the soldier. As we are drawing into the fifth or sixth year since the conclusion of actual hostilities, the time is coming for a consolidation of some of the departments of government, and the one which is due first for consolidation is, I think, the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment My suggestion to the minister and to the committee would be that before this House meets again, arrangements should be made whereby this department, the Pension board attached to it, and various other suborganizations should be consolidated in the Department of National Defence. The figures in regard to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment are startling. They have been prepared and handed to me, having been taken from the Auditor General's report of last year. The total expenditure for the year 1921-22 was $17,818,646.70. The most striking thing about it is that $6,922,432.62 has been expended in salaries; in other words, 38.84 per cent of the total vote for the year 1922 was paid out in salaries. Then, for administration of the department, the sum of $3,957,045.26 was disbursed, or 22.7 per cent of the total vote. Now we come to payments and allowances to the soldiers themselves, and we find that the total for that year was $6,940,168.82, or 38.89 per cent of the vote. That is to say, 38.89 per cent represents the total amount which the soldiers received out of that large expenditure of $17,900,000 odd. It strikes me that the cost of administration is exceedingly high; the amount spent in salaries is something enormous. The idea of spending nearly $7,000,000 in salaries for the administration of $17,000,000 seems entirely out of proportion. It may be that these figures, representing as they do the year ending 1922, will not be fully applicable to the year just closed. The year just closed may indicate some saving in this respect, and therefore a somewhat better showing. But my information leads me to believe that the same proportion will be maintained this year. I have not the figures for the year just ended; the auditor's report for that year has not been brought down.

Now, I would be the last man to object to any increased expenditure for the relief of soldiers who might need that expenditure, but 1 would point out that the soldiers themselves are getting very little of the amount expended; aproximately 39 per cent only is going to the soldiers, while 38 per cent is spent in salaries, and 22 per cent for purposes of administration. Does not the minister think that the time has come when he might consider the question of closing up all the outside institutions? In the city of Ottawa, I am told, an arrangement is made with the hospitals whereby they take soldier patients at a rate of $3.50 a day. They give them excellent care and attention at an annual rate of less than $1,200, which is far below the amount spent by the department in connection with patients who are not in civic hospitals. I am also informed that the various hospitals throughout the country are glad to get such patients. There may be a few branches of the department in connection with which special institutions will have to be maintained for a number of years yet to come, but in the majority of instances, I am satisfied, the patients can receive equally good, if not better, treatment at a great decreased cost by adopting the method which has been followed in the city of Ottawa and in some other cities, of utilizing the civic hospitals and arranging a fair basis of payment for these institutions. If this were done, a very large part of the salary list would disappear, and more money could actually be expended on the soldiers themselves. At all events, I am satisfied from the figures before me that the salary list is entirely disproportionate to the work done by the department. I bring the matter up now because the present clause of the bill seeks to increase the number of those persons in the department who will receive salaries. I think it is very proper that these boards should be appointed and the salaries paid, but, at the same time, there is great room for improvement in the old salary list, and the minister would do well to look it over before parliament meets again, and reconsider the matter to the end that a better showing may be made next session.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
On the very day I took
charge of the department I myself was amazed by the size of the figures representing the amount that was being paid out in salaries in the department. However, after some days' study of the question I realized that this was a department in which naturally a large proportion of the expenditure would have to go out in salaries. Just one moment's consideration of the circumstances will lead my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) to
D.S.C.R. Act Amendment

agree with me in this regard. All ex-service men who are seeking treatment must first of all be examined by a physician or medical man. That, in itself, requires a very large medical staff, to say nothing about the men who require treatment in the hospitals of the department. So much for the question as to the treatment of the men. Let us look at another feature of the work of the department,-the pensioners. A very large proportion of the pensioners are not permanent; they are subject to periodical re-examination. For the proper discharge of this work it is obvious that 43,000 pensioners would of necessity require a very large medical staff. This does not take into consideration the men who are seeking pensions and who must also be medically examined.

I think the pension
costs are in addition to the figures I have given. I have a note here from which I gather that the cost of administration has been deducted from the figures I gave a moment ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
refer to the amount paid in the way of pensions?
No, I am referring to the cost of administration of the pensions; the sum of $58,373 for this purpose has been deducted from the figures I gave.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
That sum of $53,000
covers clerical assistance to the Board of Pension Commissioners in Ottawa. The board do not pay salaries to any of the medical men who are examining soldiers ail over the country. This will immediately convey to the mind of the hon. gentleman and to the House generally that quite naturally in this department a very large percentage of the money must be spent in salaries. Now I come to the figures themselves, which have been taken as a basis for observation by my hon. friend,-the $17,000,000. That was for the year 1921-22. The expenditure was large during that year, but I do not think it was too large. In the following year, 1922-23 this amount was reduced by $3,000,000 if I remember rightly. For the next fiscal year 1923-24 we are asking about $2,500,000 less. This is a substantial reduction. Whether it is as large as my hon. friend would like to see effected I do not know, but it is an honest effort in that direction.
I understand that through 1922-23 the expenditure chargeable to administration was maintained in proportion to the money actually received by the soldiers?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I am not in a position to state whether the proportion has been maintained or not. We have enormously reduced the number of employees of the department. My impression is that this is not a permanent department, and I hope the time will shortly be reached when cases which have become chronic in their nature will be dealt with in homes rather than in hospitals. This policy, of course, is a subject of study for myself and the officials of the department at the present time. How soon it will be possible to disband the department remains to be seen.
My hon. friend has stated that the hospitals of the department should be closed as far as possible. I agree with him. A number of our hospitals have been closed and we have been contracting our operations. My hon. friend may be aware that we have made preparations to close the branch hospital at Burlington, near Hamilton, where we have about 130 patients. A delegation waited upon me some days ago to stress the advisability, if not the necessity, of keeping this hospital open. This request is typical of what we may expect when we begin to close any of these hospitals. But the intention is to contract the service as much as we can and within a few years to confine the care of ex-service men mostly to homes in two or three places in the Dominion. I realize that if we confide the care of our soldiers to the civic hospitals it may be less costly. We are doing that in Ottawa, in Regina and in Winnipeg, with the exception of a small hospital, and I think also in Victoria. I take these suggestions made by my hon. friend in the best possible spirit, and I can assure him that it is the object of the government to contract the service and to disband the department entirely without undue delay. How soon that can be accomplished I cannot say.

On section 3-Clause 8: Official Soldiers' Adviser.

Besides, I may point out that we are the agents of the Imperial Ministry of Pensions. This power to administer oaths would apply only to officials of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I desire to invite the attention of the committee to several items of the customs tariff which were under consideration before and concerning which some suggestions were offered. These suggestions we have given some attention. It will be remembered that I stated that representations had been made, supported here by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), that the wording of our clause with respect to the application of the British preference did not adapt itself to the manner in which the trade was conducted on the Pacific coast. We provide for a discount of 10 per cent as applied to goods which are imported by direct shipment. It is pointed out that there is not very much direct trade of that kind between Pacific ports and England; that British imports at Vancouver, for example, are largely brought by way of Hong Kong and transshipped. The wording of our clause, therefore, would not, it is felt, admit these goods to the benefit of the preference. After some consideration we have come to the conclusion to propose an amendment which will cover that case. I therefore propose to insert the following words in the resolution respecting the British preference, after the word "Canada" in the first paragraph thereof:
Provided that goods entitled to the benefits of the British preferential tariff shall be entitled to the discount authorized by this section when such goods are shipped on a through bi!U of lading consigned to a consignee in a specified port in Canada, when such goods are transferred at a port of a British colony or possession not enjoying the benefits of the British Preferential tariff and conveyed without further transhipment into a sea or river port in Canada.
That is, if the goods are consigned to Canada and are transshipped at Hong Kong, that will be deemed a direct shipment.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is one other item I wish to deal with just here. I propose to provide for a drawback in connection with items 583a and 583aa, as follows:
1031. Artificial sik tops and waste or artificial! fibre silk, artificial silk yarns or filaments, enumerated in tariff liitems 583a and 583aa, when imported by manufacturers to be further manufactured in their own factories before the first day of July, 1924; portion of duty, (not including special duty or dumping duty) payable as drawback, 60 per cent.
That is the time at which we expect the new operations in connection with the manufacture of artificial silk to take place. This is to provide in the meantime that the manufacturer using these articles may be entitled to drawback. I think my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) suggested it.

That is quite true; I did raise that question. I do not know whether my hon. friend is going quite far enough. Of course, if he did not go this distance it would mean that we could not have spinning done in this country because the outside spinner would have a direct advantage. As I explained before, the botany yarns are made of a combination of wool with an artificial silk top. The artificial silk top itself is of practically no value. It is broken artificial silk stuff and is merely a finish that gives a lustre to the wool. I would like my hon. friend to consider this point again though it may be that we can put it over now in view of what he says that the sections will not come into effect until after he has had a chance of considering it next session. But in view of the fact that the wool top is worth twice as much as the artificial top, and in view of the further fact that our tariff unfortunately provides for a 99 per cent drawback in connection with these yams, the present position is that the spinner of wool yarn in Canada for hosiery purposes-jerseys and the like, and that is the only thing these yams are used for-has absolutely no protection. Further, that section, coupled with my hon. friend's changes in the law this year looking towards the installation of a new industry here, has the further effect of putting the Canadian spinner at an absolute disadvantage as against his competitor overseas. Because in these botany yams you have the composite article, you have the product of two articles. And the imported yarn base, which is of wool, and has twice the value of the artificial silk, will be entitled to the 99 per cent drawback notwithstanding the fact that artificial silk is used in it, while our own producers will be obliged to pay the duties provided by my hon. friend's budget in the production of

Mrays and Means
the botanies, and so they are put by this parliament at an absolute disadvantage. What my hon. friend is doing to-day, while not removing that disadvantage, postpones it and I would ask him for how long a time it is postponed. Is it postponed for a year, or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This takes place on the 1st of July, 1924.
Then it would be postponed long enough to enable some rational, reasonable treatment to be given the older industry to prevent it from being put out of business just to help the new.

While we are on the question of spinning yams, I want to draw the attention of the minister to the question of linen yarns. There never has been in this country any duty on linen yams. For three years we gave them a bounty. The industry had never been established in Canada. It took its start from the demand which arose during the war for aeroplane cloth. We were making aeroplanes here and we could not get the cloth. There was an embargo on foreign yams coming in. Two industries were started in Canada for the manufacture of linen yams from the home-grown flax. A bounty limited to $25,000 was granted for a period of three years, and these two industries were established and were making some headway. Last year the bounty ran out, and the minister announced in his budget speech that it would not be renewetj- Now the position is this. The manufacturers of linen yam have absolutely no protection at all, and negotiations are going on to-day to remove the factory at Guelph, and I think the other factory, to Massachusetts where the United States government gives them a duty on linen yams of 35 per cent. They find that they cannot compete in this country against Belgium, France and Ireland in the manufacture of linen yams. If we are going to protect the silk and wool industry, as I presume we are to some extent, why not the linen yam industry, a yam made from home-grown flax for the purpose of using it in Canadian linen mills? Why should that industry not receive some consideration? My information, received this week, is that negotiations are going on now for removal of this business, employing two hundred men, from Guelph to Massachusetts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is largely correct, but not exactly so. Linen yams for certain purposes are free where they enter into other manufactures, but for other purposes there is a duty now. There was both duty and bounty, but the bounty has expired.
My recollection is that it was not used to any large extent, that only a small amount of the bounty was claimed. The duty in part remains.

The people who gave me my information are the manufacturers, and they said they did not have any protection on their yarns. I did not look the matter up in the tariff, but I would rather assume that they knew what they were speaking about.
They were quite right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is free for certain
purposes but not free entirely. I have no doubt the manufacturers intended to give my hon. friend a correct statement, but I think he must have misunderstood them on that point.

Is not the real trouble-I am speaking from my recollection of the tariff inquiry-that in so far as these linen yarns are concerned, while we start out with a duty on linen yarn the rebating sections of the tariff are such as to bring about practically the situation that the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Gutherie) points out? The minister says it is only for certain purposes that rebate is given. That is true, but these are practically 4 p.m. all the purposes for which the yams are used. They are not used for anything else, and you might just as well take away the protection altogether in most of these cases. It is just like the botany yam; I am more familiar with the botany yarn situation, and I know that one mill has already closed down, and if it had not been for the partial relief now given would have been moved out of this country. I do not think my hon. friend can give the hon. member for South Wellington any real demand for these yams except the demand which is covered by the drawback provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is one of those cases where one man's raw material is the other man's finished article. I might point out that there is no change in this respect. The bounty has expired, but we are making no tariff change as respects linen yam. Item 543 in the tariff covers:
Linen yarn, when imported by manufacturers of towels, damask, or seamless linen fire hose duck, for use exclusively in (the manufacture of such articles in their own factories.
This comes in free. It is the raw material of the manufacturer and if you put the duty on there I suppose it would make trouble
Ways and Means

for the other. The only change that has taken place here is that the bounty has not been renewed.

These linen yams have been produced by two or three mills in this country, but the industry has never been a great success here, chiefly, J. think, because it has never received reasonable protection. The supply of linen yarns became critical during the war, when we could not get the yarns at all. There was nothing left to do but to go ahead and make it in Canada, and in order to encourage them the government of that day gave them a bounty for three years. It takes some time to establish an industry and only a small part of that bounty was paid to them. It is not an industry entirely by itself. It is on the same plane as the woollen industry or other industries in Canada, and if the principle of protection is fair-and I submit it is fair in this country and has been in force for many years-why should linen yarns be singled out for no protection? Why should a concern employing a couple of hundred men, just now getting well under way, using their own yarn in their own business, making towels and sheeting and table cloths and the like, be put in the position in which they are now, with no bounty and no protection, having to import their linen yarns from Europe for the purpose of manufacturing them into goods in their own factories, when they could do all that work at home? The result now is that they are just pulling up stakes, and I think within the next thirty days they will be located in Massachusetts, manufacturing there, employing American labour, paying American labour, and sending the yams back to Guelph which should have been made in Guelph. I think the case calls for immediate action on the part of the minister and the government. If this budget is not a protective budget I do not know what it is; and if it is, then it should take care of the flax business and the linen business, just as well as any other industry. I believe my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Forrester) probably knows as much about this question as I do, and can throw more light on it than I can. I am satisfied the matter is one of great interest to a large proportion of the people of Ontario. They want to grow flax and to have it manufactured in Canada, but under the circumstances the industry is bound to die in Canada and be transferred to the Stales.

It is not a matter of a drawback, as I thought. It has been carried right into the' tariff, in the provisions as to manufacture. I do not think my hon.

friend can point out any use to which linen yarn is put-that is any quantity of it-which is not covered by other tariffs. I refer to item 543, which is a free item, and 543A which is another free item. I think in the result it may fairly be said that, so far as linen yarns are concerned, there is no tariff at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is wrong in stating that this industry has been singled out. We are not touching this industry at all in this tariff, and, not having made any changes, I have not studied the figures closely.
You touched it last year. Last year's touch was the last straw.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At all events, it is one of the cases which illustrates the difficulty where one man's raw material is the other man's finished article. Here is the item:
Linen yarn, when imported by manufacturers of towels, damask, or seamless linen fire hose duck, for use exclusively in the manufacture of such articles in their own factories.
They are free. If we put a duty on these things, then the manufacturers who use them now and get them free will feel that they are entitled to compensation, and it is a difficult problem to handle. It cannot be settled by saying you will put a duty on these things, because when you do it you are disturbing other things. However, previously the bounty was a war measure, but it did not appear to be used to any considerable extent. It died a natural death, and we are nyiking no change in that. Any criticism my hon. friends can offer-and there may be something in the criticism-should have been offered in the past, because we are not making any change.
The minister announced in the budget, "We do not propose to renew the bounty on linen yarns.''

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely.

If he had renewed it, as he gave it to copper and the like, I do not think there would have been much complaint, but to lower the bounty will result in the industry leaving us. Thoroughout the whole tariff they bracket together cotton and linen goods, that is, we find the same rate of duty in respect of them, treating them practically as the same article. But when it comes down to the yams, the one has a duty and the other has not. We do not grow cotton in this country, but we do grow flax, and I submit if cotton yarns get a duty linen yarns should have it.

One of these industries
is in the county I have the honour to repre-

Ways and Means
sent. There are only two, as I understand it, in Canada. The other, and larger one, is in the county represented by my hon. friend to my right (Mr. Guthrie). The complaint made to me is that last year there was a small tariff, a very low tariff, one that had obtained against the real competitor, and that is always the tariff that counts1; what there may be against some country that really is not a competitor does not matter at all. The complaint was that the actual duty against the real competitor was cut down on linen cloth to so small a percentage that there was no possibility of it reaching the consumer. It was small to begin with, and was among the lowest of our schedules. The amount taken off has made it impossible to continue in any scale at all. I think about forty of the looms are idle now, and my information comes from the head of the firm, who has been a linen man all his life. He came originally from northern Ireland and established both the industry that my hon. friend speaks of in Guelph as well as this one. My information from him is that there is no possibility of continuing at all-not in the least. I venture to say that, after we have this establishment here, and they become competitors with the foreign linenmaker for the trade of the country, and have become established, and have the homes of the workmen established, if they go away and the industry dies, then it is not a matter of waiting three or four years, but it is probably a matter of waiting thirty years before there will be any commencement made again. This is an indigenous industry. It is not like the illustration the Minister of Finance gave some two years ago of an industry that he said was indigenous and was entitled to support merely because it was based on the brain and inventive genius of one man. I refer to the illustration as to marmalade produced in Dundee. This is an industry built upon raw material, produceable and actually produced in large degree in Canada. A very serious responsibility is taken by the Minister oi Financ.3 when he so allows things to remain, leaving the bounty to go, leaving his reduction of a year ago to go. This is not for the good of the country. Does he imagine that after the Guelph industry gets down to Massachusetts, and after the industry of the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) goes to the south of us, we are going to get any cheaper linen than before? Not a chance in the world. Why, the minister is going to lose more revenue because of the loss of the hands of that factory at Guelph than the
bounty he pays. I do not favour the bounty. It may be all right for a short time, but the proper thing is when we have a system to have it complete and fair. The minister says, "oh, but this is the raw material for some other manufacture." So is everything; you can apply that argument to anything at all. These things are adjusted in the tariff by having a lower duty on what is the raw material for the purpose of manufacture and having it a little higher for the goods that do not become the raw material at all. He has done that himself in this tariff in introducing the new protection for artificial silk. He has so arranged it to cover the very objection he is raising now. Why does he not do the same in this case of an article that is, at least, as indigenous as silk, I think more so, and that certainly is far more indigenous to this country than many articles upon which he is maintaining a protection as against the real competitor. I refer to cotton, which is where he found it when he came into power? The real competitor is in the United States. The minister amended the duty on linen cloth a year ago, and it is now only 15 per cent, 2j per cent off. The small bounty that was paid is gone; there is no protection for the yam whatever, that is on the yarn as used for the purposes for which it is made here; and we are facing the consequences to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend states that there is an import duty except for the purposes for which it is made here. It is not classified in the tariff separately, it is classified under twine and cordage. How much would be linen it would be difficult to say. Let me repeat this point again. We are not by this tariff dealing with that at all. There are many cases where an argument could be put forward in regard to a particular industry and we have no desire to do an injustice to any particular industry. As I say we are not making any change in the tariff to-day with respect to linen and that is why I have not the figures at hand. The matter might be worthy of consideration at another session.
The parties interested in the manufacture have waited on the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think so.
The matter has all been laid before him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think so.

The minister says that he is not making any change on the duty on linen. He overlooks the British preference.
Ways and Means

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not on linen yams.

Linen yarn is one item; the manufacture of linen is an entirely different item. Linen yarn goes into shoemakers' supplies, threads, fishing nets, certain kinds of cloth and of course into linen. This industry that I speak of in Guelph has had a hard time for the last fifteen years; but finally it is in a pretty fair way; it has become a very large industry employing five or six hundred men two hundred being engaged in the production of the yarn which is then manufactured in the mill. They have reached the point where the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways in their dining cars use their make of table napkins and table cloths which are very excellent. The leading hotels of the country buy their linen made in Canada from Canadian flax. The United States have undertaken to protect that industry in that country very handsomely. They give a duty of 60 per cent on linen towels, we give 15 per cent and, I believe the result of the recent cut, if the reduction applies to linen towels, is to cut it down to 12J per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not if it is 15 per cent.

If it is 15 per cent, I understand, there will be no reduction. On sheets and the like, I am told, the United States impose a duty of 45 to 50 per cent; we impose a duty of anywhere from 15 to 17i per cent. The difficulty is simply this. The linen workers in France to-day are earning 80 francs a week-that is the average wage of girls making these linen fabrics in the factories of France. That means $8 in our money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is nearer $5.
It is $5.60.

We are paying $15 to $18 a week to the girls making linen goods in the Guelph mill. I think this mill was started in 1903, and after 15 or 20 years' experience in Canada, we think we are in a position to make a very high class of linen from Canadian-grown flax. It has been a slow process to reach the goal which we have now reached. The situation is so disastrous as regards the tariff, that I doubt very much if the industry can survive. In the United States they realize the situation, and they have so adjusted their tariff as to make the linen industry there a far more marked success than it is in Canada. The question all comes back to this: Is it worth while to make your home-grown flax into your own linen, 
or is it better to buy linen in another country? For my part, I want to see it made in Canada.

I wonder whether the thought has occurred to hon. gentlemen that the protection they quote in the United States and again in Canada is one of the reasons why the despicable wages are paid to those girls in the factories in France. The matter cannot be interpreted in any other way. The higher the protection goes either in the United States or in this country, in order that French manufacturers may compete, the lower will be the wages paid in those French factories. The hon. member brings in this humanitarian question again.

Supposing we have no factories in Canada and they are in Massachusetts where the protection remains the same, does the hon. member think the addition of the Canadian market to the output of the Massachusetts factories in addition to the United States market will lower wages in the Massachusetts factories?

If we as a nation presume to become competitors in a financial way with the United States, there is nothing to prevent the United States from using her tariff weapon and raising the tariff by 50 per cent, bringing about the same conditions to-day complained of by the hon. member for Sou.h Wellington. This is only a vicious circle. I am very much interested in the manner in which the three hon. gentlemen are presenting their case to the Minister of Finance to bring this about. The more concessions are given to these industries, the worse conditions obtain both here and in the Old Country. What is the matter, in my humble opinion, as regards conditions in Canada, is that the purchasing public has not the means to purchase the article. This is only an artificial standard we create by giving this protection to that industry.
I should like to ask the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) what were the tariff conditions which surrounded, from 1903 on, the industry which he spoke of as starting in 1903.

I think in the manufacture of linens the duty was 20 to 22J per cent. You can take it as 5 per cent higher all along the line. There was in this country no industry for the manufacture of linen yarn until 1919, and in order to induce manufacturers to go into that and to use Canadian hemp, a bounty was given for three years. The bounty has run out.

Ways and Means

Do I understand that this particular industry which has been manufacturing linen cloth has recently started to manufacture the threads for which a bounty was given for the three years which have expired now?
That is right.
The contention is that the bounty should be restored?

I would press for a reasonable duty on linen thread or for a bounty, one or the other, but I have had no communication from my people asking for a bounty. They ask for the same reasonable protection for their manufacture as others in the same list are getting, just as the new silk industry is getting, just as the Minister of Finance is giving to the artificial silk people. This is more important than artificial silk. If the principle is right as regards artificial silk-and I agree with it-it is right in this also. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) must bear this in mind, the great competition in linens is not from the United States, but from Ireland first where probably the finest linens in the world are made, then from Belgium, then from France, and now there is a very heavy competition from Japan. In all these cases the wages are nothing as compared with wages which have to be paid in Canadian mills. It is to meet that competition that we ask for some reasonable tariff protection. If we get it, we can hold the industry here. If we do not get it, I do not think we can.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only items remaining, I think, in the customs tariff are the two resolutions touching the question of reciprocity with the United States. These have not yet been adopted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is one item on

speechtext: I thought it had been passed.

speechtext: No. It refers to oil used in the manufacture of manila rope.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
