Customs tariff:
8B. The Governor in Council may authorize any Minister of the Crown to enter into negotiations with any authorized representative of the government of the United States with a view to the making of a commercial agreement between the two countries on terms that may be deemed mutually beneficial. Any agreement so made shall be subject to the approval of the Parliament of Canada.

I do not suppose this resolution and the one following will be received by the committee with the same attention and earnestness that would be accorded them if they were considered to mean very much. I can assure the minister that those who are opposed to the idea underlying the resolutions would be in much greater evidence if it were believed for a moment that they were anything more than a mere gesture at this time; and I venture to say that the minister might be surprised at the variety of sources from which that opposition would come. I want to comment, first of all, on the first section. This, of course, while there is precedent for it, yet as a piece of legislation is of no effect whatever. It is merely words; it is merely surplusage in a statute It does not mean anything, because the minister or anybody else in the world could negotiate on behalf of a government without authority to do so; the only thing that he cannot do is to effect something. And thi* of course, does not give him power to effect anything. I suppose it is harmless; if I did not regard it in that light I certainly would oppose it in this House at all consequences The second one is somewhat different, however. It provides-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is the hon. member
treating them together?

I fancy it would be just as well to do so; at least one cannot discuss the general subject unless he takes the two sections together. The second one provides:
If the President of the United States, under authority of the United States Tariff of 1922, determines to reduce by 50 per cent-
Those words are struck out, I understand.
-determines to reduce the duties imposed by such act on the following articles, that is to say:
Cattle; wheat; wheat flour; oats, barley, potatoes, onions; turnips; hay; fish as enumerated in paragraphs 717, 718, 719, 720 of the said Tariff Act of 1922, the Governor in Council may by Order in Council make such reductions of duties on similar
Ways and Means

articles imported into Canada from the United States as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for such reductions on Canadian products imported into the United States.
This provides for more order in council government. But even this, I think, is harmless. Nevertheless, it has a meaning; it enables the government to do something finally without recourse to parliament, in the event of the United States President acting, as the section states, under the provisions of the United States Tariff Act of 1922. My first comment is this. I do not think the minister has carefully studied that Tariff Act if he really attaches any importance to this section. A reading of that Tariff Act would indicate that there was no possibility at all of anything being done with respect to these articles in relation to Canada. I read the act pretty carefully myself, and while there are two or three sections that cover contingencies, the result in effect is this. If the president becomes convinced that owing to differences in the cost of manufacture in other countries, owing to a disparity of cost of production elsewhere as compared with the United States, the duties imposed by the Fordney-McCumber Tariff are not representative of that difference, he may vary them up or down with a certain limitation in either direction upon his power of variation, that limitation being fifty per cent. But he must have not only the fact established that the duty itself is not representative of the variations in the cost of production, but also a certificate of his tariff commission. Well now, really, does anyone imagine that this is ever going to apply to , wheat, barley, wheat flour, and so forth? Does anyone think that any tariff commission is going to go into the cost of production of these articles in Canada and in other countries, and suggest to the President of the United States that the duty they have in that country to-day is not representative of, does not correspond with, these variations, this disparity in the cost of production? Why, if hon. gentlemen, particularly those from the West, are right about our cost of production, as I think they are, then how in the world can any tariff commission ever find that the duty now levied in the United States is not representative of the difference in cost of production? I do not see how any recommendation is ever to be made. For the matter of that-I give the opinion for what it is worth-all the variations downward which the President of the United States will ever make under the authority of the United States Tariff Act will not amount to anything at all. If he made any variations they would be more likely to be upwards. Even supposing, however, that I Mr. Meighen.)
there is any remote possibility that he would make variations downward, then I venture to suggest that they would not apply to these particular things that the minister has selected for the purposes of this resolution. Consequently the minister is playing pretty safe in respect of his proposal for reciprocity. But he takes other precautions. On this subject he has very frequently dilated on what he conceives, or rather on what he says he conceives, to have been a very grave injustice done to this country by the rejection at the hands of the people of his treaty of 1911. I have lately thought that his lamentation was more apparent than real, that his courage as to a new treaty along these lines was not quite as great as he would have us believe. I wonder why he limits this section to ten articles. He had hundreds in his treaty of 1911. Why are these few selected out of those hundreds? Why are all the others left out? Articles of the greatest possible importance, a list of which I had before me a short time ago, are not included here at all. For example, let us consider fruits	for	a moment.	Whyare	not fruits	in	this list?	Whydoes	the	minister	ask for power	withrespect to wheat but not with respect to fruits? If his courage is really as great as he would have us believe, why does he not ask parliament to give him autiiority, in case the United States is ready to admit fruits	free	into Canada,	as well as wheat,
wheat flour, barley, oats and potatoes? No single case could better illustrate the weakness of the minister's position. But I might go on-meats of all kinds, for example they were within his treaty of 1911. Why are they not here? Why does not the minister ask for power now to do again what- he wanted to do in 1911 with respect to meats in case we are met by the United States? There is perhaps no single article of greater consequence. Going on, I find tomatoes, oatmeal, cornmeal, peas, bran, macaroni, biscuits, maple sugar, pickles, cherry juice, mineral waters, essential oils-and then a whole long list of manufactured or semi-manufactured articles, they are here by the pages, all of which he had in his treaty of 1911, but none of which he has in his request for power to-day.
Now, if the minister has the faith that this country is anxious for his 1911 treaty, why does he not ask for power to make it again as respects these articles? In a word, what puts the special nine he has selected in a class by themselves? In fact as to the main commodities, that is, wheat, wheat flour, products of wheat, potatoes, we had reciprocity within the last five years and we

Ways and Means
have already seen the treatment the United States accord to reciprocity agreements in respect to those articles. Why does the minister want to put us on our knees before the United States for another agreement? They only allowed about six months' operation of our reciprocity arrangement on wheat, wheat flour and potatoes, when they got tired and cancelled the whole thing. But in case they change their mind again the minister wants to go down and offer to them reciprocity on these articles once more in order that they may cancel the arrangement once more. Does he think that a good tariff policy for this country? In fact outside of those and two or three other articles, he mentions no other in this resolution.
Now, if his courage was equal to his protestations he would put every other important article covered by the reciprocity offer in 1911 into this resolution. But he knows just as well as he knows public opinion-and he is not always a bad judge-that if today he brought into this parliament a resolution for power to do what he wanted to do in 1911 he would never carry the country with him. So he goes very cautiously about it, and includes nine articles selected from this list of several hundred, and says "I am willing to take that step," and he knows when he says it that the chance of the contingency arising which he mentions here is so remote that the stoutest Canadian who fears any renewal of a reciprocity agreement need have no misgivings. The first clause is merely words. The second clause is a request for power to act. It is applicable to only a tithe of the long series of articles he included in his treaty of 1911, and the inevitable condition attached, of course, is such that the possibility of the event ever materializing is remote in the extreme. Consequently, I do not see that the insertion of this clause in the bill need give rise to any very serious apprehensions. But I warn the minister again that there are evidences not a few, and some that might surprise him, that if he came forward at this time with his proposal of 1911 he would confront just as strong a current of opinion as he confronted then, and with the same result.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend has been kind enough to say that I am sometimes not a bad judge of public opinion. After all. we can only offer our own opinions, and I offer this simply as my own opinion for what it may be worth, little or much-that if we had an opportunity to-day of getting from the United States the Reciprocity Agreement of 1911 three-fourths of the country would demand and would be rejoiced to get it.
I am glad to have the assurance of my hon. friend that these resolutions are harmless. Well, that is a great thing; if we cannot do any good in this wicked world, let us not do any harm. Now, are they no good? How much vaue should be attached to them? I have not said that I attach very great value to them myself as to accomplishing anything.
I have explained that I thought it was right and proper that the undoubted intention of this government to seek reciprocity should be proclaimed in a formal way in the resolutions of this parliament. I think there are good reasons for that view.
Why is not fruit in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will come to that. We do not get fruit at the beginning of dinner.
Sometimes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I suggest to my hon. friend that I will follow him, if I can, in the order of his speech. He says that these resolutions are no good, that they accomplish nothing. Well, he ought to have a little more reverence for the historic policy of the Conservative party, for the glorious days of Macdonald, Tupper, Tilley and other illustrious men. In the great National Policy-which we sometimes refer to yet-we find there was a standing offer to the United States just as we have here, not in the same words but the same in principle, a declaration in the Customs Act of that day that Canada was ready to reciprocate with the United States on a large list of articles.
It proved no good then, either.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Exactly, it did not prove any good. But that does not prove that the offer was not honestly made; I am willing to believe that it was honestly made. In saying that it was not any good, my hon. friend is casting a reflection on the honesty of that clause of the National Policy and of the great men of the Conservative party who have passed away.
But why do we embody the offer in this resolution? To accomplish something. And I say it has accomplished more to-day than I expected it would. It has aroused a state of opinion in the United States which is of the utmost value. We declare our wish for reciprocity. There is nothing new in this, but by putting it in the solemn form of an act of parliament we are bringing it before the American people in a manner that they could not have noticed before. It has had that effect. I say the attention these resolutions have received to-day in the public
Ways and Means

press of the United States and from their public men is vastly greater than I ever expected. I did not expect to accomplish everything at once.	-
Does the minister mean a friendly or an unfriendly reception?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Certainly, some of the greatest newspapers in the United States have given the offer a friendly reception, and have warned the Republican party that if they do not pay attention to it they will have to bear the penalty by and by. Undoubtedly the offer has had a good effect in that way.
Our friend asks: Why do we not include fruits and many other commodities? Are we bound to put every item that appeared in the agreement of 1911 in our offer to-day? I expect the Clerks of the House would object to such a long list, if nobody else did. We say we are prepared to make a general offer to negotiate with the United States, and we do not limit it to anything, we do not bind ourselves. We say we are willing to open the door for a fair discussion of the whole question without any limit. Fruit and everything else is in the first clause if the Americans see fit to come forward and so propose. But that would require an act of congress. We knew that, we knew that if anything was done under that section at all it would have to be done later by act of congress, and congress will not meet for some months. But there is something the President of the United States can do now. Our friend says that he will not do anything; I do not venture to predict what he will do. The President has power under the American tariff of to-day to decrease or increase duties to the extent of 50 per cent. He can do that without going to congress. We do not care anything about the methods by which he will do this. But if the President desires to act he can get all the necessary information from the tariff commission. Now, with the knowledge that he has that power, we say, "Mr. President, we realize that you cannot make a general treaty with us without the consent of congress, but congress has given you the power to do these things now and if you are willing to act as respects this list of commodities, we Shall be happy to meet you."
It may be asked why we mention these particular commodities. They happen to be staple articles, articles that interest both the East and the West. I mentioned the other day that cattle in the West and fish in the East are articles of paramount importance. The failure of the United States to admit Canadian cattle into their country is the cause of one of the gravest difficulties

that our western friends have to meet, and the refusal of the United States to admit fish into their markets at reasonable rates, or free, constitutes one of the gravest difficulties existing to-day in the lower provinces. The exodus that has been taking place in Nova Scotia to the United States is largely from the fishing districts, due to their being shut out of the American market. I do not say that we are going to accomplish a very great deal; I do sny distinctly that when we put this offer before the United States we are putting it in the most effective way; we are helping to educate the public opinon of the United States on the subject. At all events we are declaring our willingness to do these things, always by way of general treaty when they are ready to do it that way, but in the meantime if they are prepared to deal with us directly under the powers given to the President, then we say we are prepared to act. In both cases we are simply making a declaration of faith, stating something that we want to do, something that would be good for Canada if we could do it; and if we cannot do it, why, we have made an honest effort in that direction. That is the whole case.

The President's powers
apply equally to every item in the tariff. Will the minister explain why he has onions in this class and has not fruit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am a very practical
person. It was pointed out by a large deputation from Ontario that the failure of the United States to admit onions into their markets was a serious matter for that part of the country. That is why we included onions.

Does the minister not
know that it is just as serious for fruit- even more so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a matter of fact the onion question has been pressed upon us very much more strongly than the fruit question. But then, where are you to draw the line?
That is what I say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We selected a number
of items; if you multiply them you may make it more difficult to attain your end. If we can get these staple articles into the United States at more favourable rates or free, well and good; if not, no harm is done by our making the offer.

The point is that onions, though a staple, are not nearly as staple a commodity as fruit. The United States

Ways and Means
market, if we could get it and pay nothing for it, would be far more important to us in fruit than it would ever be in onions. It only illustrates this:	In respect of every
single one of them there is always a price to pay; the minister selects those where he thinks the price will be the least; those that they would undoubtedly ask for over there he leaves out, thereby disclosing the hollowness of the whole reciprocity case. That is the point I sought to make: the minister's courage in proclaiming his fidelity to the old pact increases with the remoteness of any chance of his being up against it as an issue in this Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be an unlucky day for my right hon. friend when it becomes an issue.
The minister snid that in 1911. His enthusiasm to-day is not one whit greater than it was during the session of 1911.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I said the other day
that there were hon. members in this House who opposed reciprocity in 1911 but who, I am sure, are prepared to vote for it today. There are scores of people all over the country who, blindly led by partisan zeal, voted against reciprocity in 1911, but who to-day are prepared to view it as an economic question and would rejoice to see the agreement of 1911 with the United States put into effect.

The minister is very emphatic in saying that anyone who voted against, him was blindly led by partisan zeal. How does he explain the action of the multitudes who left the party that he then led, or nearly led, to vote against him? Were they blindly led by partisan zeal, too? When the minister designates the attitude resulting from an election he calls it a grouch, but he has been grouching since 1911 over the result of that election, and I fancy if he had another on the same issue he would have another grouch for the rest of his political career.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am, however, inclined to think that one of these days there will be another election on that issue, and time will tell the result.
The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) I understood, has suggested the amendment of this resolution by substituting the word "such" for the word "similar" in the fourth line.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: An amendment ha3 been submitted that on the seventh line of paragraph 8c the word "similar" be struck out and the word "such" be substituted therefor. The question is on the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that would be dangerous. I hope my hon. friend will not press that.

What does this mean? I am glad the hon. member brought it up; 1 had not had the point drawn to my attention. The minster's answer would lead me to think that he understands by the word "similar" as it is there now that in the event of the United States reducing the duties on the articles named in the clause he and his government will have power to reduce anything else in the whole tariff schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Well, then, will they havj power only to reduce in the case of the articles named in the clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would say so.
Then would not the amendment suggested be right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I do not think the word "such" is objectionable. It really means that we offer reciprocity in these particular articles, so that on the whole I can accept the amendment. I do not think it makes any material difference.
That gives effect to what the minister said. Personally I do not think anything makes much difference so far as this proposal goes.

If the intention is to deal only with the articles specified, then the amendment certainly is an improvement. But I read the resolution somewhat differently. I was going to ask the minister whether his intention was that the proposal should be in relation only to these specific articles, or whether it should extend to any articles of a like nature. I understand him to say now his intention was that the Governor in Council would be permitted to reduce the duties on these particular commodities and on no others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that ought to be the meaning of it, yes.

I want to say in connection with both these paragraphs that I am heartilv in sympathy with their general purpose, but I am afraid they will not get us very far. I believe the minister is entirely in sympathy
Ways and Means

with the proposal for reciprocity betwteen Canada and the United States; I only wish I had as much confidence in those that are behind him so far as their support of the principle goes. I am inclined to think the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) is considerably astray in his estimate of public opinion on this point. I would like very much to see this issue decided on its own merits. I have some very distinct recollections of the election campaign of 1911, and I know of no election where there was so much confusion of issues as prevailed on that occasion. I have never regarded the decision then taken as being in any sense a decision on the merits of reciprocity. In conclusion I just want to say this: If we do not have commercial union with the United States in a reasonable time I do not think we are likely to be able to maintain the Canadian confederation. In my judgment we may have political union instead with the United States. I do not want to see that. I would like to see the experiment in confederation work out, but I do think that a very large measure of commercial union with the United States, with all that that involves, is an absolute necessity if we are going to preserve our political integrity.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendment is carried. Shall the resolution as amended carry?
I thought we might have the benediction or other comment of hon. gentlemen on the aspirations of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good). The silence is really oppressive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Silence gives consent.
What to? Commercial union or political absorption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To the principle of the best possible trade relations with one hundred and ten millions of the richest people on earth who live next door to us.

I had expected
that we would have heard something from the government side, just some little thing as to the Canadians and the Canadian people; that even under the present administration every man in Canada could go to sleep knowing that this country can continue to function, and that we were not yet bound to deliver ourselves up to a commercial union on the one hand or a political union on the other. I thought I would have heard that from my friend, but it did not come. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, there is really only one

thing that I object to in connection with this whole matter, and that is that to-day under the circumstances in which we now are Canada ought to be in a little bit better position than that of a beggar holding out her hand. I would have thought that my friend today would have learned the lesson which he professed to have learned in his budget, that he was wrong in connection with the French treaty in trying to trade without something to trade with, and that he would have had something to offer the Americans, who were described from the other side as good men of business in connection with their dealings -some reason why they should give reciprocity to a country whose markets at the present time they now to a tremendous extent occupy and enjoy. In a small matter my friend learns a lesson. He says that in connection with Australia we needed something to trade with, so we have put a duty on raisins. But there is absolutely nothing done by my hon. friend with regard to the United States, apart from the begging attitude into which we are put-we, next to Great Britain, the greatest national buyer in the world to-day from the United States, we who to-day are giving her the benefit of our markets to 68 per cent of our national purchases. There is not a single gesture from the minister to show that we have any independence of thought or liberty of action or courage-not a single gesture. Something is said about Nova Scotia and fishing. There is one thing to be done for Nova Scotia and fishing. Here you have the cod fishing beds close to Canada. There was a modus vivendi there, and you 5 p.m. have now a tremendous tariff on fish. After that tariff on fish is effective you have the statement made that the American ports cannot be and shall not be open to the Canadian fishermen, and you have this government saying at the same time that Nova Scotia is depleted. You have this government allowing the American fisherman the full advantage of the Canadian location. Our ports are entirely open to him. He gets the advantage which we have by reason of the contiguity of our ports to the fishing banks. That is all right, we are told- everything is all right. Now, if my hon. friend wants to do business, why not try and do business in a businesslike way? Why not show that there is some object in having reciprocity with the Americans? If he is going to try and do business with them I would suggest that when he starts doing it he should have just as much to offer the fishermen of the United States as he wants for the fishermen of Nova Scotia. I would suggest that

Ways and Means
he do not go down there and ask that we get something for our fishermen which the American fishermen already have. I would suggest that when he is looking after our agriculture he put himself in the same position, for example that when he is trying to work out any treaty of reciprocity he should have something to deal with which would help that agricultural industry for which so much concern is professed. You will not get anything by requests and prayers. Take, for example, butter. I think it would be a good thing-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What about oleo?

I will come to that in a minute, I am glad my hon. friend gave me the suggestion. We have a four-cent rate on butter and the Americans have an eight cent rate. We have any amount of American eggs coming in here to-day at a rate which is half the American rate. Is reciprocity to be just a continuation down the line in these percentages? If it is not to be, I would suggest that my hon. friend ought to have an answer to the American tariff.
My hon. friend says, what about oleo? If there is one thing I want to congratulate my hon. friend upon it is his stand on the oleomargarine question. But he took his stand I think only half way. He said that oleo should be imported and manufactured, and he was perfectly right, under fair terms. The Americans have a duty of eight cents a pound on oleo. We have no duty; and if oleomargarine is to fulfil any real useful purpose outside of the purpose of being a very great necessity-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it is prohibited what is the good of a duty?

My hon. friend is quite right. The Americans do not prohibit, and my hon. friend would not prohibit, nor would I, but I am pointing out that the Americans had that duty of eight cents, and I was further going on to point out that if there is anything that oleo would be a good thing for outside of the help it gives to those who cannot, unfortunately, at times get butter when they need it, the thing would be to give a market for the amount of beef fats produced in this country and which run up into the millions of pounds. The Americans see to it that none of these beef fats get into the United States, while we had a provision under which everything could be rebated that was used in the manufacture of oleo. We require just a little reciprocity in tariffs at the present time if we are going to
put ourselves in a position to do anything. We must have a little equality. And I think that if my hon. friend wishes to do that, he will put this House in the position in which he put it in relation to Australia. What is right for Australia cannot be wrong in connection with larger issues.

I think the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) was a little unhappy in his use of the term "commercial union" in his remarks a few moments ago. I hardly know what is implied by the term myself, and I doubt very much whether he knows. However, I am inclined to think that the idea he had in mind was reciprocal tariff arrangements. If that was what he meant, I very willingly give adherence to that view. If he meant commercial union, I say that, as far as I am personally concerned, I do not know what it means. It may mean a great deal more than he thinks it means, and I should hesitate to pledge myself to support that view, at least until I know what it means. Reciprocal tariff arrangements with the United States is one thing. Commercial union may be very much more, but just what I would not undertake to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The discussion this afternoon emphasizes the fact that, as regards the ex-Minister of Finance, his preaching is substantially different from his practice. He has again and again advanced the proposition that if you want to deal with somebody you have to have something to deal with. He referred to that again and again in connection with the French treaty. I would remind him that he sent his colleague, Sir George Foster, and others over the waters to negotiate a treaty with France, and he did not arm them in the way he says they should be armed. He sent them helpless, and they brought home a treaty. I am not finding fault with that, but the hon. member preaches the doctrine that if you want to deal with other nations you must jack up your tariff. He did not do that. That only proves that my hon. friend, when he talks this way, is not as much in earnest as he is in some other matter. As to the policy of increasing the tariff against the United States, have not hon. members made it a virtue in this country that they did not increase the tariff? Have they not tried to persuade the country at certain public gatherings that they had reduced that tariff, and that they had a tariff almost the same as ours? They undertook to prove that their tariff was lower than ours by some small fraction, and now we are told that the true doctrine is that if you want to negotiate you must jack up the tariff. My hon. friend's
Ways and Means

practice and his preaching are widely different. I do not think he would ever go before the country and proclaim the doctrine he has proclaimed to-day.
I am afraid that my hon. friend and I are never going to get this question of precept and practice settled. But there is a great distinction between my hon. friend and myself.
Hear, hear.

Yes, and we will come to it; hon. members need not be at all alarmed. There is a very great difference. So far as I know, at any rate, we have tried to put into effect the precepts that we taught and preached. So far we have not sought to discard any principle upon which we stood, for the sake of continuance in office. If we have done so I would be pleased if the minister would point it out. I have not the honour of being in the position of my hon. friend. He has asked "Why did you not do things when you were in office"? Why, my hon. friend knows perfectly well that when Sir George Foster went over to France the House was not in session. The budget was not pending. He knows also perfectly well that it was merely a temporary arrangement. Then he says "Why did you not do the same thing with the States? Why did you not raise the duty?" Surely, my hon. friend knows perfectly well that when we were in office the new rates, the prohibitive rates-and they were not even then as prohibitive as they are now -were brought in as a temporary measure. We desired to do nothing-and Mr. Chairman I think we were absolutely right in the attitude we adopted-which would give the slightest excuse for our friends to the south in proceeding in what we thought was a mistaken course. My hon. friend would have done exactly the same thing if he had thought the tariff was absolutely too low. He has raised some tariff items since he has been [DOT] here. He has raised some items in this very budget. But if he had been where I was, and where the late government was at that time-never mind whether he thought every single bit of American goods coming into Canada was coming in at too low a rate- he would not, I venture to say, have raised a single tariff item. He would have been just as anxious as we were that the tariff wall should not be continued. I ask my hon. friend, were we wrong?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is wrong now.

Were we wrong thinking it was a good thing to give no reason

or no excuse for a continuance of the Ford-ney Bill? To-day the matter is turned into a question of permanent tariff legislation, and it is my hon. friend who has to do it to-day. He says he does not believe in having something to trade with. Why did he advance the tariff rate on raisins? Why, of course, he knows there should be something to deal with; and if it were not for the fact that my hon. friend to-day feels that he is tied here and tied there with commitments in this direction and that direction he would see to it that his tariff arrangement was such that he could look for doing business on a proper basis with the United States as well as Australia.

I think after the remarks of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) I should perhaps make some explanation of what I meant by commercial union. I certainly did not mean reciprocal tariff arrangements. That might mean 50 per cent duty on both sides. What I meant by a large measure of commercial union was the obliteration of the tariff barrier between us and the United States. In connection with what the hon. ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) said as to the use of the tariff for bargaining, that might be all right if we were looking at it wholly from the standpoint of the producer. But it is a two-edged sword, and if we attempt to retaliate in matters of this sort we may be advantaging somebody on this side of the line and we may be correspondingly disadvantaging somebody else. We must, I think, look at these matters from the standpoint of the consumer as well as the standpoint of the producer. Reference was made to butter for instance. The Americans had a duty of 8 cents a pound and we had a duty of 4 cents a pound. That seems unfair. It depends on whether you look at it from the standpoint of the producer of butter or the consumer of butter. I think the inference is obvious.

The hon. member for
Brant (Mr. Good) is frank, and what is more, he is logical in his definition of the term "commercial union." How it could mean anything else, I cannot understand. What I want the committee to understand is that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), in approving the words of the hon. member for Brant used a definition meaning exactly the same as the hon. member for Brant said, the closest possible tariff relations with the United States.

Trade relations.

Ways and Means

That means, no tariff
between the two countries.

That is surely
a little different.

The hon. member for
Halifax is becoming apprehensive. I see that he is roused. I am glad he is. Does he think there is anything closer in our trade relations with the United States, than no tariff at all? The Minister of Finance saye that commercial union means the elos-[DOT]est possible trade relations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I never said anything
of the sort. I will speak of that in a moment.
I thought I had it exactly. I will put myself in the recollection of any other hon. member. If that was not what he said, I do not know what it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let me say at once
that I did not catch the words "commercial union" from the hon. member for Brant, and therefore I could not have had any reference to that. What I said was that I was in favour of the best trade-I do not know whether I used the word "closest;" I will use it now-the closest trade relations with 110,000,000 of the richest people on earth. That means trade relations, and only an unfair person would say that I had contemplated any other relations whatever.

I did not intimate that
the minister contemplated any other relations than trade relations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The right hon. member
said that I had approved commercial union.

Yes, because the hon.
member said that was what the hon. member for Brant meant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I said what I said, not
what he said.

The minister said that
the hon. member for Brant meant the closest possible trade relations with the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not say what the
hon. member for Brant meant at all. I said what I meant.

I do not like to contradict the minister but my memory is pretty good. However, this does not matter. That is what he wants himself. He does not mean anything except the closest trade relations only. The closest trade relations means no tariff at all.
Oh, oh.
Not necessarily.

What would be closer
than no tariff at all, I ask those who interrupted with laughter? There could be nothing closer. If the Minister of Finance meant what he said, he wants no tariff at all between this country and the United States.

Commercial
union might mean a great deal more than even that.

It would eventually, in
my judgment, as I have often said-and I know this is the judgment of the hon. member for Halifax too-but the hon. member for Brant does not think so.

What is in
my right hon. friend's mind is not the same as what is in my own at the moment. I know what he means-political union subsequently.
Yes.

It would mean also that the United States and Canada would have the same tariff as against every other country in the world, inclusive of Great Britain, and this would be in conflict with the declared policy of hon. gentlemen directly opposite. It was for that reason that I wish to dissociate myself with that view of commercial union.
I think we have things straightened out now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not exactly.

I thought the Minister of Finance would want to correct something again. The intimation of the hon. member for Halifax is that the closest possible trade relations, meaning, as I stated, and as he does not contradict, no tariff, free trade between us and the United States-
I did not say that.
He would not stand for that.
I did not express my opinion at all.
Will the hon. member express one now?

I did not express an opinion on that poipt one way or another. I protested against the use of the words "commercial union," because I said in the first place that I was not quite sure what that meant, and I also expressed the opinion that the hon. member for Brant does not know

Ways and Means

what it means. I repeat that. I like to give adherence to the things I understand, or partially understand at least.

I cannot get the hon. member to say what his opinion, stated by himself, of free trade with the United States would be. The hon. member might just as well speak out. He would fight that with all the strength of his being, the same as I would.
The subject was not before the committee. I was not thinking about it.

He might just as well say. What is more, the Minister of Finance would not have it, although one would gather that from what he said, and the hon. member for Brant had a right to comment on it in his remarks. The fact is that those things are impossible. Let me be understood anyway. I agree with the Liberal leader of 1890 who went out from his office, because he knew anything of the nature of commercial union could never stop with commercial union and was bound to lead to a far more disastrous outcome.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like to be judged by what I say and not by what my right hon. friend says I said. He said that I had approved commercial union.
I did say that in effect but not in those words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend did say that.
In effect that is what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He also said that I was in favour of no tariff between the United States and Canada. These are both inventions of my right hon. friend. I have talked often, perhaps too often, on the question of trade relations between the United States and Canada; but I challenge the right hon. gentleman to show that I ever said anywhere that I expected there would be no tariff between the United States and Canada. I have never had such an idea. I do not believe in it now; I never believed in it. The right hon. gentleman would have difficulty in convincing people that I said such a thing.
I did not think the minister meant that, but his reply to the hon. member for Brant-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not reply to the hon. member for Brant: I did not catch his remark.
His comment on the speech of the hon. member for Brant would lead hon. members of the House to think he did believe that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was commenting on what my right hon. friend said.
A minister who gets up and says that he believes in the closest possible trade relations with the United States-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
-has a right to have hon.. members understand from that, that the Minister of Finance believes in no tariff between us and the United States.
Whether it is the closest possible or not.
It is the closest possible.
I say it is not. It may not be possible.
Certainly it is possible.
I question if it is possible.

It may not be the greatest wisdom on the part of either country, certainly not of ours. The closest possible trade relations mean no tariff. What I protest against is this loose assumption, for the attraction of those whose minds lean that way, that hon. members are really in favour of the closest possible trade relations between us and the United States. They are not, and hon. members on all sides of this House, at least on two of them, know right well what the ultimate consequences of such a relationship would be.
As regards what the minister said, I want to say only one word before I sit down, because I think I can make the matter clear to the committee. He says: "If we were in earnest when we said that before he went over and placed himself in negotiation with France, he should first of all have had something to trade with by way of a higher tariff on luxuries, we would have done the same thing ourselves." The real central fact is this: The whole French treaty did not go out of effect until the session of 1921 was over. We had no prospect of a new treaty with France. We had to make a temporary arrangement in the summer after the session was passed. How could we have had the tariff raised unless we did that by order in council as the minister is taking power to do very often? We could not raise the tariff. So the minister's retort is entirely without any basis, entirely without any reason behind it. The minister went through a session, during every day of

Ways and Means
which he knew he had to enter into trade negotiations with France. He let the session go by, and therefore he put himself in a position where he had no answer to France at all. As a consequence we have a treaty to-day which I think is the most unfavourable, the most unequal, and to us the most disastrous that we have been compelled to enter into in the history of our country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman sent a colleague to negotiate a treaty with France; whether that treaty was big or little, temporary or otherwise, is not of great importance. He sent him, not armed, as he said we should have been, but simply to negotiate a treaty as best he could, and there was every opportunity, before Sir George Foster went, of raising the tariff.
Not at all; that is the point. The old treaty was in effect in 192021.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But you got notice that the old treaty was to terminate.
We also got notice later that it was not to terminate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, well.

France retracted her position and it was while I was in England that we got notice that the treaty was to terminate. There was no opportunity to come to parliament, and the hon. gentleman's contention has no force.

I am rather glad that I used the expression "commercial union" because it has led to some illuminating confessions. I do not know what it means in ordinary usage, if it has any such usage, but I know what I meant by it: I meant exactly what the minister said when he suggested that we should have the closest possible trade relations with the United States. I do not suppose that we can reach the ideal, at least in any short time, but I do think that the political independence of this country is conditioned very largely upon our getting the closest trade relations that can possibly be brought about with the United States. And in that respect I take issue absolutely with the opinion of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). I am sure he is entirely honest in his views in that regard, but although this is a very complicated question, which I do not pretend to argue now, I certainly feel convinced from my study of the situation, and of history generally, that unless we can secure a large degree of commercial union, of close trade relations, or of reciprocity-I do not care what
249i
you choose to call it, but I hope the House understands what I mean-then it will be difficult for us to preserve our political independence. If we do get such a condition, it will of course be comparatively easy for us to maintain that independence.
Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Has the minister any assurance that this arrangement will be sufficient to have the industry established?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should not be justified in giving that assurance, but I expect that it will. Of course, the people who seek bounties generally want more than we are able to give them, and they rather convey the impression at first that the thing cannot be done unless
Ways and Means

we can comply with their wishes to the fullest extent. I will not say more than that I am hopeful that what we propose will accomplish its purpose. I cannot give any assurance.
I assume that the extension of time now given is the result of further negotiation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. It in part meets their desire, but it does not provide all that they want.

Are their wishes met in regard to the extension of time? I take it that they probably wanted to have more in other directions, as well as respects the extension of time. But so far as that particular is concerned, have they been given just what they want?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So far as the resolution goes it is entirely in line with their wishes, except that it does not go quite the length they would like to have it go. There is one month of difference between the time at which we begin and the time they propose; we want the round calendar year. Otherwise the resolution is in accordance with their wishes.
I am referring to the question of time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are taking the calendar year rather than the month of December, for convenience sake.

I owe it to the minister to express approval of the attempt being made here, though he has not chosen the method which I think would in the end be best for the country. He has chosen one method which I earnestly hope will succeed. If we can make the growing of hemp in western Canada a real success, that is to say, if we can make it a competitive crop with the others, it would be a great thing for that part of the Dominion. That I am sure of. I do not like the bounty system. I do not think it is a sound one. There may be special cases where it can be justified, but I do not believe that you can get these things that have a strong foothold in other lands started in a new country, where all the experiments have to be undertaken and all the dangers of a new venture encountered, if you let things take their course, as some would advocate. Consequently, I join with the minister in the earnest hope that this will result in starting the hemp industry here, and that from this commencement the enterprise will go on and prosper.

I cannot persuade myself that the minister is at all convinced that this is 
in any sense a successful attempt to establish this industry in western Canada. I do not know that we are justified in concluding that the project will be proceeded with. I am absolutely convinced, from intimate experience, that if this factory is established in Winnipeg, or anywhere else in western Canada, it will end in utter disappointment and disillusionment.
What are the actual facts? We are importing into Canada at the present time about 90 per cent of the binder twine used here. I have been informed on reliable authority that the binder twine interests in the United States cannot extend their markets into Europe. That market is pretty well served at the present time by European concerns, particularly by the Belfast Rope Works, the largest of its kind in the world. We are importing within 90 per cent of the actual binder twine used. Let us suppose that this industry is established on this basis, what is going to happen? Price-cutting immediately; the price of binder twine in western Canada will fall anywhere from 4 to 6 cents a pound. So that in the last analysis this is a direct subsidy to the farmers of western Canada. In no sense can it be looked upon as a subsidy to the industry that is being established. An hon. member in close proximity to me said a few days ago that he was opposed to this subsidy because the government did not subsidize him in his farming operations. But that is exactly what it is going to do if this resolution passes. There is going to be drastic price-cutting, and the only one who will benefit is the farmer. I would not support the resolution from that point of view, because I do not think that in the last analysis the western farmer can be helped by subsidies.
There might be some hope for the success of this firm if it were the mere expansion of an American industry, but as it is being backed by British capital it seems to me that there is absolutely no hope of its success. Are the American interests going to surrender their market in western Canada at a time when there is no hope of extending their markets in Europe without an attempt to crush this rising concern? If there is anything more cruel in modern civilization, anything that might be comparable to the thumbscrew age, it is an attempt to establish an industry in a protected country on a free trade basis. I heartily agree with the right hon. leader of the Opposition that if you are going to have a protective system you must extend that system, you must round it out. These people will pay duty on all the

Ways and Means
machinery they import, they will pay duty on their belting; not only that, the agriculturist who is to grow the hemp will pay duty on his plows and his harness; and then if the argument of our protectionists is true, that protection increases wages, here you have an industry established on a free trade basis coming into the labour market in competition with protected industries. Now, I am 'absolutely convinced that this industry cannot be established on such a basis.
If it is the desire of the government and of the people that a binder twine factory should be established, other ways and means will have to be devised. But I am not sure that the establishment of this factory is an imperative necessity. Let us remember that for every acre grown in hemp there will be an acre less grown in wheat and oats, for the production of which western Canada is peculiarly adapted. The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) is not present, but I have understood from him that the growing of hemp in Manitoba can only be successfully undertaken in certain sections when the land is absolutely free from noxious weeds. It seems to me that this matter should have received much more careful consideration before any attempt is made to establish an industry on this basis.

Mr. Chairman, I dissent from the opinion expressed by the right hon. leader of the Opposition in his criticism of bounties as a form of protection. I do not believe in the protective system, but if we are going to give protection to special industries I do think that a bounty is better than a tariff. It is open and aboveboard, and we know what we are paying; we only pay for what we get as we get it. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) has pointed out the peculiar condition surrounding this particular industry. Very frankly, I question the whole policy of subsidizing industries. It seems to me that when conditions are right capital and labour will be applied to natural resources to produce whatever is needed, and we cannot for any length of time subsidize an industry with any national advantage. But supposing that this is a desirable industry, then when conditions are favourable there is no doubt at all that those who are interested will invest in it and carry it on if there is any probability of its being successfully established. If, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Springfield, the industry is doomed from the start- I do not pretend to pass an opinion upon that, but I think his argument is certainly worth considering-if that is the situation, then it simply means we are passing over a certain
amount of our money to people who may undertake an enterprise of this sort which will sooner or later collapse and our money will have been wasted.
Is this money to be paid to the farmer who produces the hemp? I think that could easily be inferred from this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I do hope that Hansard had the repeated "hear hear" of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) to the contention of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) that bounties are much better than a protective tariff, because I fully expect that next year we shall find his influence prevail in the government and there will be a bounty on artificial silk and we shall also find that the boot and shoe manufacturers hereafter will be granted a bounty and the duty will be entirely taken away. We have every reason to expect that from the interruption of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, especially in respect to boots and shoes.
I would urge that the minister might give me his opinion at least as to whether, if a bounty is to be paid on the production of hemp, it should not be paid to the man who produces it.

If we have to choose between a protective tariff and bounties, I certainly prefer the latter, but I do not rise to commend the action of the minister in this respect. Viewing it from the most favourable standpoint, and assuming that this industry would be successful, I can conceive of this company to which the bonus will be paid coming to parliament in the not very far distant future and demanding that a duty be placed on binder twine. That would naturally be the next step, and the farmers in western Canada are not prepared for anything of the kind.

Mr. Chairman, if we are
to have anv new industries established in Canada we must expect to give them some
Ways and Means

help at the start. I am more than surprised that the farmers of the, prairie provinces object to this small bonus to assist this industry, as it is they, more than anyone else, who will receive the benefit of its establishment. And if the industry is established the people of Canada as a whole have nothing to lose by it, the firm itself takes all the chances; we pay no money over until the factory is in operation and turning out the finished article. Not until then does any bounty become payable. I think it will be one of the best things for western Canada that has taken place for many years. It will keep at least $10,000,000 of Canadian money in Canada, and that means something.

I do not doubt the
sincerity of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) but that is the same old protectionist doctrine that has been preached in this country for the last seventy-five years. But let the industry become partly established and then there will be sufficient reason for your protecting it still further. The industry will still be there; the plant is in operation; if the protection is withdrawn large numbers of people will be thrown out of employment-that is the argument. I say that now is the time to begin. If this industry is what it ought to be; if it is indigenous to the prairie country, it will develop without any bonus.

If the hon. member for
Cariboo was logical I think he would support my contention that this bounty is being paid to the wrong parties. If he wants to bring about the production of hemp, surely he would urge that the bounty should be paid to those who produce it. To my mind it is a most illogical proceeding.

Mr. LeSUEUR:	Before the committee
passes upon this resolution I would like to place before hon. members, in as exact and as concise a form as I can, the facts surrounding this industry and the results which I believe must inevitably follow the adoption of this resolution. I think we should first get a clear conception of the two basic ideas on which I believe this resolution is founded. The first idea in the cancelling of these bounties is that the treasury of Canada might otherwise be called upon in a large measure for the payment of bounties on account of a possible large production of oil in the future in western Canada. My conclusion in that respect is based directly upon the remarks of the Finance Minister himself in his budget speech. He said:
The total amount paid in the form of bounty in 1922 was $93,636. The amount is not large, and if we had to consider only the conditions which existed when the bounty was applied it might not be worth our while to make any change. But oil hias been found in our western country. There is a widespread conviction that we are on the eve of great oil discoveries in the far west and north. The development of great oil wells in that country would of course be in one way a blessing, as adding so much to the natural resources of the Dominion. But from the Dominion treasury's point of view that which might seem to be a blessing would be little less than a disaster. If there should be, as may very likely occur, great strikes of oil in the western country, the bounties we are called upon to pay would be a very serious charge upon the treasury. We are proposing, therefore-
And then follows an outline of the present resolution. I submit, therefore, that the primary object of the cancellation of these bounties is to prevent a call upon the treasury for large sums on account of the discovery of oil in considerable quantities in the West. The second object of the resolution is based upon a recognition of the fact that grave hardships and serious dislocations in industry will result from the repeal of the bounty; it is an attempt to ameliorate the conditions which would naturally be expected to follow from the repeal. I propose to show just what the withdrawal of these bounties means to the industry in question and to point out that both these objects can be accomplished in a workable and inexpensive way without causing any hardship to this industry.
First let us look at the exact position of the oil-producing industry in Canada. The output in 1922 of the oil producers of Canada

Ways and Means
was about 178,567 barrels. Nearly 93 per cent of that production, or about 164,500 barrels, took place in western Ontario; in the county of Lambton alone the production was about 119,000 barrels, or 67 per cent. I mention these facts simply because I am well acquainted with the actual oil operations in Lambton county, which has 67 per cent of the total production. But when I describe the conditions of the oil fields in that county they may be taken, I believe, as applying generally to the oil-producing industry throughout Canada. In western Ontario, which produced about 93 per cent of the Canadian output, they are operating about 3,547 wells. About 216 power plants are being used to operate these wells. The investment in the industry is upwards of $2,000,000, exclusive of the value of the land, or the value of the leases, as we would call them.
The operation of these oil-fields is more or less along these lines. Most of these fields are old fields but the wells must be cleaned, the casing must be replaced from time to time, the pumping and the power transmission must be maintained, and the result is that it is a fairly expensive process especially when we remember that the 164,500 barrels of oil are produced from 3,547 wells. That means a rather small production per well. In addition none of these wells are flowing wells. In each case the oil has to be pumped and raised to the surface and then gathered to your central tank. That adds to the expense.
I would also point out that these operators are composed of farmers and small producers. They are the owners of a few wells. _ In no case is there a big powerful company in these fields. They are all small operators.
Now with regard to the cost per barrel of that oil, inquiry has been made among these operators, and they are men who have been in the oil business practically all their lives. Their method of operation is economical, and I believe the figures which I am going to give are accurate and can be accepted by the House with confidence. In fact, I have discussed these figures with independent authorities who have every reason to know whether they would be accurate or not, and I am told that they are. We have here the report of one property covering forty wells. It shows that in 1922 the average cost per barrel was $2.40. Another property operating sixty-three wells shows an average cost per barrel of $2.42. Another property operating fifty-seven wells shows an average cost per barrel of $2.51. Another operating 138 wells shows an average cost per barrel of $2.54; another an average cost of $2.58; another an average cost of $2.70, and another an average cost of $2.94 per
barrel. That will give some idea of the cost per barrel of the oil produced in that country.
Now as to the price received for that oil during 1922. The average price received in Petrolia was $2.62^ per barrel, in Oil Springs, being a slightly lighter oil, the price was $2.69£. The price of Canadian crude to-day is $2.58 per barrel. The point I wish to make is this, that the margin between the cost of that oil per ban-el and the average price received for it is very small at the best, and in some cases the margin is entirely supplied by the bounty of 52£ cents a barrel which this government pays. Now if this bounty is removed as this resolution proposes, what will be the result in that field in western Ontario? The result will be that a certain proportion of these producers will not be able to carry on without that bounty. Their costs are equal to or higher than the average price which they receive.
