Mr. LeSUEUR: Before proceeding with my remarks I will, with the indulgence of the House, briefly summarize what I have said, so that this matter may be presented with some degree of continuity. We are dealing with the resolution on petroleum which is proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). The bounty at present is 52f cents per barrel. The objects or purposes of this resolution are, in my mind, two; first, the primary and controlling one, namely, to prevent any large or substantial call on the federal treasury by reason of the discovery of oil in quantities in Canada and especially in western Canada. If it were not for that danger, and if conditions were to remain as they are and were, I take it from the budget of the Minister of Finance, there would be little object in taking off this bounty, as the payment for bounties is only $93,666, or possibly one cent per capita per year for the inhabitants of this Dominion. The other object of this resolution in taking the bounty off in two steps is, I believe, to create as little hardship as possible in the results which must inevitably follow this legislation.
I have briefly explained the oil position in Canada; that a great part of the oil produced in Canada to-day is obtained from western Ontario: that is production, representing 93 per cent of the total production of the Dominion, is approximately 164,000 barrels per
Ways and Means

year, produced from about 3,547 wells, owned by small operators, no big companies being concerned, and that the oil must be raised, as there are no flowing wells. This oil must be raised and gathered, and owing to the small production per well, the large number of wells compared with the total production, the average cost per barrel is heavy. I pointed out in detail that these operators, who have been oil men from their youth upwards and know how to handle wells, show that their costs run from $2.40 per barrel to as high as $3 per barrel, and that the average Canadian price for crude oil in 1922 was $2.62i per barrel in the Petrolia district, and $2.69i in the Oil Springs district, there being a slight difference in the specific gravity of the oil. The result is that possibly the majority of these oil operators have no margin of profit, except the profit offered them by the bounty of 52i cents per barrel, and that there are a large number who have a small margin of profit without the bounty.
That was the point at which we had arrived when the committee rose at six o'clock.
I should like to point out the result of the taking off of this bounty. The immediate result will necessarily be that a large portion of these oil producers must cease operations. A careful estimate has been made, and it is estimated that possibly between 50 and 60 per cent of the producers will have to cease operations, and this would mean a cutting down of possibly 50 per cent of the production in western Ontario. But it goes much further. That is simply the primary result. I would like to explain to this committee the method of handling oil after it is produced. In those fields there are receiving stations, and the oil is taken to the receiving station, or pumped to the receiving station, by the producer. From that receiving station the oil is then gathered to the central, larger tanks in the town of Petrolia. There it is taken by the main pipe line and driven by pumps for a distance of about 16 or 17 miles to the Imperial Oil Company's refinery at Sarnia where it is refined. That is the process of transportation.
That transportation system, I would point out, involves these receiving stations and their operation, and the gathering from the receiving stations to that central tank; this involves the measuring of the central tank or the strapping of it, as we call it. It also involves the pumping stations and the driving of that oil through a pipe line for 16 or 17 miles to the point of consumption. That means a very considerable investment, a considerable staff to operate the transportation system and 
a considerable overhead expense. This is the point which I am arriving at: If that production is cut in half by the removal of the bounty, as it certainly will be-there can be no other possible result-you then have a production in that western Ontario district of possibly 80,000 to 85,000 barrels, or not more than 250 barrels a day. What I say to this committee is that with a production of only 250 barrels a day, you have not sufficient oil to transport, to carry the overhead involved in that transportation system. Your 250 barrels a day will not support the keeping of the staffs at the receiving stations, at the central tank, and on the pump and pipe line operation. I can assure this committee with every certainty that if the production is cut in two in that way, it must necessarily mean the dismantling of the pipe line transportation system and the salvaging of what there is there. That will without a doubt be the result of the removal of the bounty.
What does that mean? You have still possibly somewhat under 50 per cent of your oil producers who have a sufficient margin between their cost of production per barrel and the average price which they receive, to permit them to continue operations; but as soon as that pipe line is taken out and dismantled, these producers must secure other means of carrying their produce to market. That means either tanking it by tank wagon or building lines of their own to stations, and erecting receiving racks and so on at those stations. That means an investment, and with this resolution in view, not one of those men will expend that amount. Furthermore, if they simply tank the oil by tank wagon to the Imperial Oil Company's refinery at Sarnia, that means an added cost which, I say, will wipe out, or very nearly wipe out, all the margin of profit they have, and the net result of this resolution means practically the complete elimination or wiping out of that oil field in western Ontario. These are facts which I do not believe can be refuted in any way. They are facts which, I believe, from close acquaintance with that field and with those conditions, make the results that I have indicated an absolute certainty.

How does the hon, member figure the cost of production in this case?
Mr. LeSUEUR: There are many items in the cost of production. One could not, in the course of an evening practically, tell the hon. member all that enters into the cost of production; but it will mean your maintenance, cleaning, possible renewals, pumping and raising of your oil, gathering, maintenance

Ways and Means
of power stations and so on. There are a hundred and one items.

Could the hon. member inform the committee whether or not there are any customs duties on well-drilling machinery and appliances necessary for maintaining the pumping stations he suggests?
Mr. LeSUEUR: There have been duties on various articles used in the drilling of wells but an amendment has been made in the budget which is now before the committee. That would not enter much into this, because this is a field already drilled, already operating, and the item of removing the duty affects more a new field which you are going in to drill, to explore and to exploit.
I have arrived at the point where, I believe, I have shown that the removal of this bounty must mean the practical wiping out of this field. Let us see just what that means in the way of results. In the first place, I do not believe much could be salvaged from those wells, and this would mean practically the wiping out of the investment of possibly upwards of 82,000,000. It would certainly mean, conservatively speaking, the wiping out of a great deal of that investment, of very much the larger part of it. In the second place, the Imperial Oil Company pays for that oil, about 165,000 barrels, approximately $400,000 each year. That money is set in circulation in that district, including Bothwell, Petrolia, Oil Springs- and so on, and it goes into every line of commerce. If this industry is wiped out, that money will be spent amongst the drillers in the midi-continent fields, which would be the natural place for that oil to be brought from if the Canadian oil wells are shut down. That is quite an item, and I would say that this is a big argument in offsetting the one cent per capita per annum on the inhabitants of this Dominion which this oil bounty at present calls for.
Another result is this: Petrolia is a town of possibly 3,000 inhabitants. It is a very nice little town with a certain quantity of pavements, with its public buildings, with a water system bringing water from lake Huron, a distance of 16 miles-. In getting these improvements, in making Petrolia a liveable place, the town has incurred a debenture debt of approximately $435,000. The life of Petrolia is practically bound up in the oil industry. If you eliminate that oil industry, you are going to do a most serious injury to Petrolia. I think, without question, you will reduce its population by, at least, 1,000, many say by 1,500. You will cut it in two, because the hardware and other stores which
furnish the oil well supplies and the centre of the oil operations are in the town of Petrolia. If you reduce the number of inhabitants, you are going to lessen the values of property; you are going to make houses and property a drug on the market, and you are going to strain very seriously the financial solvency of that town. You will hurt the whole district around. That will be the inevitable result of the closing down of the oil fields in that county and in those districts.
There is another angle from which to view this, and that is, this bounty had for one of its objects originally the encouragement of further drilling. There is not much further drilling in western Ontario, though there is more than one naturally thinks. There are, I think, at present some wells being put down near Colborne, possibly one near Melrose; there is one in York county; in Lambton there are several; in Sarnia township there is one, in Bosanquet township also and at Thedford. But these are more or less shallow wells in western Ontario going into what we call the coniferous formation which is a shallow formation and which is the usual well strata in those districts. If this bounty is taken off, I believe, at least, for all purposes of shallow drilling, this will produce a most detrimental effect on further exploration work. It will put a wet blanket on all .parties who are either drilling now or are contemplating drilling for oil.
The great fear of the Minister of Finance in this matter has been that there will be a large production in western Canada. But that fear is unfounded; for while there has been spent in western Canada by one company several million dollars in oil operations, up to date the results have not been encouraging and the prospects are not bright. I understand that the president of that company has officially stated that they are not and never have asked or expected to receive this bounty, they are seeking for production on a large scale. That, of course, has nothing to do with the possibility that oil may be found; and I am quite in accord with the Minister of Finance in any measures he may adopt -to safeguard the treasury against large drains from big producing wells. But I believe that this object of the minister's, as well as the purpose of assisting those who are look-for oil, can be most satisfactorily attained by a method which will avoid the hardships which the present resolution must inevitably impose on local industry in western Ontario.
The method which I feel sure will do this is the principle of limiting the bounty to so many barrels per well per day. For example,
Ways and Means

I suggest that the bounty be paid only on the first five barrels per well per day. For example, the bounty would be paid on the first five barrels; and if a well produced any more than that, if it produced ten or a hundred or a thousand barrels per day, bounty would only be paid on five barrels in each case, nothing further would be paid. That would provide complete protection against the fear which the Minister of Finance seems to entertain and which apparently underlies the main purpose of this resolution. I offer that as a principle for the minister's consideration. He may consider that five barrels per day per well is not a wise standard; he may think it should be ten or twenty-five or any other number. That is a matter for him to consider. But I suggest that five barrels per day per well would be a fair amount on which to pay royalty.
Let me indicate a few points in relation to this proposal. In the first place this resolution confines the bounty to those who have already been receiving it, that is, to a particular proportion of the oil producers of the Dominion. The proposal I submit to the committee would treat all oil producers equally, and as a matter of fact it is the principle that is recognized in all countries. I am convinced of the soundness of it, and I do not think there can be any question about its being quite fair. It makes no distinction between the oil producer who has received a bounty in the past, and the man who is looking for oil and may find it later on. The proposal to pay a bounty on the first five barrels only would not only safeguard the treasury but, which is an equally important consideration, would extend the same treatment to all who are interested in oil. Some hon. members may think that this is more theoretical than practical, but it is something to be considered.
I submit, however, that the system is essentially feasible; and it is inexpensive, which is the second point I want to emphasize. We already have inspectors at these various points and they know the fields thoroughly. We have reports in the Department of Mines and in other departments giving accurate data on the wells, besides many other details, and while I do not know whether it is the fact in Canada, I know that it is quite the usual thing in oil fields for the government to be furnished with maps showing the location of wells, and so forth. I feel certain that the government inspectors at these different points are fully acquainted with the different wells and their production, and this system that I suggest, or at all events one similar to it, is more or less in vogue in other coun-

tries where it works satisfactorily. I am not speaking of bounties now; I am referring to the system which is indispensable if a proper calculation is to be made of production.
In the third place, I would point out that the payment of the bounty on the first five barrels only would save the oil industry of western Ontario. I am sure it would. Some of the wells produce over five barrels a day, and they can take care of themselves; but the man who is especially hurt is the very man who would be saved by the payment of a bounty on five barrels a day. This would throw no burden upon the people of Canada. As I have pointed out, only $93,000 is paid per year by way of bounty, and that is less than one per cent per head of the population of Canada; and under this five barrel limit there would be practically no danger of that sum being increased, because nothing would be paid on any production exceeding five barrels. In that way the treasury would not be called upon to pay any substantial amount more than is paid at present.
The Minister of Finance very plainly indicates in his budget speech that if it were not for the fear of great production in the West he might not consider it worth while interfering with the bounty. So far as there is any fear from the West, I submit that it is completely dispelled by the limit that I have suggested. If they do get a large production there, as we all hope they will, the government will pay only on the first five barrels, and on nothing more; and that would not amount to a bagatelle. I submit, therefore, that the proposal I have suggested offers the minister a reassurance which must remove the fear he has of the public treasury being drained by reason of large productions.
Let me assure the minister in conclusion that I am not offering these remarks in any hostile or critical spirit. Far from it. But in view of my intimate acquaintance with these fields of western Ontario I think it is only my duty to state the facts as I know them, and, in as clear a way as I can, point out to the committee the results which I know must inevitably ensue from the enactment into law of this proposed resolution. I have tried to outline what I believe is a practicable, an entirely feasible and, at the same time, an inexpensive solution of this question, and one which, if adopted, would meet the end which this legislation is intended to serve, namely, the guarding of the treasury. More than that, it would alleviate the hardships which must follow of necessity if such legislation as this is carried out.

Mr. Chairman, I listened very attentively to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) had to say, at the time he introduced his budget, respecting the abolition of the bounty on Canadian petroleum, and, if I may say so, his reasons thereon were not convincing to me. He then said that he desired to do away with the bounties on certain articles, including petroleum, because he thought that these bounties had served their purpose. Are we satisfied that that is so? The purpose of a bounty is to encourage an industry in such a way that it may be made financially successful. Well, is petroleum produced in Canada to-day in that large and satisfactory volume which we would all like to see? I do not th.nk any hon. member will say that it is, and I do not think we would gather from the remarks of my colleague from Lambton (Mr. LeSueur) that that is the case. Certainly I can say that oil is not being produced in satisfactory volume in New Brunswick. Indeed, the minister himself in the course of his budget speech stated that the operations carried on for the production of petroleum in Canada were never very large. They were chiefly in Ontario, and later in some degree in New Brunswick. Then comes this important statement:
The operations have dwindled considerably.
I have no doubt that this statement is correct. And if operations have dwindled considerably, is this not an argument for-continuing the bounty rather than withdrawing it? The minister added:
The total amount paid in the form of bounty in 1922 was $93,636.
He admits that this is a small amount, and that were it not for certain future developments he would be disposed not to disturb this bounty. His words are:
There is a widespread conviction that we are on the eve of great oill discoveries in the far west and north.
Is that sufficiently definite to justify the abolition of this bounty on petroleum? It seems to me that this is too indefinite. There is no doubt sufficient evidence to warrant the hope that in the future there will be a copious supply of oil in the far west and north, but, as the minister says, we are only "on the eve of these discoveries." That is too indefinite,
Ways and Means

I think. In that case we are depending on the future. The experience of everyone in mining is that there are many disappointments; we can only count on the actual mineral production when we see it and when we have it. I quite understand there should be proper safeguards in the event of there being a tremendous discovery or production of oil, but that is against a future eventuality. That condition does not exist now, and in the meantime the bounties are being diminished or removed from industries that are struggling on, and before any considerable number of large, rich oil wells have been developed. I think this action is premature and I hope it will be possible for the minister to give some further consideration to the matter with a view to continuing the bounty or to taking such steps that those engaged in this industry may not have to look forward to its being cut off in two years, especially when there is no assurance of any substantial production for the future. I have heard from the manager of the New Brunswick Gas and Oil Fields, and he expresses the opinion that the removal of this bounty is likely to strangle the production of petroleum. One may ask, why all these difficulties? Why should the wells in Canada not be as rich as the wells in the United States? The answer is a very obvious one; we see it in everything. We have a great production of wheat in the West; why is it there is such a small production of wheat in certain portions of the Maritime provinces? Simply because there is a difference in the condition. You may have a fertile wheat producing country, or you may have a country which is not suited to the production of wheat. You may have rich oil wells, or you may have oil wells of low grade, and so it is with ours, or at any rate with a portion of ours. For instance, in New Brunswick it requires a depth of about 3,000 feet to reach oil, and at that the wells are of small productivity. It is plain, therefore, that there are variations in the wealth producing possibilities of different countries and of different parts of the same country. I urge, therefore, that this reduction of the bounty be not proceeded with; I certainly think it should not take place until we actually have the production of oil that is forecast, but which may never occur. In the meantime those industries which have been built up under the advantage of the bounty and which are now operating should not be disturbed. Capital has been invested in these properties, the work in connection with which is going on under the aegis of the bounty, and I urge most strongly that we should be slow to take action which may lead to very great loss and even disaster.

It has impressed itself upon ms that this is another "infant industry". It does seem that when the term of the contract with all these so-called infant industries expires they always have individuals who will appear before the government and ask them to break the contract and to make further renewals of the privileges extended, whether they be in the form of subsidies or bounties. As to the oil wells in Lambton county, I may say that that is my own old county, and I recall that back in the year 1890 the production of oil there was a very flourishing industry. Even in those days oil was drawn past our home up in Warwick township and sold from door to door in the rural districts at 10 cents a gallon. The wells were bored at that time; they were a going concern, and later the prices were enhanced. A lot of people believe it is because of the imposition of these bounties and duties that the price has been enhanced. In any case, since they did all those things in the early days, why should they ask for a special privilege at this time? It is difficult for me to conceive that if there should be an unprecedented flow of oil from the wells of western Canada the consumers of oil would receive the benefit. I would like to see the day when the people should be getting some of the benefits of the natural resources of this country. But we always have someone, to argue for a retention of bounties and subsidies, even in the face of the facts that I have submitted-that in the case of this industry they drilled wells and made a success of their operations as far back as 1890.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I say a word first in regard to the observations of the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. MacLaren) ? He advises that we keep this bounty on until we "strike ile", as the saying was some years ago in the West, and then stop it. Well, if my hon. friend will reflect for a moment he will see what the result would be: If we should then say to the West, "We have been paying bounties to the East for twenty years, but the moment you get any oil we stop them all," I would not like to have to answer the criticisms that would come from my western friends. One difficulty incidental, I suppose, to any system of protection, whether it is by bounty or by duty, is that the parties benefiting from it easily train themselves to depend upon it, and then if at a given moment it is deemed to be in the public interest to reduce or abolish that protection, instantly you are told that the industry is going to be destroyed. I suppose they believe it in all sincerity; they educate themselves to believe that without

Ways and Means
this assistance they could not live. Now, we sometimes talk of infant industries. The oil industry is not an infant industry; why, it has almost attained its full age of twenty-one years; it is almost old enough to vote. As to the merits of bounties generally there is a difference of opinion, as we know from the discussion to-day, but I think we will almost all admit that we do not want a system under which a bounty must be perpetual. If there is anything to be said in favour of bounties it is that they may be put on at a certain stage to lend a helping hand,-even that would oe debatable, I suppose. But surely it is pretty generally agreed that nobody wants a perpetual system of bounties. This bounty was granted nearly twenty-one years ago-in 1904. It was originally a very considerable industry. It has now, as I stated, dwindled considerably, but an industry that has enjoyed a bounty for such a long period as twenty years I do not think should make a great fuss if we find it necessary to stop the bounty. We are doing it very gently. We are giving them two years' notice before we stop it, and I do not think a strong argument can be put up against that. I differ entirely with the hon. member for St. John, who thought he had a simple solution-just abolish the bounty when the West gets any oil. We have been paying bounties for twenty years to the eastern oil fields, and I would not care very much to be Minister of Finance if the moment oil is found in the West I had to say: Now we are going to stop the bounty. I would not like to make a proposal of that nature. I hope and believe that the people in Ontario interested in the oil industry and in New Brunswick where they have the shales will be able to carry on. I think they magnify the trouble. They easily persuade themselves they cannot live without this artificial aid. I believe it will be found that notwithstanding the abolition of this bounty this industry will still have a fair chance of living. It is a waning industry in any event, and I believe it will be found that my hon. friend from West Lamb-ton has magnified the danger of the whole thing.
Reviewing what has been said, a bounty has been given to this industry for twenty years. It has not been ungenerously dealt with, nor is it being dealt with ungenerously to-day, when we are giving them two years longer before the bounty is taken off. I think on the whole that the industry has been generously dealt with, and that there will be no ground for complaint if we allow this resolution to take effect.

Would my hon. friend tell us what the objection is to reducing the bounty by fixing the limit at five barrels per well as has been suggested? I think that would make a very large reduction in the expenditure and it would place the small operator in the position of being able to carry on. It would help the small producer; it would help the actual farmer who is carrying on operations. It would be of no help whatever to the large corporations. The larger interests have been getting the benefits of this bounty. Why not make a reduction by fixing the limit at five barrels per well and at the same time aid the small producer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the people who [DOT] are getting the benefit of this to-day are the ones who have been getting the benefit of it for a great many years. I do not think there has been any material change. I have not the list at hand, but I think the interests enjoying the bounty to-day are substantially the same as have been enjoying it in bygone years.

My'hon. friend does not catch my point at all, not in the slightest. I am not referring to the man who is getting the bounty to-day and the man who got it yesterday. We have had bounties paid without limit in connection with the production of oil. If a well had a capacity of one hundred barrels a day it received payment on the whole output; in other words, if you had a well with a capacity of a hundred barrels a day as against a well with a capacity of five barrels, it got twenty times as much. Now the proposition whereby the treasury can be helped, whereby reductions can be made, whereby no large demand can be placed upon the treasury by the discovery of large gushers that need absolutely no bounty, whereby also the small producer is enabled to carry on-I ask my friend to look into that and see if it is not worth while to try and save that small producer. It seems to me it is worth while to save him and at the same time save the country's money, but if my hon. friend does not think it worth while I am not going to press him any more. But I do not think he has the figures. I do not think he can now tell us what is the largest capacity upon which bounties are being paid, or how many small wells would benefit by fixing the
9 p.m. limit at five barrels per day. Let me put it in another way: Rightly or wrongly a community has been built up in that part of the country. Improvements have been made and you have there a community that will continue to function perfectly well I think from what the local member has said, if the small man is looked after. Now is it
Ways and Means

not worth while to see if the country cannot protect itself and at the same time enable this community to continue and these small producers to carry on? If my hon. friend has any real reason, I could understand that, but I am sure he would want to have some real reason other than the mere fact that the solution is suggested by the local member. So far we have not had any reason given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have had representations from the oil interests, and all the facts that can be suggested in the matter have been presented to me. They have not commended themselves to my judgment. That is all I can say.

Will not my-friend tell me this: What is the real reason why this reduction cannot be made by limiting the bounty to wells with a capacity of five barrels per day, instead of cutting the bounty in half? Why cannot it be done just as well that way?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only tell my hon. friend that having considered all these things his suggestion does not commend itself to my judgment.
Then I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, we do not get very far. The hon. gentleman will give us no business reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought I had given reasons, but my hon. friend thinks I have not.

My hon. friend will bear with me. He did give reasons pointing to the necessity for a reduction in bounties. Here is another way in which the reduction can be made and at the same time the small producer can be protected. Now the question I am putting to my hon. friend is this: What is the reason why the reduction cannot be made in that way? He says he does not like it, but that is not a reason. Of course, if he does not want to give me a reason, I am not going to press him any more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have answered my hon. friend.
Mr. LeSUEUR: I do not know whether I make myself clear to the minister, but the one object which the Minister of Finance clearly puts forward as practically the sole reason for the changing of this bounty is this, to give his own words:
The amount is not large, and if we had to consider only the conditions which existed when the bounty was applied it might not be worth our while to make any change.

Then he goes on in the budget speech to say that practically the one reason for this resolution is the fear of big production in the West and the consequent drain on the treasury. Now fixing a limit of five barrels per well will certainly avoid all danger from that source, and at the same time it will save the dislocation which will inevitably follow in western Ontario from the introduction of this measure. I submit that we have sufficient dislocation of trade in Canada today without causing any more, and if we can get a solution which accomplishes the object of the hon. Minister of Finance and at the same time avoids further dislocation- I say that dislocation will follow; the minister may not think so-it will in any event avoid the possibility of it following, it will be taking the safe business course. Therefore I submit that we should put into effect a measure which will accomplish both objects.

When the budget was brought down it contained three or four proposals for granting certain bounties. I looked upon these bounties a little more favourably than I did upon the idea of imposing tariff duties, because it did seem to me that a bounty could be removed much more easily than a tariff. But apparently I made a mistake. It is just about as difficult to take a bounty off as it is to lower the tariff. At the same time a bounty should be arranged in such a way that it will be reduced until it finally ceases to be, and I see no reason why at the present time this item should not carry.
I am glad to find that the other bounties that have been suggested will be gradually reduced to the minimum, and that they will be put on the free list. I have much pleasure in supporting the resolution.
Resolution agreed to.

Customs Tariff:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend The Special War Revenue Act, 1915, and amending acts and to provide:
1. That the maximum amount of stamp tax payable on a cheque, bill of exchange, promissory note, advance on securities, overdraft, receipt by a person for money paid to him by a bank chargeable against a deposit of money in the bank to his credit, express company's money order or traveller's cheque, or post office money order be reduced to one dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I direct the attention of the committee to this resolution, and I desire to make some changes, to which I will call attention. The resolution is somewhat comprehensive. I do not know whether we will be able to dispose of all the items to-night. In the first place, there is a proposal to

Ways and Means
reduce the stamp tax on cheques. The maximum tax was $2 and we have reduced it to $1. According to the wording of the resolution, the reduction would apply to other things than cheques. It would apply to notes of hand and so on. We desire to amend the resolution so that the reduction will apply entirely to cheques. The item would then read:
That the maximum amount of stamp tax payable on a cheque, bill of exchange, payable on demand, or within three days after sight, receipt by a person for money paid to him by a bank chargeable against a deposit of money in the bank to his credit, express company's money order or traveller's cheque, or post office money order, be reduced to one dollar.
The effect of it is that the reduction will apply only to cheques and not to notes. I would therefore on that point move that resolution No. 1 of the resolutions of May 11, 1923, respecting the special war revenue act be amended to read as above.
The effect of this is to keep the promissory note with the unlimited stamp; that is to say, without any maximum.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the reduction applies only to cheques.

I want to have a word to say about that, not from a party standpoint, because I know it is lower than the rate that applied in the days of the late government, and that there was no maximum as respects promissory notes. Really, I cannot see the justice of that tax at all. For the life of me, I cannot see why we tax a man because he owes money. I know that you do not tax a man because he pays his debt. For my part, I do not think there is any justice in the cheque tax. It should be merely a tax commensurate with the advantage given him in paying that way. Even that is a mighty small justification or reason for it. But when you come to tax a man because he is in debt, I cannot see any justice, rhyme or reason in it. I hope I am not actuated by the fact that I have to pay considerable of a tax myself.
Fortunately, the hon. member has the money in the bank.

If ever there was an illogical tax, it seems to me it is that tax. It is not pretended that it should be paid by the creditor. You say to a man "If you are in debt, we will jump on your back and make you pay a little more to the treasmy than the fellow who is not in debt."
Oh, no.

lam not arguing this particularly against the minister. All he has done is that he has doubled it. If it is wrong in this case it was wrong as we mainta. ued it ourselves. My attention was not particularly called to it then and indeed that feature of it escaped me personally entirely. I will call the minister's attention to the inequity of the whole thing. According to this principle, why not tax a man because he wears bad clothes?
Does my hon. friend contend that because a man gives a cheque he is in debt?

I am not speaking of the cheque tax now. I do not think the minister's plan in regard to that is right. I think the plan of the late government in that respect was right, but I am not dealing with that now. I am on the promissory note or the overdraft at the bank. If a man owes the bank $20,000 or $30,000 he has to pay $10 for the privilege of owing it every month or so. Here is another instance. Supjpose a man goes into the bank on the 29th or 30th March and borrows $20,000, on the next day there is a tax against him of, say, $4 or $5. He is assessed that amount because he is in debt. Suppose he goes in the next day and pays it off, the minister puts it on again. He has to pay for going into debt and has to pay to get out of debt. There is a toll as he goes in and as he goes out, even though he only owes the debt two days. The reason or the coincidence of it is this: That the banks collect every three months. The act must compel them to or they would not do it. That is to say, at the end of March, at the end of June, and so on, they collect, and if a man owes the money only a day before the end of March he is assessed the percentage of the note at the end of March. If he pays it a day after he is assessed again the same amount. If he does not, and waits until before the hammer falls at the end of June, down comes the minister with another tax on him, and if he pays two days after the minister is down on him again. Of all the utterly unreasonable taxes, I think this is the worst of all. It is wrong to mj mind in principle, and the incidence of it is wrong. Why in the world a man who goes in debt on the 29th of March should be taxed far more than the man who goes in debt on the 29th January is a mystery to me. And why the fellow who pays his debt quickly is taxed still more I cannot understand. The man who pays on the 2nd April is taxed far more than the man who pays on the 2nd
Ways and Means

of May. If there is rhyme or reason in that, I would really like to have the minister explain it.
What do you suggest?
I suggest wiping it out.

Where would you get your
revenue?
I mentioned some methods to-day but I did not get much open support from the Minister of Customs. I think I have more support in his heart than in his expressions.
My heart is with the hon. member all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am really afraid that I cannot give any other reason than this one, that we need the money. I propose to move an amendment at a later stage. At present there is no date fixed for bringing the provision into force, and it is desirable that the date should be fixed. I propose that the reduction shall take effect on the 1st August. That will come up a little later.

If the minister has to have this, no matter whom he takes it out of, why not, at least, have some common sense in the method of imposition? Why make fish of one and flesh of another? Why make it a mere matter of chance whether you pay $20 or $10? The minister might just as well collect by a lottery. That would be just as moral and just as sane. The way the matter stands now, it all depends when you happen to make the note and when you happen to pay it. One man may have a note for three months and pay a certain amount only; another man may have a note for three days and pay twice as much. I should like the minister to look into the matter and make it rational, for to-day it is utterly irrational; there is no common sense to it at all. In my judgment, the Whole idea is wrong; it is founded on a principle utterly wrong from the beginning. But if the minister is bound to keep it up, why impose these foolish regulations that fall with utter inequality upon debtors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend says that this is inequitable. He is not alone in that criticism. I do not know of any item in the customs tariff that someone does not say is inequitable. I have no hope that we shall ever get taxes in any form which will be admitted to be generally equitable.

Could the minister not do this? This is not a matter of somebody saying that the tax is inequitable; it is a matter
IMr. Meighen.]
of whether the tax is inequitable or not. If the inequality is clearly shown, why continue it? If the minister is bound to tax men because they are in debt, all right; tax them according to the length of time. The length of time now is supposed to be the measure of tne tax, but it is not at all. This is just a mere matter of chance. Why not say that a noi.e that stands for six months will pay so much, a note that stands for three months so much, and so on? Make the tax proportionate to the time. There is no common sense to t'h'3 from whatever angle you view it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is my right hon. friend contending that because a note is liquidated in three days, it should pay a different tax from one liquidated in three months- one that runs the full tenure?

The way the matter
stands to-day, a man might make a note on the second day of January and carry it on to the 31st day of March, and he pays the tax once. That is three months all but a day. But if he makes it on the 30th of March and pays it off on the 1st of April, he pays a tax twice, although he has had the money for only two days.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is the tax net on the instrument itself?

No, it is not. It is the minister's regulation. In one case the man has a note for three months and he pays the tax once. In the other case, he has it for two days, and he pays it twice. The minister says he has to continue that because he has to have the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: While the rate has been increased, the wording of the law is precisely the same as it was before. I do not think this is a new feature. We have increased the amount of the tax; but the method is pretty well established; people get used to it, and I think we can look to have it a little while longer.
One can get used to having one's teeth pulled.
No, one cannot; I have had experience.

I venture to say the
people have not gone into the matter and learned the meaning of it. It is the minister's regulations that are at fault, not the law. Why should such a thing as I have described be continued? One hangs one's head in shame before a debtor when he comes and complains. The thing is ridiculous. Let the minister make

Ways and Means
the tax proportionate to the time if he wishes to continue the tax. A change in the regulations should be sufficient. The way the thing is now, actually one can hardly have the patience to discuss it, because it is not only inequitable, but grossly absurd.

I also think this tax is inequitable, but on different grounds from those advanced by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). I do not think that his point is well taken in the illustration that he gave *of a man who borrows money on the last *of the month and repays it in the early days *of the ensuing month, and he draws from that the suggestion that the man should pay stamp tax for the length of time he has the money.
It all depends on the month. One month he pays one thing; another month, another thing.

The same argument might hold good as regards postage stamps. 1 might argue: Why should I pay three cents to mail a letter to Hull, when three cents would take a letter to the Pacific coast? The argument is the same. The time for which the note is drawn, whether for a shorter period or a longer period, has nothing to do with the tax; the tax is a tax on making out, the note, in the same way as the postage stamp is applied in a generic way.
The objection I take to the clause is this: The Minister of Finance has said that there is an absolute necessity to obtain revenue, hence this clause. Why not leave this clause out and let the tax go on at two cents for [DOT]every fifty dollars as the amount increases? Why reduce the maximum from $2 to $1? That will produce, not more money, but les3 money. In its very essence and nature, the tax is unjust as between the small man and the man who handles money in large amounts. A man pays two cents every time he draws a cheque under $50. That applies if he draws a cheque for $2, and the leader of the Opposition might object to that. Let us take an average and say that his cheques average $25, that is for everyone who draws cheques under $50. That would mean that he would pay [DOT]08 per cent on the amount of his cheques. But if a man drew a cheque for $5,000, he would pay only -02 per cent. That means that the small man pays four times as much as the man who is able to draw a bigger cheque. From the point of view of inequality between the tax on the small man and the tax on the big man, and from the point of
view of revenue, I can see no reason for ths change in the maximum from $2 to $1.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The object of the reduction was this. There are many transactions in which the same amount of money passes through two or three hands. Really it is the one transaction, the one deal, and the cheque has to be given two or three times. Representations along that line were made and we were impressed with them so that we reduced the maximum from $2 to $1 largely to meet cases of that kind.

I admit there is a distinction between the position of the note and the overdraft and the cheque. Indeed, I think it is because there is that great distinction, that the cheque tax becomes all the more abominable. The cheque is an instrument which is drawn by the bank's customer who deposits the money which renders it possible for business to be carried on. He is the man who renders it possible for the borrower to get his accommodation. The one man is taking advantage of somebody else's assets for the purpose of carrying on his business. The man who draws the cheque is the man who makes it possible for that business to be carried on. There is a great difference in principle between taxing the man who discounts his paper and has his overdraft at the bank and the man who draws cheques. But my chief quarrel with the cheque tax is because it is perfectly without rhyme or reason; it cannot be supported on any principle, while you can support the other two taxes that my hon. friend is referring to. You cannot support a tax on a cheque of any idea of value given on anv ascending or other scale. I object to it not only on that ground, but on the ground that it is not being and cannot be equitably carried out, and the minister himself does not know what the law calls for. I can make that statement without fear of contradiction by anybody who has made a study of this legislation. The government are not collecting this; they cannot. It is being collected by the banks, and if there is one there must be thirty rulings given by the department from time to time on the different matters that come up. It is a difficult thing to know how to charge these stamp taxes. Just to see whether I am right or wrong, I am going to ask the minister a few questions. Take the tax on cheques and drafts. What stamps have to be affixed; first, on a draft for $50, payable at sight or within three days thereafter? Secondly, on a draft for $50 payable in ten days?

Ways and Means

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be 2 cents.

The minister
says 2 cents; I am afraid he is incorrect. To start with, it would be $2.
Two dollars on fifty dollars?
I said $50,000
You said $50.

Then, I beg
your pardon; I meant to say $50,000. Let me again put the question. What stamp must be affixed on a draft for $50,000, payable at sight or within three days, and on one payable in ten days? What is the difference, if there is any? How many managers of branch banks could answer that question? The Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) does not know now, and it is his department that is concerned.

We do not determine the
amount of the stamps by the length of time involved. It is the amount of the money on which the tax is to be charged that determines the quantity of stamps, and the charge on $50,000 will be as many two cents as there are multiples of fifty in $50,000, whether the time involved is three or four months. My hon. friend was referring just now to an overdraft. Well, the law provides that he who draws on the bank or gets an accommodation for, say, $50,000, shall pay as many times two cents as there are multiples of fifty in the total.

Just as I
thought, the Minister of Customs knows absolutely nothing about it.

I am following the lead
of my predecessors, and I do not wish to put them to shame.
The hon. gentleman's predecessors gave him no such lead. They had no system of multiplying taxes.

They may not have done
that, but very often they knew nothing at all of what they were doing.

The simple fact is that no one would know anything about this matter unless he had made a special study of it. The difference is that a draft for three days is a cheque, but when it is for ten days it is "time," and you have the $2 limit in one case, while it does not apply in the other. Now, you have these instruments going up and down the country and no one knows anything about the matter. In fact, the minister who is in charge of the whole business does not know. Let us take another illustration.

Does the hon. member
say that a draft for three days is a cheque?

Yes, sight or
three days.

Under the special War
Tax Revenue Act?

Under the hon. gentleman's act. Let me take another simple case. What stamps must be affixed to a bill of exchange for $10,000: First, when the bill of exchange is drawn in Canada on a person in a foreign country payable on arrival of goods? Secondly, when the bill of exchange is drawn in Canada on a resident of Canada payable on arrival of goods? And, thirdly, when the bill of exchange is drawn in a foreign country on a resident of Canada, payable on arrival of goods? I know that my hon. friend cannot tell me, and it is not fair that we should wait for an answer. He does not know. Yet you have that sort of conundrum put up day after day under this precious system of multiplying stamps on cheques and bills of exchange all over the country. Let me get something really simple. Have stamps to be attached to bills or drafts when delivered to the bank for collection, or need such stamps not be affixed until such drafts are accepted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend might
ask me fifty questions of that nature, and 1 should have to have time to consider them. It is a difficult matter to interpret the act on the spur of the moment. The hon. gentleman really magnifies the trouble, for I have not heard of any difficulties. The banks make their returns and we get the money. However, if he is really earnest in the desire to obtain information, if he is putting these questions for the purpose of eliciting information that he wants, I will take them into consideration. But I do not want to interpret the act right off the bat.

But this is not
doing it right off the bat. Here we have an act that has been running for over a year, and the Minister of Customs, who is enforcing it, knows nothing about it. I do not blame him at all. The whole truth is that we have an act which is enforced here and not enforced there, and you simply cannot help it. You have such a mixed up state of things that it takes a Philadelphia lawyer to answer the questions that arise in consequence. My hon. friend says he has heard of no difficulties. Apparently they do not come to his notice, but he would find if he went to the Bankers' Association that there has been any amount of


Ways and. Means
trouble. He would find the same thing if he went to the Department of Customs; he would discover trouble there.
Oh, no.

The hon. gentleman says "oh, no." He has dodged the trouble; he has officers who do the work for him. But I know about the matter because I happened to be held up in connection with stamps on one of these documents. The bank said they had to make the charge under the act, and I pressed for the authority. The authority came in the shape of a ruling from the Department of Customs and Excise, and my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, takes the only safe position that he can possibly take when he says that I might ask him fifty questions and he would not be able to answer without having an opportunity to consider them. He is absolutely on safe ground, because that is the literal truth. But if the Minister of Finance, the author and creator of these ascending stamp taxes on cheques, cannot tell you, then how on earth do we expect anything like uniformity of enforcement throughout the thousand and one branch banks in the country? The fact is that we are not getting it. I could go on piling up illustration upon illustration in proof of this. The tax is wrong in principle and is unfair in application; and it is not and cannot be enforced evenly everywhere. Just as my hon. friend has trouble in arriving at conclusions, so will others experience the same thing, and in greater measure. Put his intellect against the intellect of a branch manager or of a receiving teller. If the hon. gentleman has difficulties, what must be the difficulties of those officers? One man thinks there is a difficulty here and he makes application to the Bankers' Association. The Bankers' Association make a ruling and they send it to the Department of Customs to see whether they know anything about it. Sometimes, Mr. Ross, of the Bankers' Association, has difficulties, and appeals to the department. Now, that gentleman is supposed to know something about the matter, but at one time he is told that he is right and at another time they tell him he kno.ws nothing about it. And yet we are seriously supposed to regard this tax as having been fairly and equitably administered. My hon. friend says he has got a lot of money out of this tax. I do not see how he can have any idea of the amount.
