speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
probably knows that in the inland revenue service postage stamps are used to a large extent. I propose to change that. But you cannot tell exactly what money has come into the inland revenue and what into the post office by reason of this tax. My hon. friend says that if I would consult the Bankers' Association I would find there is a great deal of dissatisfaction. I have not consulted them, but I am in contact with them frequently and I am not conscious of any difficulty in administering the act. My information is that the act is working satisfactorily.
The hon. minister tells me first that he can ascertain what money is being obtained from this tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As between the two
departments.

Then he tells
me that postage stamps are used in the one case and not in the other. Surely my hon. friend will admit that it is impossible for him to tell to-day what revenue he is getting out of this tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because of the difficulty as between the postage stamp and the inland revenue stamp, that is correct. We can tell what amount of money we are getting on cheques from inland revenue stamps and from postage stamps, but we cannot allot the revenue between the two departments. We propose to change that: by our amendments to-day and cease the use of postage stamps for the purpose.
In other words, my hon. friend cannot say how many cheques have postage stamps on them. And he is quite right, nobody can.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend had
the same rule.

In connection
with what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Postage stamps.

In connection
with a single stamp on each cheque.
Ways and Means

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the difference in principle?

Everything. We made arrangements for the embossing of cheque stamps and were getting in a position where we would know pretty well. I admit we did not have a complete check, but it is something to get an idea as to the number of cheques so stamped. It is a comparatively easy thing to do that.

No, it is not an easy
thing.
But it is difficult to get an unknown multiple of stamps.

The stamps are there to
show if you can get the cheques.

But I suppose
my hon. friend has tried to do that?

I only try to do things
that have sense in them.

As a matter
of principle should stamps be affixed to drafts when delivered for collection, or not until after they are accepted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I said to my hon. friend a little while ago, he can ask very many questions of this nature which I prefer not to answer by way of interpretation. If debatable questions, I shall be very happy to deal with them. I suppose when he puts them that way he regards them as debatable.

I tried to get
this information before in order to advance matters so that I would not have to bring it sup now.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no recollection
of any such attempt.
I put a question on the order paper and was told there were not any such rulings.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When.

At the earlier
part of the session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no recollection
of it, but I will look it up.

I am not pressing the question, but I do not want it to be understood that I have held this matter back just to bother my friend. I tried to get the information in the proper way. I also tried to get these questions on the order paper so the government would know just exactly
{Sir Henry Drayton.]
where they were, but I was informed that under the Speaker's ruling these questions were out of order because they involved an interpretation of law. I thought it would have been easier for the government if the matter had been so dealt with. But I am not asking for an interpretation of the law, I am asking as a matter of principle. No matter what the law is, is it right? Take this case: Drafts sent in for collection-not accepted- returned with notification-new drafts drawn by the same drawer and sent back to the same bank; should there be a duplicate set of stamps?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whether the draft is paid or not, I think it would have to bear the stamp. I do not recollect the question my hon. friend put on the order paper. My desire is to see that every information he sought on any public matter should be given to him in all due courtesy, and if he asked any question of that kind, and it was not fairly answered, I shall be glad to look into it.
I am not complaining.

I put a series of questions with respect to these rulings on the order paper, and they were returned by the Clerk of the House with the intimation that they were out of order because they involved an interpretation of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they had not been out of order, and they were addressed to me, I would certainly have declined to give any interpretation of law in that way. I do not think it is the business of ministers to give interpretations of law.

I was referring to an older question than that again, to a question I put in the early days of the session as to what rulings had been made in connection with these very stamps. I was told there had been none. I am quite sure that was an oversight, and I am not making any complaint in regard to it. Does my hon. friend think as the author of this tax whether, as a matter of principle, there should be two sets of stamps affixed to the transaction I mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is a very legitimate means of raising money for public purposes, yes.

Then, Mr. Chairman, I just want to show what is being done. A draft is sent in to a bank, and under the rulings, not of the department in the first instance, but of the Canadian Bankers' Association, endorsed by the department, that

Ways and Means
draft, which is not a completed instrument until it is accepted, has to have stamps attached to it to the full amount, if it be a time draft, before it is sent for acceptance; and if that draft is not accepted and returned, under the rulings of the department a duplicate set of stamps have to be placed upon another draft for the purpose of effecting one and the same transaction. Does my hon. friend really think that is right?

If my hon. friend will allow me? When a draft is sent and not accepted for cause, I suppose the party who draws the draft has to put a stamp on it. Can the party who accepts a draft send back this draft again without putting any stamp on it?
Under the rulings each is looked upon as a separate transaction. I venture to say that in nine cases out of ten that ruling would never be followed by any banker in ordinary practice.
It is generally accepted by banks.

There are any amount of others just to show how hard it is to administer this stamp tax. Take for example where an American bank deposits cheques, drafts, travellers' cheques, money orders, notes and other items on which the stamp tax has been duly assessed, is such American bank entitled to withdraw the same by settlement draft without further tax, provided said settlement draft is payable to order of another bank?
Another little question: In case of customers borrowing under section 88 of the Bank Act, and who conduct a sales and purchase account, is it in order to debit the sales account with the amounts to be applied on the loan, instead of obtaining cheques or bills of exchange to which stamps would have to be affixed?
Another question-and I might go on ad infinitum-upon the request of a customer, may his account be debited with the cost of drafts-foreign or domestic-sold to him, without obtaining from him a cheque or any other form of requisition on which stamps would have to be affixed? Another question: In case stamps have to be affixed to cheques or other requisitions for drafts, must similar stamps be affixed to the drafts also? I do not suppose it is worth while going on with the mess, Mr. Chairman. I will ask this question: Under this mixed-up law, in connection with which so many questions can arise and so many different rulings can be given, how is the collection of the tax checked?
Does my hon. friend want to know the amount we get from the tax?
No.
What, then?
How is the collection of the tax checked?

Does he mean by that,
how do we collect on cheques?

No, I did not
ask that. I know you do not do the work; I know the banks are doing it. But how do you check the work of the banks?
That I cannot answer.

I was quite
sure that my hon. friend could not answer, because it is not done.

The law provides for that. A banker is not to accept a cheque unless it bears the stamps. Does the law not say that? Now, the bankers are a lot of men whom I think we ought to have confidence in. My hon. friend seems to have, anyway; their rulings are accepted by him as the law. Now, we cannot check smuggling, although smuggling is against the law, but whenever we catch an offender we punish him. If the banker accepts a cheque to which no stamp is affixed, he is liable to penalty. We presume the bankers are doing their duty; they are helping us to collect the revenue of the country. Unless they want to render themselves liable to penalty they do not cash cheques unless the proper stamps are affixed thereto.
My hon. friend says the bankers' rulings have my respect. I am not giving them any. It is my hon. friend's department that is doing it.
What?

Giving this
great respect to rulings of the banks.
Yes, you have.
Now, I wish to ask another question.
I will not be cross-examined here.

Well, my hon.
friend may not be willing to answer the question; nevertheless I will put it and he may answer it if he likes. He has said there is a penalty in connection with these stamps. Will he tell us what that penalty is?

The cheque is no good; that is the penalty.
Ways and Means

The penalty is mentioned
in the act. If the cheque bears no stamps, he is liable to penalty. If it bears only a two cent stamp, there is no penalty; it was omitted last year.

Of course it
was omitted.

My hon. friend thought
he was going to catch me.
No, because-

Is my hon. friend going
to say that he told me about it? He did not tell me; I spoke to him about it. I asked him how he would draw the amendment.
My hon. friend said a moment ago that there was a penalty.
Yes, there is.

There is no
penalty except that which is provided for failure to place the initial two-cent stamp on the cheque.
Yes.
There is nothing provided as a penalty for the omission to affix any stamps in excess of two cents.
I admit that.
Very good; now, what is the penalty as against the banker?

Oh well, if my hon. friend wants to play that game; if he wants to get smart, let us go out in the open, get a mattress and have it out. This is not carrying on the business of the * country. He knows very well that the penalty was imposed by himself when the law respecting the two cent stamp tax was enacted.

As to the two
cents it is all right; but where is the penalty on the bank for not seeing to it that the proper amount of stamps in excess of two cents is affixed?

I will ask my hon. friend
a question:	When the law respecting the
two cent stamp tax was enacted, was that his law or not?
Yes.
Was a penalty put on them ?
Yes.
Then it is there, and he knows all about it.
Yes.
Then what is the use of keeping that knowledge away from the public?

The whole thing is too plain for words. There is a penalty for not affixing the two cent stamp, but absolutely nothing in respect to the multiplication of stamps involved in the tax above that amount.
I admit that was omitted.
It was. Now as I say, it is unnecessary to go on multiplying instances-
We know what your knowledge is-now quit.
If my hon. friend wants a lot more questions I will give them to him, but a moment ago he said he did not want to be examined.
No, I do not want them. You had better answer them for the benefit of the House and of the public.
I am not supposed to tell the government what it is to do in all these things; in any case, they would not take my word for it.
You are supposed to tell us what you know, anyway.

It would take too long if I told all I know about the mismanagement of this administration.
Mr. BUREAU Publish it-Webster's dictionary.

I submit in all seriousness to the Minister of Finance that he has a tax which has not been and cannot be equitably enforced. He has a tax which is illogical, a tax the receipts from which he himself does not know, a tax which-he will correct me if I am wrong-is not imposed in any other civilized country. So far as the stamp tax on cheques is concerned, the minister is putting Canada just where he claimed the vote on oleomargarine was putting it the other day. Why should a tax of this kind be further insisted upon? My hon. friend has given some relief; he has taken the maximum tax on cheques down to one dollar. Why not make a fixed rate on cheques. Why not have two cents for cheques up to $50 and five cents, if you like, for all cheques in excess of that amount? Why not, at any rate, have some specified amount so that everybody will know what the law is? And if that cannot be done, what logical

Ways and Means
reason in the world is there for giving the relief upon cheques of the larger sums instead of the smaller sums? Why not leave the cheques in the higher registers as they were and absolve from this multiplication of stamps all cheques, for example, under $500? If there is to be any relief, let us have it where it will do some good. Why stick to relief in the upper registers instead of the lower, instead of in those cases where the people concerned are those who really require assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is imagining difficulties which to the best of my knowledge and belief have no existence. He suggests that the tax is not being and cannot be collected. All I can say in that respect is this:	The information that has come to
me is that the tax can be collected; it is being collected, and it is a very considerable source of revenue. As for the action of the banks in the matter, my hon. friend may have seen some banker who disapproves of it, but I believe the banks are doing their duty in collecting the money, and there are penalties if they do not do it. I say that my hon. friend is imagining difficulties for the sake of offering criticism.
I cannot understand my hon. friend saying that when a moment ago he told me I could easily ask him fifty questions that he could not answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I said fifty; make it one hundred if you like. You can ask all sorts of questions with regard to the interpretation of any act that for myself I would not undertake to answer. If my hon. friend has any real questions to put; if he really wants information, I shall be happy to inform him as best I can. But I do not think my hon. friend does want information. He is as capable of judging these disputed points as any person else, and I am quite sure that he knows more about these matters than he is willing to admit.
The minister does not get my point at all. What I am saying is that we have no right to have a law that is so complicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter of opinion, not of fact.

It is not that I want the information. I have it; I have looked it up. But I am going to give my hon. friend these questions, and by the time he has gone through them and got the answer* right he will find that this is a complicated thing and complicated in a way in which it ought not to be.

I do not wish to assume the attitude of matching my puny financial knowledge against that of the Minister of Finance. That would be absurd, but this question is one that interests everyone. It comes right home to us all. I have been trying to digest the answer the minister gave me half an hour ago in connection with changing the maximum on big cheques from $2 to $1, and if I have followed his answer right it is this: He said that in certain transactions it became necessary to issue a cheque for the same amount practically two or three times, and consequently the parties to that transaction paid two or three times over, which was really unreasonable, and therefore he made this change. Now I cannot see-it may be my lack of financial ability-that that is logical. I recall a case some months ago in which I was involved in a transaction for $1,700 or $1,800 as near as I remember, and before that transaction was complete somebody had to pay the stamps three times on that $1,800. Under the amendment proposed by the Minister of Finance to-night I will still have to pay three times on $1,800, or three times if the amount was $3,000 or $4,000. That gives me and people of that class no relief whatever. If we were allowed to add these three amounts together then it would be logical, but it does not say that. It says if you have any transaction involving the payment once, twice or three times of a sum under $5,000 you will pay it every time, but if it is only one transaction you will only have to pay once. It is not logical either as applied to the big man, because he will have to pay three times the minimum anyway if the transaction involves two or more cheques. I cannot see how it is logical on that argument to make the change. In view of the necessity of money-and I am not aware there is any intense demand for this change-I would be willing to vote for an amendment to leave the amount at $2.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I might mention that an argument was used that on the border where accounts might be kept on one side of the line or the other, the effect of this tax was to induce people to withdraw their money from Canadian banks and keep it on the American side. I thought there was some force in that although possibly the argument was strained.

Does the minister think he is meeting that objection by reducing the tax from $2 to $1. I think the reason will still prevail and that accounts will be withdrawn to American banks. That is a very
Ways and Means

real condition on the American border. A great deal of money on deposit in Canadian banks by American citizens residing along the border has been withdrawn just as a result of this stamp tax.

I wish to endorse the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi. If it were a matter of equity alone I think the Finance Minister would be more warranted in making the maximum tax $3 instead of SI. As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has pointed out, in the case of the individual who writes a cheque below that amount, more particularly the man of small means who cannot write cheques for large sums of money, the same argument applies. The argument of the Finance Minister is just as applicable to cheques of $10 and $25 as to cheques for a larger amount. I have some sort of an idea in the back of my head that in the case of individuals who are favoured with a $1 tax on a $5,000 10 p.m. cheque the law of gravitation applies, and perhaps that is the only benefit a smaller man would get. In sending out a cheque covering co-operative shipments, for instance, they would get the benefit in being able to send out a large sum of money in one cheque but it would be made up of a number of small cheques going to the parties who make up the shipment. As one hon. member has suggested, in the case of a man who is obliged to go into debt and borrow money to meet an obligation, it does seem to me that he should not be fined for that. It is bad enough for the individual who is fortunate enough to have money on deposit. We will not have very much sympathy with him if he is fined, but the man who has been obliged to go and borrow money to keep himself in business standing, and I speak from experience, is fined at the present time. I think it was earlier in the session that I pointed out that this government was not the only one that might be termed guilty. The former government when individuals bought school lands, for instance, and made a solemn contract with the government to pay 5 per cent, and through some visitation of Providence they were unable to meet their obligations, increased the rate of interest two per cent. That is the thing that people are protesting against, that when in difficulties over which they have no control the powers that be sit on them and fine them a greater amount. I do not think it is fair or just that people who through no fault of their own get into such circumstances, should be obliged to furnish the revenue of this country, when in my humble judgment other and better means could be found.
IMr. Hanson.]
Can the minister give the committee an estimate of the reduction in revenue that will be caused by reducing the maximum tax on large cheques from $2 to $1.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not at the moment. I am not sure whether it could be done at a later stage or not. I doubt if it could be done. If it could be done I would be very willing to get it for my hon. friend, but offhand I could not tell him.

I would just like to join with the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) and the: hon. leader of the Independent group (Mr. Neill) in voicing my protest against the special privilege given to corporations, companies and financial insututions in this reduction from a maximum of $2 to $1. I find by figuring that the largest sum of money on which a company will pay a tax at the rate of 2 cents for $50 is $2,500. They will pay a tax of $1 on that sum. If a farmer should be fortunate enough to ge>, that much, on the basis of paying 2 cents on an average of $25, he would pay $2, or double the amount. On a cheque for $10,000, and many of our large corporations pay $10,000 cheques quite frequently, the maximum amount they would pay would be $1, while if a farmer should by some unknown method be able to realize $10,000 in a year's operations and pay it out on the basis of $25 amounts he would pay a tax of $8, or eight times the amount that the strong financial corporation would pay. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this is unduly penalizing "the under dog," if I might use the expression. Of course, the "bark" is pretty well out of the under fellow now. He might not "bark" very much at this moment, but there is a little "bite" left in him, and he may "bite."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The arguments of several hon. gentlemen would almost lead to the idea that we should have a graduated tax without limit on cheques and documents. I confess that at one stage that seemed to me to be a fair proposal, but on further consideration it was found not to be expedient. Therefore the maximum was fixed at $2, and now it is proposed to reduce it to $1. I think my hon. friend is mistaken in imagining there is anything in this that is levelled at the farmer. We are all interested in the larger transactions of business. We do not want to crowd big business all the time, and I think the concession that is given, whether it is big business or not, from $2 to $1, is a reduction which ought to be accepted by the House. At first glance a tax graduated simply according to the size of the cheque might appeal to some hon. gen-

Ways and Means
tlemen, but I think on reflection they will find it would not do at all.

I think the general consensus of opinion here is not only against graduating indefinitely, but against graduating at all. If we could only get a small flat tax we would all know about it.
I propose to move in amendment the following :
That no addition be made to the 2 cent stamp on cheques until the amount of such cheque be $500 or greater.
The effect of that would be that there would be no graduated scale on cheques until $500 is reached.

I hardly know what to say
about this amendment, but I did think in the first place the maximum might be reduced to $1 on the larger amounts. It seems to me it would be a good thing to start at the other end also. I do not know about the transaction of $500 with the 2 cent stamp, but there are a great many smaller transactions, say, of $4 and $5. It would be lifting a burden from the poorer people if the stamp tax were removed altogether, say up to $20 cheques. I find that in the case of the family man the stamp tax sometimes leads to what might be called a little extravagance. For instance, I notice that in the West, when a man receives a certain amount of money for a shipment of grain, instead of placing that money in the bank and utilizing the bank, he keeps the money at home, with the result that very often money is expended on things that would never be purchased at all if the money were safely deposited in the bank. If the minister can see his way clear, not only to help the financial interests by reducing the maximum stamp tax to $1, but also to have the stamp tax taken off altogether in le-gard to cheques under $10, I think it would be a great benefit to the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With reference to the
amendment proposed by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton); at the present time a cheque for $500 would pay a 20 cent tax. My hon. friend proposes to reduce that tax to 2 cents. I do not think the House ought to make such a reduction. I think we need the money. I do not think it is a proper motion, and I hope the committee will not agree with my hon. friend.

I desire to oppose this tax on the grounds already stated and on two additional grounds. It i= well known that taxes generally are unpopular, but this is certainly the most unpopular tax ever levied in Canada. I know that the Minister of Finance must have the money and I appreciate the situation in which he is placed in that regard. If it is necessary to impose taxes in some other way, all right; but relieve us of this stamp tax on cheques. I know that the Minister of Finance in the past has considered suggestions made to him, and while I would not offer him advice, I would like to present the most urgent plea. My first objection to this tax is one *hat has not been given voice to in the House tonight. We find cheques with a score and more of these stamps on them. The minimum cheque tax is 2 cents, and the provision starts with a 2 cent stamp tax. Then in the case of a larger amount, the cheque will have a number of these stamps affixed to it, and it is a disgusting and unsanitary nuisance to have to affix these stamps to cheques. It is irritating in the extreme. I hope the Minister of Finance will live a long time, but after he is gone he will be well remembered, and the only thing that will militate against his reputation will be when these cheques are produced, as they must be hereafter, in generations to come, the people will wonder why, in 1923, we ever submitted to the disgusting practice of affixing stamps to cheques, and why it was that we could find no better way of raising money. The minister intimated that he did not know that the bankers objected very much to this. I heard, within a very few days the manager of a bank refer to this taxation as "Fielding's filthy licking stamp tax," and those who have had experience know exactly what that means. We would gladly pay for that irritation, if we could get rid of it. It is all very well if you can indent the stamp on the cheque, but to go through the practice with ten or twenty stamps is very irritating, and I think the Finance Minister, in the kindness of his heart, should relieve us of it.
I have another objection. There are many bills that have to be paid by a certain date. In the city we have the taxes, the water rates, and the gas bills to pay; and the merchants at times avail themselves of discounts if they can pay before a certain date. At least three instances have come under my notice where a very considerable sum was lost by reason of the fact that after office hours, and after the banks were closed and stamps were not available at the post office, the cheques could not be sent out. A direct loss resulted on account of the parties not having sufficient stamps. You cannot tell what provision to make in a case of this kind, and the result is that the irritation is repeated. Loss results, and the whole thing is so unpopular that I submit, in the interests of the country, of business, and of the Fi-
Ways and Means

nance Minister's immortality, this tax should be removed.

I would like to ask the hon. mover of the amendment if he is really accomplishing the purpose he seeks to accomplish by it. Suppose, for instance, the amendment were given effect to, and a man wanted to issue a cheque for $2,500; at the present time he would be called upon to pay $1. If the amendment were in effect all he would have to do would be to issue five cheques of $500 each, and he would be called upon to pay a tax of 10 cents. It seems to me the amendment is not effective for the purpose the hon. member has in view.

The hon. member has not caught the idea of the amendment, which was, in the first instance to help the man who I thought required assistance in this country-the man who was issuing small cheques. I wanted to keep the tax down to 2 cents. I think $500 would fairly cover all these small cheques. In the second instance, from the other end, the absurdity of this graduated tax on cheques is abundantly shown. Of course, it is all right to show the absurdity at the other end, just as was shown by the hon. member for Kinders-ley (Mr. Carmichael) a moment or two ago -quite all right to show that the $10,000 cheque in the one instance pays $1 and the $10,000 cheque in the other instance pays $8. It is all right to show the anomaly there. Of course, you show the anomaly when you pay it at the other end just the same, but that is no answer to it. The answer is that there ought not to be a graduated tax on cheques, and if you are going to get away from the graduated tax on the small cheque, there is no other way of doing it.
Amendment (Sir Henry Drayton) negatived.
I should like to say, in prefacing the amendment which I intend to move, that the remark has been made tonight that this is a very unpopular tax. I suppose all taxes are unpopular.
This is the most.
Perhaps it is; but I can recollect for fifty years back seeing stamps on cheques and receipts. That has been an old-established custom in Great Britain for many years.
One stamp only.

I cannot remember; I cannot go back and make any statement as to the amount; but as long as I remember I have seen stamps on receipts and cheques. I move, however, in amendment:

That the words "reduced to" in the fifth line of clause 1 be struck out, and the words "two dollars" be substituted for the word "one dollar" cn the same line.
That is putting the maximum tax back to two dollars as it was before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I suggest to my hon. friend that while he can move a reduction in the tax, I do not think he can move to increase it. He is supposed to be in favour of reducing taxation, not in favour of increasing it.

I suggest to the minister
that he accept the proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You can take almost
any item of our system of taxation and show that it is very unpopular. My hon. friend is right: all taxation is unpopular. Please keep this in mind: We need the money, and if you are going to reduce the revenue from this source, you may have to find it somewhere else. We cannot afford to give up any considerable revenue A this kind, and I am bound to say from all the information I have-
This will produce more money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think not in this case. I think not. There are cases where reduced taxes will produce more money-my hon. friend is right at times-but I think in this case it would not. I think the proposal to reduce the tax to one dollar is a reasonable one, and I earnestly ask the committee to consider the matter and to accept these changes.
Dp I understand the minister to say that he thought reducing the maximum to one dollar would bring in as much as if it were two dollars?

That might
very well happen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The point I raised was that the hon. member (Mr. Forke) could not move to increase the tax. I think it is possible the maximum of one dollar may produce as much money as the two dollars. There are cases where reduction of taxation brings in more money. On the merits of it, however, as a fair tax, I think one dollar is a very moderate charge to make, and I might reasonably ask the committee to stand by it.

I wish the minister
would have that view with regard to the tariff.

The minister
wants more revenue. A ruling has been given in connection with receipts. We are not chang-

Ways and Means
ing receipts at all now apparently, and I suppose this is the best place to refer to it. More money is required and there has been a ruling in connection with receipts, in connection with certain forms of letters, forms of printed letters and the like, postcards, which obviates the necessity of paying a tax on the receipts, on the idea that the same instrument has already paid a tax. If my hon. friend wants more money, that is one thing he might consider.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That will be considered.

Another thing that the minister might consider is this: The receipt stamp, having regard to cheques, is disappearing entirely. My hon. friend is really losing money in connection with his receipts. This is a form of cheque which is now used by railway companies. The face of the cheque reads:
In full payment for services rendered during the month of....
The endorsement reads:
This cheque is accepted by me in full payment and satisfaction of all claims for services rendered as specified in the body of the cheque. I also hereby acknowledge to have received the amount this cheque calls for.
According to the ruling of the department, there is no stamp attached to that.
There is to the cheque. The same ruling applies.

Owing to the ruling of the department, no stamp whatever is attached to the receipt, because the department rules that the instrument, that is the cheque, has been stamped. The instrument has never been stamped at all. The cheque is one thing and the receipt is another. If we are really going to have fairness in connection with the enforcement of the law as regards receipts, we must see that this is not merely an endorsement of the cheque for the purpose of drawing the money. It reads in so many words that it is an acceptance-
In full payment for services rendered during the month of. ... I also hereby acknowledge to have received the amount this cheque calls for.
There are some 300,000 of those cheques issued monthly in Canada with those receipts which under the ruling of the department, have not to be stamped. But there is another thing my hon. friend will find is going on throughout the country. I am reading the form now from a sample invoice. There is a new way of getting out invoices that are perforated at the top. The customer is asked'
Kindly return this part of the statement with your cheque.
That is just the top part of the invoice. You retain the invoice which shows you what you have. At the bottom of the invoice is printed:
An endorsement of cheque is your receipt. No other acknowledgment will be forwarded unless specially requested.
So you have to send a special letter now in many cases if you want a receipt. The whole fact of the matter is that, under the present rule the department is losing money on its receipt law and regulations. Why, instead of getting answers now, you do not get any answers at all. You send a cheque with a bill and you do not get any reply. The government loses the two cents which it would get for the postage, or if the letter is sent out of town, three cents, and it is not getting the additional two cents. It is plainly printed upon the top of the statement:
Kindly return this part of the statement with your cheque.
Under the statement is printed:
An endorsement of your cheque is your receipt. No other acknowledgment will be forwarded unless specially requested.
I am afraid this is only another way of annoying the public without raising revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend imagines that you can put on the statute books any law that somebody cannot evade for a time, I have no such confidence. Every law is evaded for a while until, in the light of experience, you can meet the difficulty, and this is not the exception. I am not astonished to find that some people are evading this law. We shall be glad to be able to deal with those cases. The mere fact of an evasion of the law is not proof that a law is wrong.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
A point of order is raised by the Minister of Finance. I quote from May 12th edition, at page 462:
The principle that the sanction of the Crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, apiplies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue. .
The footnote, No. 5, states:
When it appeared from the debate that an amendment proposed to a resolution reported from the Committee of Ways and Means would increase the charge, the Speaker ruled the amendment out of order.
As this amendment is to increase the charge, I rule that it is not in order.

I would suggest the following amendment which I think would be in order:
Strike out the words "reduced to one" in the fifth line and insert the word "two", and add at the end of the line "and the minimum amount to be two cents on one hundred dollars."
Ways and Means

The effect of that will be to reduce the revenue sufficiently to bring the amendment in order, and yet it will make no substantial reduction. The smaller cheques would pay only two cents on $100, and on the larger ones the maximum would be $2 as it is at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the same thing in another form.

It cannot be
the same thing in another form, because one does one thing and another something else. The one is objected to because it raises revenue, but this is a reduction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendment proposes to strike out the words "reduce to one" in the fifth line, and to add at the end of the line the words "the minimum amount be two cents on $100."

I do not think you have
quite correctly read the amendment, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps my writing is not as good as it might be. The amendment proposes to strike out the words "reduce to one," and insert the word "two" in the fifth line, and to insert at the end of the line the words "and the minimum amount shall be two cents on one hundred dollars." The effect is very simple. You san isisue a cheque for any amount up to $100 for two cents, and above that the present law would operate, of two cents for every $50; and when it came to large sums the maximum, as at present, would be $2 instead of $1. The general effect would be to ease the tax on the small amounts, and to keep it as before on the large amounts; but in the total the reduction would be very little.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member proposes to make $2 the maximum.

That is only a part of the
amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But that part I have
correctly stated.
That is only half of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It therefore does increase the taxation-from one to two dollars.

But the amendment should
be taken in its entirety.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely.

I want to raise a point of order myself. I think we are all under a misapprehension. This does not come into effect until the first of August, so that it is not yet within the inhibition of the ruling. We are not raising the tax; we are simply keeping it as it is to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The ruling applies to
the papers before us.

I think not; I think we are ruling on the effect of the papers before us, and the basis of the ruling is that if the motion were given effect to we should be adding to the rate of taxation, which we are not doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the first place, the
first of August clause is not yet adopted; but I do not dwell on that point. The question is as between the motion that is placed before the Chairman and the amendment and there can be no doubt about the effect of the amendment.

I rather think that the
question must be decided by the burden to be imposed on the people. The proposal would be all right so long as it did not increase the burden on the subject, and that theory must be borne out by the authorities. I invite the committee to consider the point, because otherwise we are reduced to a state of abject helplessness.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the point is
debated any further, I desire to cite May for the information of the committee. At page 462 there appears the following:
The principle that the sanction of the Crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, applies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue. No motion can therefore be made to impose a tax, save by a minister of the Crown, unless such tax be in substitution, by way of equivalent, for taxation at that moment submitted to the consideration of parliament, nor can the amount of a tax proposed on behalf of the Crown be augmented, nor any alteration made in the area of imposition.
On the same page there is a quotation from the House of Commons Debates of the British parliament. I shall read it:
Thus on the 12th April, 1916, the Chairman, in allowing an amendement to be moved in committee on the Finance (New Duties) Bill with the object of altering the method of levying a new tax, insisted that the amendment should be so framed as not to increase the charge that would be imposed on any individual payer of the tax
When it appeared from the debate that an amendment proposed to a resolution reported from the Committee of Ways and Means would increase the charge, the Speaker ruled the amendment out of order.
The question arises whether the amendment now before the Chair would increase the taxation on any individual taxpayer, or would alter the area of imposition.

Does it not
rather turn on the question as to whether or not the increase has reference to a tax that is now existing and not to any charge proposed to be made effective?

Ways and Means

May includes taxation
proposed.
I think the rule has reference to new taxation rather than old.
The quotation which the Chairman read from May refers to proposed taxation, which is the present case.
No, to taxation in existence.
We are not discussing taxation now levied, we are discussing proposed taxation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Let me just quote again the last words of the authority I cited:
Nor can the amount of a tax proposed on behalf of the Crown be augmented, nor any alteration made in the area of imposition.
That clearly refers to proposed taxation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must rule that the amendment would in effect augment taxation and alter the area of imposition. It would increase the taxation on some individual taxpayer, and I must therefore rule it out of older.

If I may be allowed to add to what I have already said, Mr. Chairman, I may point out that while the amendment will increase taxation on some individuals, we must remember that although in the maximum he would pay a little more he will get the benefit of the minimum provision, so that what he loses at one end he will gain at the other. As regards the area of imposition, the amendment proposes no change whatever. If I were suggesting the infliction of a tax on a man who owns a motor car that would be changing the area of taxation, but it cannot for a moment be considered that you are changing the area of imposition in this case because it is confined strictly to the original class of taxpayers affected namely, those who issue cheques. I therefore do not see how the amendment can be ruled ont of order on that ground; and as I have already indicated, the taxpayer ultimately will not have to pay any more, but rather less.
It affects the individual taxpayer so far as the amount is concerned, because it increases the maximum from one to two.

In an individual instance, yes. But I maintain, and I think it will be admitted by everyone, that while the taxpayer may pay a little more at one end he will in the long run gain what he lost in that direction. because of the saving in regard to the
lcwer amounts. The general result must be to reduce taxation to the individual. I submit that the amendment must be taken as a whole. You cannot discuss one section of it for the purposes of one line of argument, and then take another part of it for some other argument. That is not logical. I say that the amendment in the end reduces taxation instead of increasing it, and that I am sure is t? e spirit of May's ruling. I would point out, however, that while this is a comparatively trivial matter, it is a matter of great importance so far as the ruling is concerned, because that ruling will govern the House in years to come.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No man can possibly tell Ikw much the individual will gain at one end and lose at the other. You must deal with the individual case, and in the individual case there is to be increased taxation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must rule upon the authorities which I have cited to the committee in the discussion of this point of order that this does increase the charge which would be imposed on any individual payer of the tax, and that on the other hand there is an alteration in the area of imposition that is being placed upon a certain class of individuals who fall within this rule; therefore I declare the amendment moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is out of order.
Amendment (Mr. Fielding) agreed to.
Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move resolution No. 2, Mr. Chairman, on the same page:
2. That after a date to be fixed by proclamation of the Governor in Council the excise tax on wines of all kinds, excqpt sparkling wines, containing not more than forty per centum of proof spirit be reduced to seven and one-half cents per gallon, and the excise tax on champagne and all other sparkling wines be reduced to one dollar and fifty cents per gallon.

I really think my hon. friend must feel it is very unkind that this resolution is printed right after the resolution dealing with the stamp duty on cheques. There was only one argument why people should pay the tax-that the minister wants the money. Then in the very next resolution, which is now before us, he is cutting in two the taxes on champagne and sparkling wines. I am afraid my hon. friend is not consistent. We all know why. We all know the mess he has got into by reason of the French treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the unkindest cut of all. Hon. members on my friend's
Ways and Means

side complained of the advantage given French wines under the French treaty, and we at once stated we would deal with native wines if they would wait patiently. Now we are dealing fairly and equitably with these my hon. friend is unhappy.
Not at all. I think it is the inevitable result of the French treaty.
What was the tax before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Thirty cents and three dollars.
This is an instance where by reducing the duty it is expected people will drink more wine and consequently there will be a greater revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is in order to place native wines in an equitable position with respect to French wines.
Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The next resolution deals with the sales tax. I do not want to go on with it to-night. I propose to proceed with No. 4 in the latter part of the resolutions.
I move:
That Schedule 1 to the said act be amended by striking thereout the items respecting confectionery and beverages.
That is one of the items announced in the budget speech and fully discussed some time ago.
Shall the resolution carry ?

Yes, resolutions 4, 5, 6 and 7:
4.	That Schedule I to the said act be amended by striking thereout the items respecting confectionery and beverages.
5.	That Schedule II to the said act be amended by striking thereout the item respecting beverages and by adding to the said schedule the following item:
"Carbonic acid gas in cylinders, per pound. . . . one cent."
6.	That the provisions of the said act respecting stamp tax on receipts be amended by providing:
(i)	That paragraph (b) of subsection four of section fourteen of the said Act as enacted by said chapter forty-seven be amended to read as follows: "(b) a receipt or document in the nature of a receipt which is taxable under section twelve of this act."
(ii)	By adding provisions for the better enforcement of said section fourteen.
7.	That the provisions of this resolution, except the provision proposed by section two, shall come into force on the first day of August, 1923.
Resolutions agreed to.

subtopic: USE OF POSTAGE STAMPS FOR INLAND REVENUE TAXES

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: USE OF POSTAGE STAMPS FOR INLAND REVENUE TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I mentioned it was proposed to provide that hereafter postage stamps should not be used for inland revenue purposes. The resolution I beg to move on that subject is as follows:
That the resolution respecting the amendment to the special War Revenue Act be amended by adding thereto the provision, that subsection 3 of section 19 of the said act, which provides that postage stamps may be used in lieu of stamps specially prepared in fulfilment of any requirement under part 3, be repealed, and that any enactment founded on this provision shall come into force on the 1st day of October 1923.
The effect of that will be that on and after the 1st October postage stamps will no longer be used, and inland revenue stamps will be required for inland revenue purposes.
Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Take No. 3, Sir, on the order with regard to sales tax. The substance of this is that instead of the varying rates hitherto imposed we are to impose practically a general rate of 6 per cent. That is the principle involved. The machinery by which it is to be carried out is set forth in the resolution and is not free from difficulty, but we think we have got it in fairly good shape.
I understood my hon. friend did not want to take up the sales tax resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I laid it aside for the moment, I had other things before me.

I am afraid
some of the members have left the chamber.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend wishes that it be postponed, I will agree.

Personally I
do not wish to postpone it, but some of the members have left. However, I do not suppose we could finish it to-night anyway. There is a lot yet to understand in connection with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In that case we had
better postpone it.
Resolution stands.
Progress reported.

The House again in committee of Supply, Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure) in the chair.
Dominion Lands and Parks-Canadian National Parks and Historic sites, $1,250,980.

Supply-Interior-Parks

Has the department come
to any conclusion in connection wi.h the matter of the granting of additional power privileges to the Calgary Power Company in the national park at Banff?

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argen-teuil, Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A good
many representations have been made against the granting of the application, but so far no conclusion has been reached by the department. I do not intend to move in the matter until I have visited the park during this summer, particularly the Spray lake3, which it is alleged, would be affected by the granting of the application.

What is the policy of the
department, either past or present, with regard to applications for power privileges in the national parks?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The present government have not adopted any definite policy. An application was granted on lake Minnewanka in the Banff national park to the company making the application in the present case. I would not like to admit that that was establishing a precedent; however, it will have to be definitely settled whether applications of this kind are to be granted, at least on certain areas that are of considerable importance. I may say that applications have been made, though not actively pressed, for the raising of the levels of Waterton lake for the purpose of irrigation in southern Alberta. Of course that is a question in which the United States government would be interested.

I may inform the minister
that I have been receiving telegrams from the West protesting against the granting of any further power privileges in these parks. It seems to be a very lively question in the prairie provinces. I simply call attention to that fact.

The public parks of
Canada have been set apart for the use of the Canadian people. I would like to ask the minister whether he thinks it is within the power of the government to grant such privileges on these areas.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, it is
within the power of the department to do so. We have a bill on the order paper which would put under the control of parliament water-powers as well as other privileges In areas set aside for park purposes, but I may not press that bill. My own inclination is in the direction of reserving these areas purely for the purposes for which they were set aside. But to lay down the hard and fast rule
that in none of these areas-and there are immense areas set aside for park purposes in the Rocky mountains-should any power privileges be given, would perhaps be going quite a long way.

I do not know just what is the minister's mind in the matter, but if I could judge from his last sentence or so, I do not think I am very far removed from him in opinion. I have read some editorial references to the application of some Calgary power company for power privileges on the Spray lakes in Rocky mountains park, or, as it is now called, Banff national park. These references are wholly antagonistic and seem to be based on the supposed principle that when a park is established as such, no use must be made of any of its resources. The point raised by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner) seems to rest on the same assumption, that is to say that since the parks are for the whole people of Canada, no use should be made of the resources therein for any practical purposes. I must support the minister when he intimates that it would be utterly impossible to follow that principle. Why, we do not follow it anywhere in Canada. I am not saying a word on behalf of this particular application. I have had no communication whatever from the company directly or indirectly. I do not know whether its application has the least merit or whether it has not; it may be quite the right thing to refuse it. But to lay down as a general principle that because a power is in a park it is sacrosanct and cannot be made use of seems to me absurd. It is a wholly wrong conception that the use of the power of a water is any less for the public than the leaving of it in nature's state that the public may look at it. I would be very sorry to see anything done in the Banff park that would seriously interfere with its value for scenic purposes or its value as a park, and it might be that no substantial use could be made of that power without such interference with its scenic value as would by no means be compensated for by the use of the water for that purpose. At the same time I would think it should not be impossible to provide by regulation for such construction as would not interfere with its value for scenic purposes, but might indeed improve it. It might not be impossible. If it is not, then unless the power is absolutely essential for public use I would not spoil the park for the power. But what I object to is this general assumption that because we have laid aside certain areas and established there parks we must shut out the hand of man and say: Here you may starve for power, industry

Supply-Interior-Parks
may be utterly without the means of sustenance, the public outside may simply be hanged, we have got to keep this thing a thing of beauty. Why, if that were done at Niagara Falls where would we be to-day?
I do not think there is any general assumption along that line.

Every argument I have seen is based on that. It is not for the sake of a company that the power right is granted. It is because the public need the power. The company has no more claim than any number of people. It has just the same, but it has no more. I have seen articles in American and Canadian magazines about the profanity, the blasphemy of harnessing Niagara Falls and thereby diminishing the flow of water down this great cataclysm of nature. Well, I consider that rubbish. Imagine the people of Ontario to-day with their own backs and hands doing the work that the falls of Niagara are doing, in order that wedding couples could see more water falling over the topi That seems to me ridiculous, and the same is true of Banff national park. I hope the minister will take the greatest care that no matter ior what purpose no great substantial injury is done to the scenic beauty of the park-I would not say no matter for what purpose, for if the purpose be great enough I would spoil the whole scenic beauty, but no purpose is great enough to warrant that. I hope every reasonable precaution will be taken to preserve the beauty of the park, but at the same time I hope solid common sense will be used and that especially in those parts of Canada where power is very scarce no rigid rule will be adopted that will shut out the utilization of power merely because it is in a park. That is all I wish to say about it. I repeat what I said at first, I have had no communication from anybody on this subject. I have not the faintest knowledge as to who the company is, but I must say that the appeals I read in the press made a very weak impression on my mind.
I would just like to suggest to the minister that the utilization of these powers be not so much for the benefit of a company but for the use of the people in any case where they are granted.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That goes without saying. I may say in fairness to my predecessors that without adding a single additional provision for safeguarding the public interest, that has been very well taken care of so far as granting water power privileges are concerned.

There seems to be a misconception about the application of the Calgary Power Company. I am speaking neither for nor against them. I am in a different position, having to make a decision, because I have in my department the Water Powers branch, who look at this matter from the standpoint of power, the standpoint which has just been enunciated by my hon. friend, that is, the advantage of having cheap power for the development of industry, and on the other hand I have also in my department the 11 p.m. Parks branch, whose business it is to preserve the scenic beauty of our parks for tourist purposes and as a playground for the people of Canada, and the views of the two branches are widely at variance on this question. The Parks Commissioner takes the ground that we should close the parks absolutely so far as water-powers are concerned. Now I frankly admit I have an open mind on this question. I am keen on scenic beauty, so much so that last summer when this question was very much to the fore I refused the application of the Calgary Power Company to further raise the level of lake Minnewanka. Anybody who has been at Banff knows that lake Minnewanka is within a few miles of the centre of the attractive portion of the park. The Calgary Power Company already have a concession on that lake, and they have increased the lake level, and their application last year was for the purpose of raising it by another ten or fifteen feet. After looking it over I came to the conclusion that it would absolutely destroy the scenic properties of that particular lake. It was very close to where all sightseers of the park come, and obviously if we are to get any return for our investment in our national parks we must keep them attractive enough to draw tourists, and on these grounds I refused the application of the company. They subsequently made application for the Spray lakes. I have not seen them. They are on the other side of the town of Banff. I am not an engineer and cannot tell from a study of the maps just what the effect of raising the level of the Spray lakes would be. However, it is rather an expensive undertaking, and in fact would cost a great deal more than the company would feel warranted in expending at the moment in view of the amount of power they could sell. I think my hon. friend from Calgary is well posted on this question. He represents the city that is most vitally interested, and I believe that the city is somewhat opposed to the granting of the application. I have a perfectly open mind on the question. I want to know what effect it would have on the scenic properties of the park and how it

Supply-Interior-Parks
would affect the river flowing out of the town, because if they draw off a tremendous quantity of water, which they would do in the winter, of necessity the river would be a very small stream for a large portion of the summer while the reservoir was filling up. The reservoir is a huge one, I would gather from a perusal of the maps and plans, but without seeing the actual ground one cannot form a very definite opinion about the matter.
I agree with my hon. friend absolutely that to say that the water-powers of the park shall not be used to serve say that huge area including all the Rocky mountains might be going very far, but on the other hand care should be taken to preserve the scenic beauties of the park. All reasonable precautions should be taken not to impair the scenic properties of our parks, which not only attract tourists but serve as a playground for our own people.

The increase in this item is really alarming, and I cannot see why it is consented to in silence by hon. gentlemen who denounced the voting of about two-thirds of this amount a short time ago. There has been an increase of I think about 20 per cent in two years. What is being done with the money? Where is the tremendous increase going? I have as high an appreciation of the value of our parks as anybody, I think. In fact, I conducted a pretty difficult battle on their behalf against the silent witnesses of this vote, but still I want to know what the extra money is going for.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend I think was not in the House the other evening when this item was pretty fully discussed. The item was left over at the request of the ex-Minister of Finance in order that the leader of the Opposition might have an opportunity of discussing it. There is considerable increase in the item. One of the very heavy increases is due to the fa\iu that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which operated the mines in the vicinity of Banff, are closing down the mines, and consequently we are unable to secure the electric light that we formerly got from this plant, and we have to take steps to construct a new electric light plant. That will represent $150,000. And indeed that is not all it represents. I think it represents nearer $200,000. We have not capitalized the charges with respect to the parks. All the expenditure being taken out of ordinary revenue, it comes out of one year's appropriation. The same thing applies in the little town of Canmore, where we had a nearepidemic owing to the unsanitary conditions, and we were forced to take precautions against the conditions there which were very bad.
We are spending $17,500 to better the sanitary conditions this year. Then at Wainwright we have the problem of taking care of more buffalo than the fenced area will maintain. The herd has grown to about
7.000	head. The area is only capable of maintaining 5,000-I think, much more properly, 3,000. But we are forced to reduce the herd, and as the buffalo are somewhat difficult to handle, we will have to spend $13,000 on the construction of a slaughter house to kill a certain proportion of the animals. I mentioned the other night that we had under consideration the advisability of taking some of the younger animals and turning them loose in the north country, with the herd that we now estimate may be about
2.000	or so, that have gone into that country and are established north of the Hay river along the Mackenzie. But unfortunately we have discovered that we have tuberculosis in the herd, and there is some question as to whether we should allow animals from the parks to mingle with those out on the prairie, where they are undoubtedly free from contamination. We require this amount for that purpose. Then at the Lamont park we have under consideration the advisability of fencing in a larger area for the animals that are there, including a small buffalo herd left there, which I believe was the first buffalo herd in the country. That herd has grown to much larger proportions, and we have to take in a larger area, which will cost $24,000. That practically makes the total increase, or nearly all of it. This might in my opinion under other circumstances be charged to capital account, but the parks appropriations have year by year, no matter what the expenditure amounted to, been charged to revenue account and cleared up in the year in which the work is undertaken. It has the advantage that you are not accumulating any capital charges.
Is the minister harnessing the water power to get the electric light?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Calgary Power Company applied for increased storage on lake Minnewanka, and there was a reservation in the agreement with that company that in the event of the government requiring water for the purpose of producing electric light for their own purposes, they were to have it; and we are taking advantage of that reservation.

I am not objecting at all. I was thinking it would be rather inconsistent for us to be harnessing the water and at the same time saying to the public of Canada, "We will not let anybody in

Supply-Interior-Parka
I do not think the right hon. leader of the Opposition is quite correct. I do not think anybody ever said that nobody could get in-not in this House anyway.
I did not say that any one in this House said it. I mentioned the source from which it came.

I see there is an increase in the item for the national parks, and possibly quite rightly too. The minister gave one or two reasons why there was an increase. He said we should reserve all historical sites, and two reasons were given why we should do so. One was to induce tourists from other countries to come to see the beautiful spots of Canada. He went on to say these sites and parks were the playgrounds of Canada. That is the point I wish to attack for the moment. If these sites or parks happen to be the playground of the people of Canada, who are the people that are able ,to look upon them as a playground? At the present time these parks are practically situated in one place in Canada, with the result that there are thousands and thousands of people in Canada who are not able to visit them. As far as Saskatchewan is concerned at the present time, I know of no national park or no national playground that we can visit. Yet we have to help bear the burden. As a large amount of money is being spent almost entirely on one spot, to induce tourists from the United States to come along the national highway which has cost a great deal of money, it seems to me, that certain beauty spots should be placed in other provinces; so that all the people of Canada would have the right to enjoy the national playgrounds, the expense of which they have to bear. Is there any possibility of having a national park somewhere in southern Saskatchewan-not eastern Saskatchewan, around the Assiniboia-but somewhere in the western part of Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was going to remark that I think it would be rather difficult even in Saskatchewan to establish a park much closer to my hon. friend than Banff. I may say to him that some of the visitors to Banff come there in Ford cars. They are provided with camping facilities. I was simply amazed to find how many people camp in that way, and visit in Banff park, at very little expense. We are proposing to do something in southern Saskatchewan, in the constituency of my hon. friend, at Estevan and Vidal, where we are making preparations for a park that will be a playground for the 
people of Saskatchewan, where there is reasonable opportunity for it, and where the cost will be reasonable. We could establish these parks in territory that is not fit for other purposes, and I feel that it would be good business to set aside these areas for this purpose.
I suggest that there is a beautiful spot on the south Saskatchewan river, in the southern part of Saskatchewan.
The minister has mentioned the fact that Ford cars go there. He means that the farmers are taking advantage of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They do not all go in Ford cars.
It would be only the farmers who would go there in Ford cars. I see how it works out all right.
Can the minister give any estimate of the amount Canada derives from the tourist traffic at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be a very difficult estimate to make, but we think that somewhere between fifteen and twenty million dollars is brought into the country in this way. That seems a lot of money but if you go to the Banff hotel and stay there for a day or so, and then go to the other points of interest in Canada and stay for a day or so, perhaps the sum would not seem so extravagant after all.

I do not oppose the granting of money for our national parks, but I would like to point out that it was my privilege to go to the Banff national park a couple of years ago. Before being permitted to enter I was charged, I think, the fee of $1. In view of the fact that we are donating such a large sum of money under this item, I do not know whether it is fair and equitable to impose on Canadians a penalty on entering their own park which is kept up by their own money. I do not see that it would be inequitable to charge American tourists. I am rather of opinion that the charge is just the same for both American and Canadian tourists. In connection with the Banff national park, I should like to know if the money charged at the toll gate on entering that park is sufficient for the upkeep of the park.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. I could say at once, without the question being asked, that it does not begin to keep up the expenditure on the park. I think my hon.

Supply-In terior-Parks
friend would realize, driving over the roads alone, that there is a tremendous expenditure in roads for the benefit of the man who pays that dollar and who takes his car into the park. That is not altogether the idea. The idea is to have a complete record of those who enter the park and a knowledge of where they are, because, while 99 per cent of the people who go into the park are careful, one careless individual or one individual letting fire loose can do a tremendous amount of damage. It must be remembered that we must guard pretty carefully, not so much the people, as the park itself, to prevent, for instance, fire from spreading Then there is the possibility of people in the park destroying animals in an endeavour to get souvenirs in the way of game heads and that sort of thing. All that work is expensive, but still it must be done. My hon. friend will realize that it is an excellent thing for the visitors to see the mountain sheep which are tame and which come down to the roads. That could not be accomplished unless we looked after the visitors fairly carefully. Perhaps 99 per cent of the visitors do not need super- * vision, but some create trouble for us.
Is it not a fact that the amount levied is the same for American as for Canadian tourists?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

In the opinion of the minister, would it not be wise that a distinction should be made, a smaller charge being imposed on the Canadian tourist and a larger one on the American, who contributes nothing for the upkeep of the park?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I must confess that I have paid the charge on entering the park, and I never thought it was extravagant. It is $1 for your car. You have a week.
Perhaps it is not extravagant for the Canadian, but for the American it should be relatively more.

The minister a few moments ago stated that it was estimated that the tourist traffic coming into Canada was worth in the neighbourhood of from fifteen to twenty million dollars. A few minutes ago we heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) say that it was very difficult to raise money.
