In view of the
memorial that I understand has just been received by the government from the Local Council, the Territorial Council of Yukon, for an increase in the membership of the council anc an increase in the indemnity, what policy has the government decided upon in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is a matter that we have discussed in council in respect to both the memorial received and the representations made by my hon. friend. It is felt that there are two requests, the request that the indemnity be increased, and the request that the membership be increased in view of the Mayo silver strike. While the population of the Yukon is not decreasing, I think within the last couple of years we cannot discover that there has been a very marked increase. For that reason it will appear that they have ample representation in the three members. Perhaps in the location of territory there might be some change, but it would not appear to be advisable to increase the number.
As regards the indemnity, I have some sympathy with the request. Nevertheless, during
Supply-Interior

all these years they have got along with this amount, and with a population not much more than that of a small-sized city, it would not appear that we would be warranted at the moment in increasing the amount. If the population should increase, then in all probability there would be something to be said in favour of increasing the indemnity.

Since the last census returns were made, the population of the Yukon has materially increased owing to the discovery of silver ore in large quantities in that territory. A very important silver mining camp has been established and will continue to grow. I have not the slightest doubt about that. An area which was practically unpopulated before except for a few explorers, is now becoming populated. Towns are being established there and permanent settlement is taking place. That part of the territory is entirely isolated from the older and more settled portions. The constitution of the Territorial Council at the present time is practically that of the legislatures of the provinces. The Territorial Council has the same power to legislate as provincial legislative assemblies have. The suggestion was that the membership of the council, which is now three, the members being elected from the city of Dawson and the town of Whitehorse and one member representing the mining community, be increased to four, and this new mining district be given a member. The indemnity is now the small sum of $400 a year. It was reduced to that sum only in the year 1918 when the late government in a burst of economy picked on that item for purposes of reduction, although they might have saved hundreds of thousands of dollars more properly in other directions. The reduction in ihis respect was entirely improper and was made without reference to any one in touch with rhe facts. It was done blindly and the matter should now be remedied. I would ask the minister to take it into consideration, with a view to making a grant in the Supplementary Estimates for the purpose.
What was the indemnity previously?

At the time of the reduction it was $600 per annum, and some years before that, $1,000. I am sure that in view of the cost of transportation, living and other expenses in that country this is not an extravagant sum.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As in the case of Banff, we are faced with a difficult proposition to give an adequate service over a very wide area. We have not a telegraph service in the Department of Interior; the service is under the Public Works department and has been rather expensive. We propose this year to substitute a radio service in the north country, putting in a station at McMurray, one at Fort Simpson and another at Dawson, which will enable us to dispense with a very expensive line service running into the Dawson territory, and as well a telegraph service reaching from McMurray northward. That will cost $55,000. It seems a fairly large amount, but fully half of it is expended in the Public Works department on repairs of lines that now give a very indifferent service and which we shall be able to do without. Then we have the expedition to the northeastern shores of Canada, to those islands in the northern sea, where we have to establish ourselves. We [DOT] sent an expedition last year for which we voted the sum of $45,000, but we found this totally inadequate end had to supplement it by a grant which will come up in the Sup-plementaries for discussion. We are asking this year for an increase over the $45,000 voted last year of $35,000. We have an old ship belonging to the Marine department, known as the Arctic, which has made several voyages into the northern sea. It is now becoming obsolete; it is very slow and is costly to operate, and it is dangerous to send into these northern seas a ship of this kind, owing to its age. However, we are sending her this year to establish a post at Cape Sabine just off the shores of Greenland, which residents of Greenland cross to Melville sound. More particularly are we anxious to establish this post because Captain McMillan proposes wintering there with an American expedition. It will be recalled that Captain Peary wintered there on one of his expeditions, and we are somewhat fearful of claims being set up to these northern islands. We are desirous of establishing a police force there to maintain sovereignty and hold the islands for Canada. It may be said that they are

Supply-Interior
not very valuable, but there is evidence of very extensive mineral deposits on the islands, and in future they may become of great value. For that reason we are asking for an increase of $35,000 to send the Arctic back into the north. Further, we have purchased from the British Admiralty a steel vessel that has a speed three times as great as that of the Arctic. That ship will be sent there annually for the purpose of relieving the mounted police force and taking in food. We thought we could put it into commission this year but that is not practicable. It was built in 1920, and is of the trawler type, with a speed of 12 knots and a large capacity for fuel. It was not built for northern waters, and will have to be reinforced in the hull.
Why not take one of the Merchant Marine boats?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We had every one of them thoroughly examined, but none of them could be converted for the purpose. Besides, they are slow sailers and speed in this matter is an important factor. This ship cost the British Admiralty $200,000 to construct. We purchased it for $55,000, and it will cost in the neighbourhood of $25,000 to reinforce the hull, but we shall have an admirable ship for the purpose for which it is required.
Where is the rest of the purchase money?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I shall have to ask for a further sum in the Supple-mentaries in addition to the $40,000.

I just want to say a few words by way of comparison of this service, which it is intended by this expenditure to inaugurate in the north country, with the present service and also as to how the cost of the present service has been distributed, and may be materially reduced. I was glad to hear the minister indicate a reduction in connection with the item. I understand it is intended to erect a wireless station at Fort McMurray, one at Fort Simpson, and one at Dawson in Yukon. This item should to a large extent take the place of item 360 under Public Works, to be found at page 62 of the Estimates, which shows a vote of $277,000 for the Yukon telegraphic system. This item, ranging from $275,000 to $300,000, has appeared in the Estimates each year for the past twenty-three years. It has been a hardy annual, and while it is perfectly right that we should pass it this year, I think this should be positively its last appearance. The cost of the administration of
government of Yukon would be substantial, if only the amounts legitimately chargeable were included, but when very large items that should be charged elsewhere are charged to Yukon the apparent cost of administration of that territory is much greater than the actual cost.
The establishment and maintenance of the Yukon telegraph line has been a great boon to the people of that country. They are isolated as it is, but without the telegraph lines, particularly in winter, they would be cut off from the world. The line is often put out of business by storms in winter and by forest fires in summer, but it has always been patched up again and communication ultimately restored.
Probably nowhere is a daily telegraphic news service so much appreciated as in Yukon. Notwithstanding the period of contraction the Yukon has passed through, the enterprise and initiative of the proprietors and publishers of the daily paper at Dawson, the Daily News has always been such since the very early days of the gold rush that that paper has never missed an issue on a working day, in addition to which they have frequently published very creditable special editions, expending money very generously to give the public an admirable news service, because you cannot get telegraphic news up there without spending money. The people are solely dependent on that line and the paper to keep them in touch with the events of the day. In winter it takes over a month to get a letter to Dawson from eastern Canada. So the House will realize how important this line is not only for news service but for all business purposes.
The line has always cost a lot of money- much more than it should have cost. It was built on a most improvident and extravagant scale in 1900-twenty-three years ago- and it has been most expensively maintained ever since, but there is no longer any excuse for this service costing the country approximately $300,000 a year. There has been little excuse for the expenditure ever since wireless telegraphy came into practical use. What has been done by this vote to-night should have been done ten years ago. I will point out how a very great saving can be effected annually in connection with this northern telegraph line without impairing the service. In fact my suggestions will, in addition to saving about a quarter of a million dollars a year, materially improve the service.
I am going to give the House a few figures which I think will be interesting, though sometimes figures are not. My authority for these figures is the Auditor General's report
Supply-Interior

for the year ending March 31st, 1922-the latest report available-and Hansard of this year containing answers to questions as to the expense of the line. In that connection I would point out to the House and to the government not only the unfairness but, I think, the incorrectness of the government's method of keeping its accounts in connection with this very large expenditure. My attention was drawn to this apparent error in book-keeping by the answers given by the government last session to questions asked by the present Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) as to the costs of administration of Yukon. The amounts stated were astonishing, and I have taken the trouble to examine and analyze the figures. In the first place let us consider the mileage on the land line. The main line in the Yukon territory is 511 miles in length, the branch lines 60 miles, making a total mileage of 571 miles; whereas the main line in British Columbia is 1,226 miles and the branch lines 1,491Y miles, or a total of 2,717| miles in British Columbia, which with the 571 miles in the Yukon territory gives a total of 3,288{ miles. So that the actual mileage of the line within the territory is not much more than one-fifth of the total. These branch lines extend between points in British Columbia having nothing whatever to do with the Yukon territory-no more to do with that territory than lines in Nova Scotia, yet the expense of them all is charged up to Yukon. For instance, the lines between Hazleton, Port Simpson and Prince Rupert, and between Williams lake and Quesnel Forks, Quesnel Forks and Barkerville, Williams lake and Bella Coola, have nothing whatever to 'do with Yukon.
The annual cost of maintaining that mile-*age within the Yukon territory for the main dine is $40,599, the cost of maintaing the branch lines is $1,660, or a total of $42,259; whereas the expense of maintaining the British Columbia portion of it is annually for the main line $142,588 and for the branch lines $79,471 or a total of $222,059, making with the $42,259 for Yukon a total for the year ending March 31st, 1922, of $264,318.

Will the hon. member
give us the figures of the revenue received from the lines in the Yukon and in British Columbia respectively?

Yes, I can and will. The total expense for the year ending 31st March 1922 was, as I have said, $264,318. The amount voted for the year ending 31st March. 1923, was $287,900, and the amount voted this year $277,000. I say of those amounts the

proportions fairly chargeable to the Yukon territory are as follows:
Annual cost of maintenance:
Yukon main line	$40,599 83
Yukon branch lines	 1,659 90

And I say one-half of the annual cost of maintaining the main line in British Columbia is properly chargeable to Yukon, or $71,293.90 -in all, $113,553.63 should be charged to Yukon. The amounts fairly chargeable to British Columbia are:
Half cost of maintaining main line in B.C. $71,293 90 Branch lines in B.C	 79,471 76

So that at least $150,765 is annually charged to Yukon that should be charged to British Columbia. This has been going on for over twenty years. As a matter of fact the Dominion government has paid out in that time for British Columbia, and charged to Yukon in connection with the telegraph line, $3,467,509. The same applies to other federal services in Yukon. Take, for instance, the mail service, about a third of the total charged to Yukon should be charged to British Columbia and for international services-in connection with the mail service in the past twenty years they have charged up over a million and a quarter dollars that should not have been charged to Yukon at all.
Another aspect of this overland line is worth considering-that it parallels the Grand Trunk Pacific line in British Columbia, 1591 miles, which stretch costs annually $47,135 to keep up, and has each year since the Grand Trunk Pacific was built-^an absolute waste of money. There has not been the slightest excuse for that expenditure since the Grand Trunk Pacific line was built.
Now, as to revenues. The revenue from the Yukon telegraph system in the year ending 31st March 1922 was $23,279, at a cost of $42,259. That is, it cost almost two dollars for each dollar taken in on Yukon business. The revenue for the British Columbia business was $65,070 at a cost of $222,059. In other words it costs almost four dollars for each dollar taken in on British Columbia business. That is the remarkable state of facts.
But what should be done? I submit that the land line should be abandoned south of the station at Tagish in Yukon and a wireless station established at Whitehorse or Dawson in Yukon territory to connect with Prince Rupert, British Columbia, where they now have a wireless station; or to connect with the wireless at Fort Simpson, Northwest Terri-

Supply-Interior
tories, and McMurray, Alberta, to be established by the vote now before the committee. The land line should be extended to the silver camp at Mayo, Yukon Territory, or a wireless station should be established at this point, thereby at once creating a remunerative system.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are going to bring down an appropriation for that in the Supplementaries this year.

In that connection
I would like to say that I have been making it my business to try to keep track of the government's plans. I have had very cordial co-operation from the officials of the Department of the Interior in the matter of their plans to lessen the cost of this public service.
It is proposed by this vote to establish three stations, at McMurray, Alberta; Simpson, Northwest Territories; and Dawson, Yukon Territory, respectively. In the meantime, in a direct line with these three stations, there has sprung up the mining camp at Mayo, which has no telegraphic communication at all; it is entirely isolated. Upon the matter being taken up with the Department of Public Works the situation so impressed the minister that he decided to put an item in the estimates of this year to extend the land line to the Mayo camp. But when it was found that the Department of the Interior had in view the establishing of these wireless stations, it was decided that a wireless station at Mayo would do all that a land line would do; that it would be less expensive and more efficient. Consequently, as the minister has stated to the committee, a vote is contemplated for the Supplementary Estimates which will also provide for a wireless station at Mayo.
I understand that the establishing of these wireless stations is being undertaken by the Department of National Defence in connection with its army work. That I think is a very fine idea; it is something of use that the Department of National Defence can put its people at. But we all know that in army matters they are supposed to "muddle through." I hope the new Acting Minster of National Defence will be able to inject into that department something like business methods. I have a letter here from the Deputy Minister of the Department of National Defence which would indicate that these business methods have not yet come to pass in that department. The original plan was to build the stations at McMurray, Alberta; Simpson, Northwest Territories; and Dawson, Yukon. Now, the stations at McMurray and Simpson are in the valley
of the Mackenzie river, separated by a great range of mountains from the station at Dawson on the Yukon river; there is no relation between the one and the other.
In conversation with officials of the Department of National Defence I found that their plan was to send one party forward to do this work, commencing at McMurray, journeying thence to Simpson and from there to Dawson. That trip would take two or three years. They could not possibly go across that chain of mountains and take their equipment. They might perhaps leave their bones on the way. This was their plan of procedure, instead of going about it in a businesslike way and sending two parties at the same time, one into the Mackenzie valley and the other up to Dawson and the Yukon, where they could put up their stations at Dawson and Mayo as separate enterprises. And now the Deputy Minister of National Defence informs me in his communication that, apparently, the department has undertaken more than it can do this season; that they will not be able to put in the four stations, and as the scheme first evolved was to put in the McMurray and Simpson stations this year they feel that they will have to proceed with those and let the stations in the Yukon valley, Dawson and Mayo, go until some other time. In other words, they are putting the cart before the horse, starting in the usual army method to "muddle through." I do hope that the Minister of the Interior will have sufficient influence with the Department of National Defence to have the matter reconsidered and that if any of the stations are to be dropped for this year, which I hope will not be the case, those in the Mackenzie valley will be dropped, because except as connecting stations for the purposes of the business originating at Dawson and Mayo, where the people are and where the business is transacted, these other stations are of no use at all. If they have no connections with these other points, Dawson and Mayo, there will be no business for them. Of course, the few people at McMurray and Simpson might listen to radio concerts from Edmonton, Calgary and Winnipeg, but from a business standpoint, from the point of view of the public service, thos'e stations would be utterly useless. So I trust that the Minister of the Interior will endeavour to induce these army people to commence at the right end of the job.
Now by this establishment of wireless the government will get an increased revenue and will actually save very large sums of money. In the first place, they will cut off from the annual expense of maintaining that land line
Supply-Interior

no less a sum than $222,000, and the annual cost, instead of $264,000 as it was for the year ending March 31, 1922, will be approximately as follows: Cost of maintaining land line within Yukon as at present, $42,259; cost of extending land line to Mayo, or to establish a wireless there, and wireless at Dawson or Whitehorse, say, $50,000-which is a very liberal estimate-making a total of $92,259 instead of $264,319. There will be a saving of not less than $172,000 for the first year, allowing for construction. The annual expenditures thereafter will be approximately as follows: cost of maintaining land line in Yukon, $42,259; cost of maintaining land line to Mayo or wireless there and wireless at Whitehorse or Dawson, say $20,000 or a total of $64,259 per annum instead of $264,000, a saving of $200,000 a year, with a more efficient service and greater revenue. If we vote thi3 item of $55,000 and about $20,000 in the Supplementary Estimates to cover the cost of constructing the wireless station required at Mayo, during the ensuing years we will save about a quarter of a million dollars annually, and at the same time give a better service. I say this is too important a matter to be overlooked by the government. No question of politics intervenes to embarrass the government or hamper efficiency; it is a plain business proposition, an opportunity to save annually a quarter of a million dollars of public money. I submit that the suggestion is a very practical one; I doubt if the government has received a suggestion much more in the public interest in the course of considering supply this session. I would also like to impress on the government the importance of that inaccuracy or error in book-keeping and that by a more equitable distribution of the expenses of administration the real cost of administering that territory should appear in the public accounts. The impression has been created, and not without cause, that the administration of Yukon has cost a great deal. But there has been a big revenue from that territory, and having regard to the amounts of the annual grants to the provinces, I do not think that when the items are properly adjusted the cost of administration of Yukon will be found to be so very extravagant after all.

I would just like to say a word in reply to my hon. friend in reference to the construction of the wireless telegraph stations. I thoroughly agree with him. Our understanding was and is that all three stations would be constructed. Indeed, pressure was brought to bear upon us

My hon. friend can rest assured that anything I can do towards pressing for completion of the stations will be done.

I omitted to say that on speaking to the Acting Minister of National Defence this evening and calling his attention to the rather unbusinesslike proposal of his department he assured me he would look into the matter at once and endeavour to co-operate with the Department of the Interior.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All I can say in reply is that certain commitments were made in respect to this exhibition when it was discussed in its initial stages, I can say frankly that, it is a very heavy expenditure at this particular time, and it is questionable whether we should continue to participate in exhibitions of this character, but we found ourselves committed to this exhibition, and we found that the other overseas dominions were making heavy expenditures in connection with it. If we go into it, it appears to me we ought do so in a way commensurate with our standing as a dominion, or keep out of it. I do not believe we would be warranted in remaining out.

I do not think the hon. member is right if he looks upon this as a legacy. I think it is his own child, but it is probably the best child he has been able to produce. I do not know why he is apologizing for it. He may have a little red blood in

his being, and he may want to stand up for it. It is not anything left over; it is the result of the visit of Colonel Belcher.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When the present government came into office, there was an undertaking, or what was virtually an undertaking that Canada would participate in the Empire exhibition. Colonel Belcher's tour was simply carrying out an understanding reached at the last conference of Prime Ministers in England.

The whole matter was entirely up in the air, in general; there was nothing specific or concrete. Canada was asked if there should be an exhibition, and we said we thought there should be. The whole thing was in the air. I do not know why my hon. friend is apologizing for the exhibition. There is nothing to be ashamed about in regard to it. I should have thought it was something the minister would say he believed was right, or else he was not going to go on with it. I believe he thinks it is right. If we go into it properly, if we are even going to have any proper understanding and to get any proper distribution of the business we require so much at the present time, particularly in view of the existing American tariff, this is the greatest hope, the best chance you have.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is to provide, just as the item reads, for the supervision of government purchases and sales. As my hon. friend is aware, there has been and is at the present time a Purchasing commission so called. As a matter of fact, the commission has never had more than one commissioner, Colonel La Fleche. He and his staff have to do with the obtaining of tenders on government contracts. As, however, the system operates at the present time, this commission acts as a body by itself, makes its report to myself as Prime Minister, and I certify whatever is sent to me in presenting matters to council to be passed by council. As a matter of fact, I have never felt that I had any real knowledge of what I was certifying to beyond the statement as sent to me by Colonel La Fleche. I think the system as it is working is anything but satisfactory. I proposed to my colleagues, and I think they are agreed, that a better supervision of government purchases would be obtained if a committee of

Supply-Purchasing Commission
council were appointed as a committee to supervise all government contracts and purchases, to which committee there should be attached a permanent secretary who, we propose, would be Colonel La Fleche himself, and that he should have associated with him such members of his staff as might be necessary to enaible them to have a supervision over all government contracts. I think that would be a more effective method of maintaining a responsible supervision of government contracts than the present system which leaves the whole matter to one head of a commission, who carries on his own inquiries without any minister being responsible for what is done.
We find now that by this reorganization we save $47,000?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

This is not a reorganization; it is a painful contraction practised almost to the point of extinction as regards real use. At one time we had a commission which did the buying absolutely without the control of the ministers. From time to time departments have made inroads into that, until at the present time, as the Prime Minister says, instead of three men, some of them at least accustomed to making purchases and the like, we now have Colonel La Fleche looking after the matter by himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That was the position when we took office.
I think the others got out just after the election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, they got out long before.
I think they read some of the things said in this House beforehand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon-

There is no secret about the attitude taken by my hon. friends in connection with the present commission. If any object is to be gained, it is quite easy to turn up Hansard. The fact is that the departments are now doing their own purchasing. The minister places his contract where he wants to place it. That is the fact to-day. If it is not the fact, I should like to be corrected. The ministers look after their own purchases now, I do not know just exactly

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Did my hon. friend say "now"?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. I might say that ever since the Purchasing commission was established, certain departments of the government conducted their own purchases wholly irrespective of the commission. Yes, when it has anything the minister thinks does not matter. Will my hon. friends say that the regular supplies in the Post Office Department, for example, are bought to-day through this commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will not be positive on that.
I suggested that this item might stand to be discussed. I am ready to discuss it.

speechtext: I would say that if there are any articles purchased by the Post Office Department that are not purchased by the commission, they will be purchased by public tender in a manner that is entirely regular.

My information is entirely to the contrary. It is that the articles have not been so purchased, and complaints have been made in connection with the department as to that. I suggest that the matter should stand until we have someone here who is looking after it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am prepared to look after it. I will get any information my hon. friend may wish.

I should like brought down to the House before this item is discussed, the advertisements for tenders for public supplies of the Post Office in the last year, the tenders received, the action taken by the commission, and when the commission first heard of the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: All right.

Before we leave this item, may we look back to a time in the last parliament, when the government of the day
Supply-Purchasing Commission

wished to load upon this country with all its shackling powers a commission to purchase everything from brooms up to cars for the railroads; and I remember a brilliant speech made against it by the late Mr. Stewart, afterwards Minister of Railways in the government, of which my distinguished, learned and hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) was Minister of Finance. I remember with what bitter criticism from his own side of the House the proposal of this unlimited commissioning of sales was greeted, and I think perhaps that what the Prime Minister suggests is a step in the right direction. We are pleased to see that there is a reduction of some 847,000, and that hope is held out for even more efficient and economical administration. I recall, too, that in the course of that interesting debate it was pointed out by the late Mr. Stewart how much more efficient the number of purchasing agents in the different departments were than people who were brought from outside, and how the worship of machinery did not of necessity bring about that efficiency desired by the taxpayers.
And the two bills were withdrawn at two consecutive sessions.
If it is a farce why continue the vote at all?
It was done by order in council without any right.

From the little information I have it appears to me that the Purchasing commission acted without jurisdiction. In any event, it seems that they are not functioning to any great extent, so far as many departments are concerned. I am interested in what the Prime Minister says because I have been under the impression for some time, and I propose to give it some effect when the report on the Civil Service committee is submitted, that not only is it essential to have some central organizing body to do the purchasing, but that there be some factor which will co-ordinate the various departments of government in order to prevent any overlapping and overmanning. In that connection I may observe that the Treasury department of England is empowered with that special function. Our Treasury board in Canada has not now, apparently, the necessary statutory powers. It seemed to me that the Prime Minister might be called the general manager of the country and the one who should be charged with the duty of purchasing and also of co-ordinating the departments of government, and that there should be an expert employed by him to look after 
both these functions. I think it is desirable, and much money would be saved in both directions. It is an urgent requirement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What my hon. friend has just expressed conveys better than my own words could what I have in mind in the proposal in view in this matter. There is in regard to appointments and different increases in the public service a treasury board before which all these various appointments and promotions have to go, apart from the Civil Service Commission. There is attached to that board an officer of the Department of Finance, whose business it is carefully to go over all appointments to see, so far as the different departments are concerned, that they are all working on a proper basis. The arrangement I am proposing is that in connection with government contracts there shall be a similar body composed of ministers who will correspond to the Treasury board; and similarly attached to that body there shall be a permanent official to be its secretary, a man of experience, with such staff as he may require, who will carefully review all government purchases and contracts and keep the Prime Minister informed on matters that are pertinent thereto. Then when various contracts in the form of orders in council come before the Prime Minister he will be in a position to inform his colleagues of precisely the position in which the matters stand. At the present time, under the arrangement that has been in existence, a recommendation comes to Council and the Prime Minister has to put his signature to it as a matter of course. He has to take the entire responsibility without having any kind of responsible supervision.

speechtext: Carried'

speechtext:

Item stands.
Canadian National Safety League, $25,000.
This is a new item. The committee would like to have it explained.

The Canadian National Safety League is a body of which Major-General Sir John M. Gibson is president, the general manager being Mr. J. F. H. Wyse. For a number of years there has been an Ontario Safety League. To be exact, it has been existence for about nine years, and 13 said to have done splendid work. It has received some assistance from the Ontario government.
Safety in what regard?
Safety from industrial cr other accidents.
From political catastrophe too?
No-
The league will be needed shortly in Ontario.

-otherwise my right hon. friend would have been more fortunate in 1921. The League in Ontario has been doing accident prevention work for some years throughout the entire province, and the statistics for the city of Toronto are particularly interesting. The ninth year of safety work was completed in 1922 with sixty fatalities fewer than in 1913, the year immediately before the league started work, in spite of an increase in population of 91,000
with its proportionate increase in industrial hazards and an increase of 32.000 in automotive vehicles. There has been a saving of 759 lives in the nine years of safety work and this is all the more remarkable in view of the large increase in the number of such vehicles. The proposal has been to establish a Canadian National Safety First League to inaugurate and carry on a safety first campaign throughout the length and breadth of Canada. Not with just the amount of money that is here voted, but with this assistance and other contributions and resources which the Canadian National Safety League is to secure, it is believed that the work will be very effective in saving Canadian lives and limbs. That, briefly, is the intent of the vote. Last year there were 1,107 fatal accidents in Canada, or an increase of 185 over the preceding year, which would appear to indicate urgent necessity for safety first education.
Who is the president of this league?
Sir John Gibson. Mr. Wyse is general manager.

What organization have
they in the province of New Brunswick?
I think New Brunswick is one of the provinces in which the league proposes to get under way a safety first campaign this year.

Mr. Chairman, I must ask the government what method is pursued in establishing this list of what might be called grants in aid? Most of these are excellent societies. The society for preventing people from being killed by automobiles or other accidents is no doubt very meritorious. But is it the duty of the federal government to pick out this, that and another society and give them grants, while there are scores of other societies just as worthy which do not receive any aid from the state? Unless the state proposes to help all meritorious societies with altruistic motives which operate to the benefit of the public-and I do not doubt that most of these societies do so operate-then I think it is poor legislation to favour them. It looks to me as if a friend of whatever administration may be in power has some pet society, and he comes and asks for a grant in aid, and sometimes he gets it. That is one point I want to make.
The other point is the utter disproportion of the amounts that are granted. Here is the Victorian Order of Nurses, one of the very best orders that we have in the country.

Supply-National Safety League
I know recently there broke out in a littls village in my riding the terrible plague of typhoid. The Victorian Order of Nurses went on the scene at the beginning and established hospitals, and did real national service. They get $5,000. Then comes along an Alpine club for the purpose of encouraging climbing in the mountains of Alberta. One would think that that alone would be sufficiently attractive without any aid, but the club receives $5,000. I protested against that time after time when I was in opposition-and I suppose when I am in opposition again I could protest with just the same effect. Then we have other societies, no doubt good in their way. But my submission to the committee is that it is not the business of the state to operate certain specific charitable societies. If it is the duty of the state to operate charitable societies in general, then there should be a general scheme. This giving small donations or large to this or that particular society is unsound legislation and should be stopped. When we have such a tremendous deficit I certainly think it is a mistake to increase the list of these favoured societies. Now, $25,000 for helping people to look after themselves so they will not be run over by automobiles is, I think, far too .arge a sum. I do not doubt it is a good society, but I do not think it is the duty of a state which has the deficit we have to go in debt to the extent of another $25,000 for this aid. If the government feels this is such a society that it should be bonused, then I certainly protest against its being bonused five times as much as the Victorian Order of Nurses.

The hon. member for
Brome (Mr. McMaster) has very largely and very correctly expressed my own ideas on this particular subject. This is an entirely new vote. To my certain knowledge the Victorian Order of Nurses has pressed the government for a larger vote. The Victorian Order of Nurses is an organization extending over the whole Dominion and doing most excellent work, but notwithstanding that it is given precisely the same grant as last year. Another national organization is the Boy Scouts-badly in need of money; their grant is not increased. Another national organization is the Girl Guides; their grant is not increased. Why, therefore, when an entirely new society comes along it is given a grant of $25,000, while these and other societies throughout Canada of a national and educational nature and of a character which we need in this country are overlooked, I do not understand. Some time ago I approached the government with a view of allowing de-

ductions under income tax statements for grants or donations to educational and charitable institutions, but I was met with the rejoinder: We cannot do it, we need money in the worst way. Notwithstanding that, when the Estimates come down we find an entirely new vote of $25,000. I protest vigorously against this vote, I do not think it should be granted. But if votes of this description are to be granted, the votes of institutions which we know of and which have done good work for many years should be increased instead of new votes being added to the list.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is quite true, as the hon. member for Brome has said, that in regard to many of these grants to particular organizations there is a certain element of chance; that is to say, the government is made aware of their needs, and naturally such action as the government takes is based upon the information it receives. But I think it is only fair to say that every one of these grants is based upon the merits of the organizations as presented to the government and in the light of the conditions and circumstances at the time. I think if my hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Marler) will refer to some of the earlier grants made to one or two of the organizations which he has mentioned, he will find the amounts may have been larger in order to help the organization, and what are now being given are contributions after the organization had become well established and well supported throughout the country. This is a new organization, but it is doing a class of work which has come to be recognized as of the utmost importance in the conservation of human life. It is true that the work in Canada is in its infancy, but if my hon. friend will take account of what has been done in the United States by the safety first organization that has carried its propaganda throughout all the states, he will find not only that hundreds of thousands of dollars have been saved to the nation, but that many hundreds, even thousands, of human lives have been saved through the greater precautions taken by the people to safeguard themselves against accident. Anyone travelling through the United States cannot but be impressed by the warnings placarded at almost every turn, designed to instil into all the people the necessity of guarding against accident.

Would the Prime Minister say whether the federal government of the United States bonuses this very excellent society?

Supply-National Safety League

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I cannot give . my hon. friend an answer at the moment, but whether they do or do not, I would say it is essentially work of a national character and in the national interest, and that if some private agency did not take it up, the government itself ought to do so. The conservation of natural resources is an important work of the government service, but I think the greatest of all the resources of a country are its human resources, and the conservation of human resources is an important part of the government's work. I believe a great deal can be done in the saving of life and the preventing of accident throughout the country by well-organized propaganda along the lines of safety first. It is not work that the government, perhaps, is as well organized to carry on as a private organization might be, but where a private organization is established with a promise of doing efficient work and rendering service to the public, and where the work is of national interest, the government ought to give it some aid. I would go further and say that I think the government should not undertake any work which can be carried on by private organizations and which it is in the interest of the state should be undertaken. But where a private organization of itself is not able to carry on efficiently the work that is in the national interest, and if that work can be made efficient through government aid, I believe it is economical in the end to supplement that private effort rather than institute the work as a federal enterprise. It is in that spirit that the government has sought to give this assistance to a work the object of which is to conserve human resources, to prevent accident and injury to life and limb.

No one would object to anything that is of a philanthropic or generally useful character; at the same time I think we ought to give just a little attention to the objects that this institution is said to have in view and the methods by which it is supposed to carry them out. In most of the provinces we have what are known as factory acts, which make very definite and useful provisions to guard against accident in industrial employment. As to the automobiles about which so much has been said, we have in every province more or less rigid-generally a very rigid-automobile law; and the criminal law of this country goes so far as to provide that if a man drives a motor car while intoxicated he may be subject to imprisonment without the option of a fine. All these things are effective; what, then, is left for an institution of this kind to do? Is it to regulate traffic on the railways? Why, every railway-I believe
the National Railway does it; I am sure the Canadian Pacific Railway does it-gives special attention to promoting conditions of safety. We have all these agencies both legislative and private, working in the direction of safety first, and before we are asked to vote $25,000, or even $5,000, we ought to have a much clearer designation of the means by which this society will operate or the results that it is likely to produce. We have simply been asked to vote $25,000 on the strength of the names of a few people who are said to have an organization in Ontario. So far as any statement submitted to this committee is concerned, I would not say that the existence of that organization has resulted in an increased slaughter of one hundred or more, but the slaughter has increased in spite of its existence, and that is not a very wonderful recommendation for an organization which is operating in that very province.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken-that increase was in all Canada, not in Ontario alone.

Then we were not given statistics for Ontario where we were told such beneficial results were being produced by this organization. In other words, we have not been given one single, genuine piece of information upon which to determine our vote upon this subject. I know where this whole thing begins and I know where it ends. You will find the same conditions Existing in practically every municipal organization organization throughout the country.

Will the hon. gentleman pardon me? I said that 759 lives had been saved in Ontario during the past nine years as the result of the work of the Ontario Safety League. The increase of deaths from accident in Canada was 185 during last year alone, due to the fact that no safety first organization is operating in every part of the country as it is in Ontario, resulting in the saving of lives.

I am sorry I entirely misapprehended the remarks of the minister; I think I have got it straight now. But by what system of investigation or of statistical record can the number of lives that have been saved be determined? I would say there are several million people in Canada who have not been slaughtered by any device known to modern science and I do not know that you can attribute their safety to any particular organization. Now, the point I want to make is this: A few well-meaning, and praiseworthy people in the community get together. They

Supply-National Safety League
have a definite and a desirable object, for the purposes of which they subscribe their own money. Sometimes it requires the rental or erection of a building, the employment of a staff, the organization of agencies to carry out their philanthropic work. They do it; they do it well, and it is a good thing for the country, a good thing for every community that that praiseworthy spirit exists. But after a while even the best people become a bit weary of well doing. The effort slackens; they do not want to see their pet child altogether deserted, so they turn to the nearest thing at hand, the municipal organization, and they ask for a grant. A little money is given; the thing is got on a kind of public footing; later a larger grant is given, and by and by the whole institution is shouldered by the municipality. That is not fancy; it is not a mere gathering of statistics, it is an absolute fact. It occurs in community after community throughout the length and breadth of this continent; it is a prevailing public tendency. This organization has succeeded very early in impressing not merely the municipality but the federal government that it is no longer capable of carrying on its work through its own efforts; it comes here as an easy means of obtaining some money. It may be all right to grant the money, but before we do I think we ought to have some clear statement as to the nature of the organization. We do not know yet whether it is something that operates by putting out signs on highways warning people to keep out of the road of automobiles. It may be that it puts up these signs we see all over the country "Dodge Brothers Car." I have never been able to understand that. I do not understand why it should not be necessary to dodge sister's car, dodge father's car or dodge anybody else's car. I do not see why it should be limited to dodging brother's car. I would like to know whether this organization has been operating along that particular line. I want to know whether it is by signs, by teaching in the schools, by lectures in the churches or what particular means they are taking. Do they form classes like the St. John's Ambulance Association? I want to know the particular method by which they save the lives of people. We have not been given one word except certain statistics. I do not know yet whether they operate within the factories of my own province of New Brunswick, whether they supplant the factory inspector and the Factory Act. I do not know whether they render useless certain provisions in our Workmen's Compensation Act. I do not know a thing that has been done by this organiza-
tion. I am not throwing cold wrater on it, I am not sneering at it, I am only referring to the inconsequent way in which this committee is invited to vote $25,000 without being told how it is going to be spent or being shown the connection between the expenditure of that money and the result which it is said is to be produced. Now perhaps I have invited, not reprisals I hope, but the distribution of some essential information.

It may be possible as some hon. gentlemen have intimated, that this is not a legitimate function for the federal government to participate in, or for it even to care as I understood some hon. gentlemen to intimate whether people are careless and indifferent about protecting their own lives and limbs and those of others. The hon. member for Brome inquired about the United States in this connection. I might say that during the war period the United States had control of the railroads and one of the first things it did was to place the most effective, nation-wide, safety first system on the railroads of the United States. It is probably the best system that has ever been used in any country in the world, and it worked with wonderfully beneficial effects in the saving of life and limb.
I would ask my hon. friend if the railroad systems of this country are not doing that very thing now.

I was coming to that. Canada has 22,000 miles of nationally-owned railroads now. Some gentlemen are talking about the expenditure of $25,000 on this particular item. I want to say as a man who has been a railroad man for more than thirty years that I think if we could inaugurate the real spirit and a recognition of safety first among the great majority of the railroad men in Canada who have to work on the Canadian National railways we would be amply repaid for this proposed expenditure.

What I want to get at is this: Is it part of this organization's work to teach the railway men of the Canadian National Railway System the principles of safety first? Does that come within what this money is being spent for?
If my hon. friend would only possess his soul in patience-
It is five minutes to one.

-I would try and give him the information I think he wants. This is not for the special and particular purpose of inaugurating on the Canadian National railways the safety first movement, but it is for the purpose of inaugurating in each of the

Supply-National Safety League
provinces outside of Ontario among the responsible citizens in all walks of life a safety first organization that will keep before the public, including the railroad men, the necessity of safety first, to co-operate with such safety first organizations as are on the Canadian Pacific, on the Canadian National and as are in the various industrial concerns in New Brunswick and the other provinces in Canada.
jet us see what accidents there were in Canada last year; 1,107 fatal accidents can be divided as follows; 141 deaths were recorded on the steam railways. I know something about how some of these deaths occur.
It is just from sheer, absolute
1 a.m. carelessness. Might I give an example? You all remember the dajrs when there was the link and pin coupler on the railroads, and when the brakemen used to connect the cars by inserting the link in the drawbar and then putting in the pin. To-day they have the automatic coupler, and what do we find? It might be your boy or mine, twenty-two or twenty-three years of age, young and enthusiastic, careless and carefree. He goes on the road and sees two cars coming together with the alignment of the drawbars not exactly as it should be. What do we find? Only too often as the records of the railroad organizations and of the railway commission will show he puts up his foot and kicks the drawbar over with the result that only too often he loses his leg, or possibly he is dragged under and killed. We want a campaign of safety first for that young fellow and the young fellow who is taking the same kind of unnecessary chances in the lumbering industry. We want to educate him by some kind of campaign that will prevent him from doing that kind of thing. We are willing to spend $25,000 as it were on immigration, to save to this country 185 valued citizens to work on the farms and in the factories of Canada each year. I am sure that it would be preferable to put up that amount of money in the protection of the lives of the citizens who are here, protecting them against themselves. Not one cent of this money is to be used for any purpose in Ontario. The sum of $10,000 has been voted by the Ontario government to the Ontario Safety league for the past four or five years, and the results speak for themselves, and only that my hon. friend has referred to the lateness of the hour I could read the records and show just what has been accomplished in Ontario in nine years, apparently by this Ontario safety first movement.
The figures, if my hon. friend had the time and opportunity to go into them, would show conclusively that the other provinces need the nucleus of a responsible safety first organization that will gather to it those interested in the railroads, in the lumbering industry and in the factories of the provinces to work together with the common end in view of having people take the first necessary precaution to save their own life and limbs. That is the campaign that is proposed to be conducted.
Last year 71 deaths occurred on steam railways through people being struck. Surely some of those deaths might have been prevented with just a little reasonable recognition by the victims of their responsibilities to themselves and their families and their country. By perhaps just a little more care they might have been saved. Some of them were run over and crushed; 24 were due to collisions; 24 to falls from cars or engines; all these last were among railroad men.
In the mining, smelting and quarrying group 168 deaths were recorded, of which 97 occurred in coal mining. We all know the necessity for safety first in those industries. Falls of rocks and cave-ins accounted for 65 deaths. 37 deaths were due to explosions and 19 to mine and quarry cars. In the manufacturing industry there were 159 deaths reported, 43 of which occurred in saw and planing mills, and 39 in iron and steel mills. In the saw and planing mills 20 deaths were due to machinery and 9 to flying objects. In lumbering there were 147 deaths reported of which 36 were due to falling trees and 37 to drowning. In the construction group there were 145 deaths, 40 of which were due to falls and 32 to falling objects. Of the total of deaths in industry for the year, explosive substances were responsible for 58 and electric currents for 41.
And, Mr. Chairman, we talked here at considerable length abotit forest conservation. Here we have $25,000 proposed for the conservation of human life and limb. We have talked about forest conservation in this House and very properly so, and I would not wonder if we will talk in this House still more about forest conservation. Shall we hold up our hands and say "Hands off, it is none of our business, pass it on to the big industries, and to the railroads and say that we will not expend $25,000 for the purpose of inaugurating in the provinces of Canada a real honest-to-goodness safety-first movement that will assist in preventing accidents with consequent loss of limbs, or death, to Canadian citizens whom we have here, and want to keep here for the

Supply-National Safety League
benefit of Canada. That is what there is in this proposal.

In what way are we
going to bring this propaganda directly to the attention of the working men whom the minister speaks about?

By the formation of
these safety-first organizations in various towns. The Canadian National Safety League has a membership in the following places; Calgary, Edmonton, Granby, Halifax, Montreal, Quebec, Regina, Shawinigan Falls, St. Jerome, Three Rivers, St. John, Sydney, Toronto, Vancouver, Winnipeg, and other places. There is a general safety-first organization in all those cities. The proposal is to extend that work.
By lectures and signs?
By education, by getting together those who are really interested in life and limb conservation to work under the direction of the safety-first organizations.

Does the minister
really and truly believe that he can get the railroad men throughout the length and breadth of Canada to come and attend these different lectures which will be given on behalf of this safety-first league?

I think that it would
probably be difficult to do so. I would imagine that this Canadian National Safety League would undertake the work in co-operation with other organizations. For example, the 'Canadian Pacific Railway has a safety-first organization and the Canadian National also has such an organization. I presume that in such towns as Moose Jaw and Saskatoon, where both the Canadian Pacific and Cana-dain National to-day have safety first organizations, those organizations would be co-operating with the central safety-first organizations in those particular towns. In other words, they would convey information to each other and co-operate in various ways. I do not know just what the plan might be, but considering the remarkable success which the figures show in Ontario, and the increase of 155 last year in fatal accidents in Canada, I cannot help but feel insistent that there is necessity for a campaign in other provinces, similar to that which has appeared to do such good work in Ontario.
How many deaths were there from automobile fatalities?

I am afraid I have not got the exact figures for the automobile fatalities, but that is very important, and there is necessity for a safety-first movement of some kind, even amongst automobile drivers.
Does the hon. minister think that the prohibitionists in Ontario will permit him to claim that all this good work in saving life is due to this movement?
The way in which prohibition works only too often I am sorry to say in Ontario-and I am just giving this as my opinion in answer to the hon. member-
Not officially?
No, but it may help to cause accidents rather than to prevent them, I am afraid.
After the very exhaustive and comprehensive interpretation of the item given by the Minister of Labour, I am sure the government will agree to the suggestion that the whole matter be dropped.

The minister says he really does not know how the system will work out, and I quite agree with him. From what I have heard him say, I do not think he knows, and I think the House is entitled to know how it will work out before we invest the money of this country, to the extent of 825,000, in the proposition.

I believe this will work out so that there will be overlapping. The provinces have inaugurated a system. In the first remarks offered by the Minister of Labour he cited Toronto. I claim that either Ontario, as a province, or the city of Toronto, should be responsible for the safety-first expenditure in the city of Toronto. I would be more prepared to support the $25,000 vote if it were used for the purpose of apprehending some of the speed artists in Ottawa and other cities. These automobile artists have persuaded the government to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to provide good roads through the country, so that they may travel on these roads, and have signs placed on them, but I must be on the lookout, and prepared to step out of the way of these speedsters. They create conditions which enable them to sweep along and kill many people in the country. Signs are placed on the road and we are supposed to get out of the way. That is the condition at the present time. I do not approve of spending $25,000 for the purpose of having signs placed up on these roads, which mean that we have to hop out of the way of the individual who comes along in his automobile and forgets to blow his horn. If this money were to be expended in apprehending some of these individuals who drive through the country and do not blow their horns, I would support it.

Supply-National Safety League

Did you ever drive a
motor car in the city or in the country either.
Yes.

Nine-tenths of the accidents are not due to the drivers of automobiles in this country. I want to endorse this vote. I have had several years' experience in driving motor cars in city, town and country, and I can vouch for the fact that you cannot drive down the easy-going streets of Ottawa without having several hair-raising experiences-do not laugh about it, because I will take some hon. members down and show them how people dodge about, cross the streets at intersections and run in front of automobiles.
It is the hair we want to see.

I have never had the
misfortune so far, and I hope never to have it. But I can tell hon. gentlemen that the need is very great to educate the people of all the towns and cities of this country as to how they should act. It is at present almost impossible to avoid an accident, and I heartily endorse this appropriation.

The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) asked for certain information. I did not give it just out of consideration for the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter) who referred to the lateness of the hour. This is a memorandum which my hon. friend should have, which explains the obligations and the purposes of this organization:
The Canadian National Safety League was incorporated in 1918 by Dominion charter, and without share capital. Its objects are:-
1.	To safeguard and protect the public, especially children from the dangers of automobiles, railroads, street railways and all forms of vehicular traffic on the public highways in the Dominion of Canada.
2.	To educate the public through schools, churches, literature and all channels of publicity upon matters pertinent to public safety.
How are you going to do that?

3.	To minimize the injuring and killing of persons employed in stores, factories, workshops and all departments of industrial and mercantile activity, by instilling into the minds of employer and employee the full meaning of "Safety Always".
4.	To co-operate, so far as lies in the power of the league, in preventing the useless destruction of life and property by fire.
5.	To advocate and secure possible remedies and preventives and to assist in the enactment and enforcement of ordinances requisite to carry out the foregoing by means of-
(a)	Bulletins, education, or any other method of propaganda that may from time to time be considered advisable.
(b)	To be the clearing house of all information, bulletin service, safety films and all literature bearing on accident prevention work, issued under arrangements to the various provincial leagues.
The operations of the corporation to be carried on throughout Canada.
Those are the purposes briefly.
I did not understand the Minister of Labour to say that this society would make a point of co-operating with railroad companies.
I should say, as my view, they would do that.
That was the minister's own view.

Yes. This is their statement:
To co-operate, so far as lies in the power of the league in preventing the useless destruction of life and property.
The whole proposal is to bring about cooperative arrangement between all who are interested in this important life and limb conservation work.

I quite understand the remarks of the minister in that respect, that it is their aim and object to do that; but I am a little concerned whether it will be possible or not to bring about that state of co-operation between the societies and the different railway corporations and their employees.
The hon. member is probably right.

speechtext:
May I say just one word further in regard to this item? When it is apparent to members of the committee that the object the government had in view in giving this support was that of helping an organization that was already established, that had been doing effective work in one province over a period of five years, which work had come to be generally recognized as a great human service, to organize similar classes of work in all the provinces of the Dominion, so that this "safety first" movement would receive the cumulative effect of all the provinces of the Dominion working together in a great educational campaign in a variety of forms towards furthering "safety first," probably the committee will be willing to let the item pass without further discussion. It is not proposed at all that this should be an annual grant to this par-

Supply-National Safety League
ticular organization. It is simply to enable an organization, which has made good in one province and which has shown its capacity to do effective work, to get similar organizations or branches formed in all the provinces of the Dominion, so that there will be a nation-wide "safety first" organization carrying on conservation work in human life and limb in all the provinces.

One would naturally concur in the view expressed by the Prime Minister as to the desirability of carrying out the objects of this society, but we have heard the explanation of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock). We heard first his verbal explanation that this was practically to do the work of "safety first" on the railways and particularly amongst railway men.
My hon. friend is mistaken.

That was mentioned. I thought that was pretty well covered by the Canadian Pacific agency and the Canadian National must have some similar organization. But when he came to read the detailed statement of the objects of the society, we found that the railway men were not specially mentioned; that they came only under a very general class, and that the primary object put forward was the protection of the people themselves from vehicular traffic. It is either the one thing or the other that is the chief point. The hon. member who asked: How are they going to do that? has struck about the right note. We have not got anything very definite about that yet. I can understand that the organization will spend a good deal of money for secretaries and all that sort of thing in the different provinces. That is very easy to do, and it does not produce very much result. The Prime Minister says that there have been good results in one province. Why not, before you ask us to pass an item of this size and character in this committee, give us a statement of just what has been done in that province. I do not know yet and nobody in this House does: or if they do, they have kept the knowledge very well to themselves. We can prove almost anything by statistics. I do not know whether the Minister of Labour is familiar with the Clemens' tables in regard to the place of death. I do not know whether he has the tables prepared by Samuel L. Clemens, who many years ago compiled statistics on the subject. I forget the figures, but Mark Twain pointed out that the most dangerous place in the world was a man's own bed, because more people die in bed than anywhere

else. That is quite in keeping with the nebulous character of the information that we have been able to elucidate in regard to this item. Perhaps this is an item to keep men out of bed in order that they may preserve their lives. If so, it has served its purpose admirably well.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
